entry.title: NOBL Wheels Launches AR Series of All-Road Wheels With Its Lightest Rims to Date
entry.content:
Yesterday, NOBL Wheels expanded its product lineup with the introduction of the AR Series of all-road wheels. The new AR40 and AR50 wheelsets are built with the brand’s lightest road rims to date, starting at just 350 grams (AR40). These new AR Series rims combine NOBL’s aerodynamic teardrop profile with 25mm internal widths and fully hooked beads to support increasingly wide road tires. The complete wheelsets are available in the more affordable Core version with NOBL hubs, or Custom builds with several hub and spoke options. 

NOBL AR Series Rim Design

First introduced on the FAR gravel race wheels, the AR Series rims utilize NOBL’s aerodynamic teardrop rim profile. This design has the widest point of the rim not at the bead wall, but slightly below it. This is intended to help with aerodynamics when used with wider tires by smoothing around the bulbous leading and trailing edges. NOBL says “It meets the rule of 105 with a 30c tire, which measures about 32mm on the AR’s 25mm internal width.” 

With a 25mm internal width and fully hooked beads, the AR-Series rims are designed for broad tire compatibility. NOBL states they are ready for tires from 28-45c and pressures up to 80 psi, with the confidence and security of a hooked bead. Riders can also ride with confidence knowing that NOBL offers a lifetime warranty on its carbon rims and lifetime service on its wheelsets, including truing, tensioning, and cleaning.

Weight

NOBL says that its new AR Series rims are its lightest road rims to date. They used T1000 carbon and their most advanced layup process to create what they say is among “the lightest and strongest 25mm internal road rims with a hooked bead.” The claimed weight of the 40mm deep AR40 rim is 350 grams, while the 50mm deep AR50 rim is a touch heavier at 380 grams. Despite the low weights, NOBL says the AR40 has passed impact testing up to 110J, while the AR50 has a 115J impact rating.

Of course, these lightweight rims result in lightweight wheelsets. The complete Core wheelset with NOBL hubs weighs a claimed 1307g (AR40) /1367g (AR50). The lightest Custom wheelset — DT180 hubs, Berd Polylight spokes, XDR driver — is claimed to weigh 1124g (AR40) /1184g (AR50). 

AR Series Specs

NOBL Core AR40 / AR50 Wheelset

  • Rims: NOBL AR40 / AR50
  • Hubs: NOBL Core Road Hub, 36t Ratchet
  • Spokes: Alpina Extralite / Sapim CX-Ray
  • Nipples: Black
  • Brake Interface: Centerlock
  • Driver: XDR / MS Road / HG
  • Graphics: 4 Colour Options
  • $1,999.00 CAD | $1,599.00 USD
  • Wheelset Weight: 1307/1367g (Alpina Extralite Spokes, XDR Driver)

NOBL Custom AR40 / AR50 Wheelset 

  • Rims: NOBL AR40 / AR50
  • Hub Brands: DT Swiss / Chris King / Hope / Project 321 / Onyx / Industry Nine / SON
  • Spokes: Alpina Extralite / Sapim CX-Ray / Berd Polylight
  • Nipples: Black
  • Brake Interface: Centerlock
  • Driver: XDR / MS Road / HG
  • Graphics: 4 Colour Options
  • Starting at $2,279.00 CAD | $1,699.00 USD
  • Lightest Wheelset Weight: 1124/1184g (DT180 Hubs, Berd Polylight Spokes, XDR Driver)

Availability

NOBL’s new AR Series all-road wheelsets are available now. Head to the NOBL website to learn more about the Core and Custom builds, or order a set today.

noblwheels.com

entry.title: The Best Gifts for Gravel Cyclists: What to Get Your Favorite Gravel Biker
entry.content:
On the hunt for the best gifts for the gravel riders on your holiday shopping list? Cyclists, in general, are tricky to buy for, and gravel bike riders can be especially tricky. It’s still kind of a new-ish discipline. And a lot of riders are still figuring out what gravel means to them.Are they a serious racer, a weekend doddler, an all-terrain explorer, or maybe even the kind of adventurer that heads out on week-long, self-supported bikepacking trips?

Any way they ride gravel, we can help find that perfect gift to put a smile on the face of your favorite gravel bike rider.

Ride Gravel For Less

Adding a complete carbon gravel bike to a gift guide sounds a bit over-the-top, right! Who has the gifting budget for that, after all? But hear us out, the carbon Ari Shafer ticks pretty much all the gravel boxes – from weekend rides to week-long adventures. And it promises solid affordability.

You get a lightweight and aero-optimized carbon frame, monster tire clearance up to 700x58mm or 29×2.25″, fully integrated routing, bikepacking-ready mounts & internal storage, and versatile all-terrain geometry. It’s a confident all-rounder. But it still won’t break the bank. “Flagship performance without the flagship price.”

Framesets are available from just €2000, complete bikes from just $2550 (direct from Ari Bikes). You can even save an extra two to three hundred bucks off a complete build now in Ari’s Black Friday deals. Or a hundred buckaroos off the frameset-only option.

Think your favorite gravel would prefer a pedal-assist version? Then, check out the Shafer HP ebike powered by the excellent and natural-feeling TQ HPR60 motor.

Sponsored Placement

Essentials At Your Fingertips

Nothing beats a toptube bag for keeping your snacks and essential electronics close at hand. Perennial favorites are those that naturally keep water out, are almost self-closing, and can be easily opened and secured shut with one hand, even while riding over rough terrain. Our first pick is an OG on the fast-packing scene in the 1L Apidura Racing Top Tube Bag with the magnetic clasp on its flap top. Pick the bolt-on version (on sale at $80 from Backcountry) if your buddy’s bike is new enough to have bolts on its toptube, or the strap-on version (66€ from Apidura, or $84 at that Backcountry link) to fit almost any bike.

Our second pick is the newer but similarly-shaped 1.1L Tailfin Top Tube Tube Bag Flip (85€ directly from Tailfin), which features a versatile mounting setup with or without bolts on the bike’s toptube. Either option is big enough to carry a smartphone, compact camera, or plenty of snacks. And having one can free your gravel grinding lifestyle from the need to wear a traditional cycling jersey with pockets. Strap a top tube bag on, and enjoy the freedom of riding in your favorite t-shirt.

Haul All Your Gear

Gravel and bikepacking go hand in hand, so it’s always important to be able to strap a few days’ worth of gear onto your gravel bike to head out on an adventure. But even if credit card fast-packing is more your (your favorite graveler’s) speed, you still want to have trusty packs to keep your gear safe. Nothing beats Ortlieb’s made-in-Germany Waterproof Guarantee.

We especially love the easy-to-attach and expandable Ortlieb Handlebar Pack QR (on sale for $181 via Backcountry) for its handy bar mount and easy packing.

And their mid-sized 11L Seat-Pack ($190 at REI) offers plenty of adjustable storage in a classic, easy-to-mount bikepacking saddlebag design. Pair the two together, in original black or new dark sand, and you’d be ready for everything from a backcountry overnighter to a week-long adventure tour.

Cover Your Butt

Riding gravel means getting dirty on drop bars. But that doesn’t mean that your butt needs to get wet and dirty, too. Ass Savers has your rear in mind with their simple, lightweight but effective Win Wing 2 Gravel fender (27-29€ from Ass Savers). The wishbone bracket straps onto virtually any bike’s seatstays in seconds, and can be topped with various fender blade designs to show off a little style while taming rear wheel spray. We’re partial to the low-key look, but feel free to express yourself when buying presents for your special gravel someone. I even like to ride one under a big bikepacking saddlepack to keep things cleaner, while getting gear in and out.

While you’re at it, does your kid ride gravel, too? But they don’t need something with ass written on it, right? Well, sister brand Bumbinos has kid’s bums protected from mud & rain, too. Bumbinos are kid bike-sized for 14-16″ or 18-20″ wheels, and come in way more fun designs than Ass Savers ever imagined. A Splash Pack (35€ from Bumbinos) includes matching front & rear fenders, plus cool stickers.

Ready When the Lights Go Out, In More Ways Than One

When it gets dark, the riding doesn’t have to stop. We love a simple bike light to keep the fun going after the sun goes down.

If you are looking for versatile on- and off-road-ready lighting, we love the 2360 lumen output of Exposure’s top-tier Zenith 4 headlight ($305 direct from Exposure). Jeremy reviewed this bright light mounted to his helmet. But it also comes with a bar mount, making it versatile for all types of off-road riding, and a sound all-around bike light investment.

If your gravel-riding loved one rides a bike with a wireless electronic SRAM drivetrain, they’ve invariably run out of juice, out on a ride. A spare AXS battery (on sale now, $58 at Backcountry) is the perfect insurance policy to not get caught out with a bike that no longer shifts. They’ll keep it charged and ready at home, and pack it in their bags for any longer trip. And they will thank you the next time the battery on their bike runs out!

Be Ready For Failure, Too

Well, at least be ready for a flat tire. Every rider of every type of bike should be prepared to fix a flat. Carrying spare tubes used to be bulky and kinda heavy. But no longer with fancy, light TPU tubes that pack down small. There are a lot of brands and fun colors out there. The trick for gravel is to get the right size – width, and valve length. Most of the time, you’ll be good with the standard 32-47mm width & 48mm long valve from tubes like the brown WTB NanoAir TPU gravel tube ($25 at REI).

But there’s a full rainbow of more good TPU options, like the blue MilKit TPU Road & Gravel, Panaracer Purple Lite, yellow Pirelli Cinturato Smarttube ($42 at Backcountry), orange Tubolito S-CX/Gravel, or transparent white Schwalbe Aerothan or Continental ContiTPU. All are great options, really. Before you hit buy, first maybe double-check if your friend’s gravel bike has deep aero wheels (which would need longer valves) or giant >2″ MTB-sized tires (which would mean 29″ MTB size TPU tubes).

Stay Hydrated Out There

The core of our being, cyclists need water to pedal. And big gravel adventures can only keep going if you stay well hydrated. The ultra-distance bikepacker’s secret weapon is the almost 1L made-in-France Zéfal Magnum Pro high capacity 975ml/33oz water bottle that fits in standard bottle cages (11€ from Zefal direct). No other bike bottle is as trusted by those serious gravel cyclists who venture far off the beaten track.

If you are looking to haul more than a couple of big bottles, bike hydration vests have become a popular off-road biking option. In our comprehensive Best Of… series, we faced off with 8 of the best cycling hydration vest offerings, comparing and contrasting their best attributes. One of our favorites is this EVOC Hydro Pro 3L pack ($140 on sale now at Backcountry) for its light and effective water & snacks carrying capacity.

Stay Safe On The Road

We gravelers may dream of car-free riding everywhere we roam, but the truth of the matter is that we often ride on asphalt in between gravel bits. On those sections sharing the road with traffic, a smart light that combines visibility with radar to warn of approaching cars is hard to beat. There are more and more cycling radar taillight solutions on the market these days. But our choice for gravel riders is the Wahoo Trackr Radar ($250 at Backcountry), as it can be set to low light output levels and a battery extender mode that won’t irritate your riding buddies with regular flashing. But it still gets bright when it detects an approaching car and has real-world run times up to 20 hours to keep you alert on even the longest rides.

Plus, it pairs seamlessly with the latest Roam 3 in our Best Gifts For Cyclists guide, as well as the Ace & Bolt, too.

Support The Local Bike Shop

We can’t say it enough. But when in doubt, pop into the local bikeshop nearest to the gravel cyclists on your gift list and get them a Gift Certificate. Almost everything above can be sourced through that local shop. And all shops are happy to get you a gift certificate suited to your gifting budget. Then, when the time comes for regular maintenance or to replace something that’s simply worn out, the local bikeshop is always a great place to start. Everyone loves a gift certificate from somewhere they actually want to shop. You can even be sneaky and ask your special gravel cyclist to recommend which bike shop they think is best in town, if you want to be sure to support the right one.

entry.title: First Look: REEB’s Next-Gen SST Prototype Rolls Into Sedona Mountain Bike Festival
entry.content:
I am of the opinion that steel full-suspension bikes are the vinyl records of mountain biking; they’re a little impractical, super charming, and always the thing people crowd around and want to be a part of. REEB Cycles is leaning into that with the next-generation SST. And you’ll be able to see the prototype make its public debut at the Sedona Mountain Bike Festival, this weekend, November 6-8.

The original SST arrived in 2022 as a 120mm flex-stay trail bike with a hardtail attitude. The first iteration of the SST won some awards from our friends, like Bikepacking.com’s 2023 Gear of the Year, Mountain Bike Action 2023 Editor’s Choice, and Pinkbike gave it a nod for their 2022 Outlier Bike of the Year nominee. Pretty amazing for a steel full-suspension bike swimming in a sea of carbon.

So, What’s Changed?

That’s a good question. REEB says the geometry is updated for more stability and confidence on technical descents. And they did that without giving up the climbing efficiency or playful handling. That’s a notable claim, because the first-gen medium already ran a 65.5° head tube angle. REEB hasn’t published numbers yet, so we’ll wait and see where the production numbers land.

The suspension on the updated SST gets revised kinematics aimed at small-bump sensitivity, pedaling efficiency, and general composure, not to mention better compatibility with coil shocks.

If you’re a coil-on-a-short-travel-steel-bike type of rider, your moment has arrived. The flex-stay layout remains the trick up REEB’s sleeve as it eliminates the rear pivot found on a typical Horst Link design. This way, the design saves some weight while eliminating one more pivot you’ll need to service.

The frame gets the bigger rework too. There’s a new additive-manufactured rocker pivot housing and an enlarged bottom bracket cluster for better alignment and a more integrated look.

A bridged rocker linkage with a collet system promises smoother, more consistent suspension action. Plus, redesigned hardware should make home wrenching less of a chore. The rocker and suspension hardware come from Prosise Metal Works, run by longtime REEB collaborator Adam Prosise.

What’s REEB Say?

“The SST has always been about getting more fun out of it than the travel would suggest,” said Jeff Lenosky, Brand Director at REEB Cycles. “We’ve taken everything we’ve learned from riding and developing the original bike and made meaningful improvements to how it climbs, handles, and responds on the trail. It’s still the playful steel bike we love, just in a more refined and capable package. We’re excited to get it out in front of riders and hear what they think.”

The frames are designed by the REEB team and fabricated in-house in Longmont, Colorado. Fabrication now lives at Hooptie Bike Lounge, which combines a frame shop, a full-service bike shop, and a craft beer bar. This is the most REEB sentence we’ve ever typed…

Next-Gen SST Details: What to Expect

  • 120mm rear travel, flex-stay platform (no traditional rear pivot)
  • Revised suspension kinematics for small-bump sensitivity and pedaling efficiency
  • Improved coil shock compatibility
  • Updated geometry for more descending stability, with climbing efficiency maintained
  • Additive-manufactured (3D-printed) rocker pivot housing
  • Enlarged bottom bracket cluster for better alignment and integration
  • New bridged rocker linkage with a collet system
  • Redesigned suspension hardware for easier maintenance
  • Rocker and suspension hardware by Prosise Metal Works
  • Handmade steel frame, designed and fabricated in-house in Longmont, Colorado

Pricing and availability: Not yet announced. For reference, and if I remember right, the first-gen SST was listed at around $6000. So, that means budget accordingly if you’d like one of the new ones. So, maybe skip the extra IPA and sock the money away instead.

Hit the link below for more details.

ReebCycles.com

entry.title: Readers’ Rides: La Fourche Cycles 2026 Concours de Machines
entry.content:
For this week’s Readers’ Rides, we have builder Tom Even from La Fourche Cycles in South Burgundy, France, the 2026 entry to the 2026 Concours de Machines…

La Fourche Cycles

I am Tom Even. I am building bicycles in South Burgundy, France, under the brand called La Fourche Cycles.

I am working with steel and stainless steel, creating bespoke bikes with an approach focused on simple and essential aesthetics, trying to make the most pleasant and performant bike to ride for one person at a time. The 2026 Concours de Machines challenged builders to create a modular bicycle capable of seamlessly switching between a high-performance road bike and an adventure-ready gravel bike, while incorporating a luggage system designed for effortless one-handed use.

On-Off-Road

The bike presented here is deliberately simple and minimalist: only the wheelset needs to be changed to switch from one configuration to the other. With 700 × 32 mm tires for road riding and 27.5 × 2.2″ tires for off-road riding, this technical choice makes it possible to maintain a very similar overall wheel diameter between the two configurations, and thus to keep the same geometry for both types of riding.

The rear of the bike takes inspiration from road racing, with relatively short 415 mm chainstays that allow 48/32 chainrings to be fitted despite the 55 mm-wide tires used off-road. The front of the bike, on the other hand, is designed to tackle rough terrain, with modern gravel dimensions: a 71° head angle and 65 mm of trail.

The front end is relatively short in order to provide excellent handling and responsiveness, while allowing the rider to put weight over the front wheel and maximize grip when descending the hairpins of the Galibier. The 165 mm crank arms help optimize the rider’s position and eliminate toe overlap, even with the larger tires used in gravel mode.

Columbus tubing is used for the frame, with aerospace-grade chromoly tubing for the stem and truss fork assembly. The rear rack is made from stainless steel. The frame is assembled using fillet brazing and silver brazing. 8.4 kg in road configuration, with a conversion to gravel bikepacking mode in under 8 minutes.

Inclusive Consideration

One of the key considerations of the 2026 Concours de Machines was inclusivity. As part of a partnership with the French Federation of ParaSports, the brief encouraged participants to consider the interaction between the cyclist and their luggage. How could the bike’s bags be removed and installed using only one hand?

The four side panniers use a three-point Fidlock magnetic attachment system, allowing them to be attached and detached with one hand. The frame bag is equipped with magnets that attach directly to the steel frame structure. Two fabric straps with Velcro then secure the bag firmly in place. The top bag on the rear rack simply sits on the stainless tubes and is secured with an elastic cord that can easily be installed and tensioned with one hand.

To take one-handed usability even further and make opening and closing the bags easier, they are designed with a roll-top system closed by an elastic cord and hook. The rear rack itself can also be installed and removed with one hand: simply remove the two upper mounting bolts and loosen the lower bolts by a few turns. The lower rack mounting tab is slotted, allowing the rack to be inserted onto or removed from the two bolts already installed on the frame.

Look Twice

I recently developed a color palette for my bicycles, inspired by the color charts created by modernist architects and designers. The idea behind the seven colors of the palette was to create muted, understated tones that are somewhat difficult to describe. For example, the blue can appear almost green, the black is actually a deep blue, and the white is grey… I like the idea that someone seeing the bike passing by might have a hard time identifying its color or defining it too easily.

The idea behind the bike’s paintwork was to exhibit all the colors of the range at the same time. The color palette was developed with the technical support of System P, who also painted the bike.

The bike was awarded three times at this year’s Concours de Machines. It won 2nd place in the concours, the Best Craftsmanship Award, and the Peers’ Award.

Build Spec

  • The bags were made in collaboration with Gamory Cycles, based on advice from Studio Ricochet
  • Drivetrain: mixed Shimano GRX and SRAM Red, 12-speed, with a 10–33 road cassette and 10–36 off-road cassette, and Extralite derailleur pulleys
  • Crankset: Praxis Doon GR
  • Power-meter pedals: Favero Assioma Pro MX2
  • Wheelsets: custom-built by Duke
  • Rotors and brakes: Galfer rotors and Hope RX4+ SL calipers
  • Handlebar: Ascent Aeroo
  • Headset: Extralite
  • Seatpost: Mcfk
  • Saddle: Prologo

 

We’d like to thank all of you who submitted Readers Rides builds to be shared here at The Radavist. The response has been incredible, and we have so many to share over the next few months. Feel free to submit your bike, listing details, components, and other information. You can also include a portrait of yourself with your bike and your Instagram account! Please shoot landscape-orientation photos, not portrait. Thanks!

The post Readers’ Rides: La Fourche Cycles 2026 Concours de Machines appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Same EP8 Name, But Lighter, More Powerful Shimano EP810 eBike Motor Is All-New Inside!
entry.content:
We already shared news of the key Shimano EP810 motor upgrades on the Honda RN0, earlier this week: 100Nm, 750W, 43V, and just 2.3kg. But now, we have the official name of the latest EP8 generation – EP810 being the big secret reveal. And there are quite a few more interesting details to explore, especially about new Auto Shift and Auto Assist features.

Plus, we can dive deeper into what drove Shimano’s development as the eMTB market dukes it out in superpower wars.

Let’s just start with What’s new?

Shimano outlines 5 key updates in EP810 vs. previous generation EP801:

  • The new quieter DU-EP810 motor now puts out 100Nm of max torque and 750W of peak power.
  • Its flipped motor configuration is more compact overall for improved ground clearance, with a magnesium motor housing cutting weight almost 15%, down to a claimed 2.3kg.
  • True Auto is Shimano’s new eBike ride concept, combining improved automatic shifting functionality (updated Auto Shift) with automatically adjusting pedal-assist support levels (all-new Auto Assist).
  • With the extra power comes smoother power delivery and more control, including new features like hill start assist, Lift & Shift for changing gears after a dead stop, and a more customizable Shimano Connect app.
  • New system integration adds a much more useful toptube display with USB-C connection, tidy wireless controller, plus upgraded batteries and chargers.

What was Shimano thinking with these power numbers?

Looking at the raw numbers, our first question was why. When Shimano was updating their ebike system from the ground up, why did they stop at this relatively modest power upgrade while other motor manufacturers have gone much higher? (For reference, real figures from most direct ebike competition average ~120Nm of torque, and peak power numbers ranging from 850-1500W.)

A “Shimano spokesman” explained to me that they set the upper limit for EP810 at 100Nm & 750W “because a balance of power, control, ride feel, efficiency, and durability were prioritized over headline power numbers.” The brand’s “long-standing philosophy” is that an eMTB is supposed to still feel like a mountain bike when you ride it, “not like a motorcycle”. Shimano thinks it is critical to preserve “the essence of cycling” even when you are on a full-power ebike. “When you ride, it should still feel like your effort is driving the bike. Not the system.“

    That’s definitely a philosophy that I can get behind, personally. But at a time in the industry when so many new bike buying decisions seem to be made just by looking for the biggest motor output numbers on a spec sheet, it does make us wonder how bike manufacturers and customers will respond. We asked Shimano what bike brands we should expect to see adopt the new EP810 motor. They were pretty non-committal about giving away too much, other than saying they “are seeing interest in the EP810 platform across the industry“. For now, we know of Honda that we reported on earlier in the week, plus a new Orbea Rise that also gets the new Shimano motor.

    Shimano EP810: 750W, 100Nm ebike motor

    While those key numbers aren’t quite as high as some of the competition (cough: Avinox), EP8 is still the top of Shimano’s ebike powertrain. Also, those figures are really a noticeable upgrade over EP801. And let’s be honest, plenty to keep it firmly in the full-power eMTB segment.

    What they were really going for here were improvements in control, ride feel, and all-around usability.

    True Auto: Auto Shift v3, Free Shift, and Trail+ Auto Assist

    Automating the ride was a big driver for Shimano in EP810: “when to shift, how much support to use, and how to adapt to changing terrain“. True Auto is a move to tame that by monitoring cadence, rider input toque, motor output torque, bike speed & terrain gradient, then “smoothly and almost invisibly” changing power output and shifting to adapt.

    Here, a 3rd-gen Auto Shift uses upgraded sensors and an updated algorithm to better match its automated shifts to real-world trail conditions. Plus, the Shimano Connect app now lets you adjust your preferred cadence (in a limited range) to better suit your own riding style.

    Frankly, I don’t really like to give up shifting control to the machine. So while I respect the capability of Auto Shift, I prefer to leave it off, even in this latest update. I did try it a bit on the new Honda RN0, and it works well once you adjust it to your own ride preference. But I still like to hit that Di2 shift paddle. Free Shift is great and still there all the time, though. And that’s really the best auto-shifting feature of Shimano’s ebike+Di2 integration in my book, anyway.

    What I did appreciate was the new Auto Assist mode called Trail+. Essentially a smarter Auto power mode, Shimano takes all that sensor data to vary assist level to match your real needs on the trail. I really appreciate a good Auto mode on an eMTB for regular riding. And this one works really well, dialing back power when you go downhill, while still letting you pick the power range you prefer.

    It’s even smart enough to offer some traction control functionality by detecting wheel slip or front wheel lift, and reducing/smoothing power output to adapt.

    New peripherals, too

    There’s a lot more new to the updated Shimano EP810 family. Part of that’s a new D-Fly+ wireless protocol. It’s faster, more secure, and annoyingly not backwards compatible – a sign of a new broader Shimano ‘connected ecosystem’ to come.

    One key new bit is upgraded displays. I liked the new color, non-touch 2.2″ SC-EN700 display in the toptube of the Honda, which offered a lot of easy-to-read info, two tactile buttons, and an optional USB-C charging port. There’s also a new EC-EM810 version of the old-style bar-mounted display, now with more data and full color.

    Another new piece of hardware is the nice new wireless 3-button assist switch, so you don’t have to worry with cables anymore, and can easily control the new displays.

    720Wh internal batteries and chargers are also all-new (and not backwards compatible) with the switch to a higher 43V system voltage that promises faster charging and quicker motor power delivery. There’s a standard 2A and a more powerful 4A fast-charger, too.

    EP810 Q&A with Shimano ebike Product Planner, Henry Bosch

    First off, yes, that is the name of Shimano head of planning for ebike system development.

    And yes, that’s hilarious.

    I wanted to know more about the new EP810 system and some of its design choices, and Shimano was happy to explain.

    Why flip the motor orientation left to right?

    “The EP810 uses a completely new architecture built around a larger, more powerful motor. To design a compact drive unit, the motor is positioned on the left side of the system, while the electronic components are positioned on the right. This layout supports the performance requirements of the EP810 while contributing to a smaller and lighter drive unit.”

    “Positioning the motor on the left side also creates more available space within the drive unit structure. This allows the motor housing to sit further outboard, improving cooling performance and helping maintain power under sustained loads. Achieving a similar arrangement on the right side would not have been possible because of the packaging constraints created by the chainring and drivetrain.”

    How did the motor lose a claimed 400g (almost 15% reduction)?

    “The weight reduction comes from several changes within the drive unit. The larger motor architecture allowed Shimano to redesign the internal gearing arrangement, using shorter and more compact shafts to reduce overall mass.”

    “Additional weight savings come from the motor itself, which uses a larger-diameter design with a lighter, hollow internal structure.”

    Was weight savings a higher priority than higher torque & power output?

    “Development of EP810 focused on achieving the best balance of power, control, efficiency, durability and ride feel, rather than prioritising a single performance metric. Reducing the size and weight of the drive unit was an important objective, as it improves ground clearance and gives bicycle manufacturers greater flexibility when designing frames. At the same time, the EP810 also delivers significant increases in both torque and peak power compared to the previous generation.”

    Will brands be able to put the new EP901 motor into existing frames, without new molds?

    “While the EP810 retains the same mounting bolt locations as the EP801, the overall shape and dimensions of the drive unit have changed. As a result, most manufacturers will need to update designs to accommodate the new system.”

    How does it ride?

    Test Riding Shimano EP810 full-power on the Honda RN0

    I got to test out the new Shimano EP810 motor over two wet & rainy days in Spain with the Honda RN0. Its EP8 name on the side may be the same. But with more power, more control, a more compact design, and lighter weight, it’s a whole new animal.

    Let’s go back to those key stats. The new EP810 cranks out 100Nm of max torque, up 17.6% from EP801. Its peak power now tops 750W, up 25% from the previous generation. And it shifts to a higher 43V system, compared to 36V of the prior EP-801 generation (and most other premium ebikes). Those all lead to a noticeable boost in power feel, and quicker motor response.

    No, that’s not the most torquey or most powerful ebike system. But, it might just be the lightest full-power eMTB motor. And I never felt lacking of power. In fact, if I had to guess based on simple math, if the motor power is a bit lower than some competition, you should get a bit more range out of that 720Wh battery, right?

    More compact, and more control

    As for 400g of weight savings at the magnesium-cased motor, I don’t think that makes much difference on a on a 22-24kg ebike. But the new flipped motor configuration is quite a bit more compact. That means you are less likely to hit it on rocks (chainrings are now more vulnerable though, and might need an extra bashguard). The new motor is also narrower from the front, which looks like it exposes more of the fins on the increased left side, which may improve heat dissipation.

    What is important to know, though, is that the new EP8 feels much more powerful than the previous generation. And while the new True Auto controls and in-app adjustability range can be a bit overwhelming, you can definitely customize the performance to how you prefer an eMTB ride to feel.

    I’ll be curious to try it out on more eMTB platforms.

    bike.Shimano.com

entry.title: Counting Milestones at GRUSK – Andy Karr
entry.content:
Set amongst ancient rock formations and a million acres of National Forest, the Gravel Ride Up Spruce Knob has become a fixture of the mid-Atlantic gravel circuit over its decade of existence. Andy Karr brought his gravel bike, a camera, and two dozen of his closest friends up to the Seneca Rocks and Spruce Knob area of West Virginia to celebrate a series of big life milestones at this year’s GRUSK.

That the Gravel Ride Up Spruce Knob fell on my fortieth birthday was serendipitous. GRUSK has been a popular event for me and my Great Eskape teammates since 2017, and we’ve routinely made a weekend of it. We usually set up camp for our teammates and other friends for Friday and Saturday nights at the nearby Seneca Shadows campground. A weekend of camping, riding bikes, and hanging out around a campfire sounded like a great way to ring in decade number four.

Forty being widely held as a milestone birthday, a fair number of friends, family, and coworkers have asked me if I “feel old” turning forty this year.

Old? Wanna know what’s old?

The quartzite and limestone that now make up the distinctive geological features on Spruce Knob and the nearby Seneca Rocks in West Virginia are formed from sediments deposited on a seabed 450-600 million years ago. The spines of Seneca Rocks are sedimentary layers upended and turned 90 degrees on their side by the collision of a chain of volcanos (now the Blue Ridge) with the North American Plate over 200 million years ago. Nothing sets the anxieties of middle age into a proper deep-time context like holding a birthday party in a setting shaped by tectonic and erosional forces over hundreds of millions of years.

For the last ten of those years, the Gravel Ride Up Spruce Knob has been bringing adventurous cyclists together for a weekend of gravel riding, camping, and companionship in the middle of the Spruce Knob-Seneca Rocks National Recreation Area and its many crags and hollows (pronounced “hollers,” around here). In addition to hosting West Virginia’s tallest point, the Spruce Knob area is crisscrossed by streams and rivers, plentiful blankets of rhododendron and laurel flowers, nearly a million acres of Monongahela National Forest, and by hundreds of miles of gravel roads and doubletrack that make for endless possibilities for gravel riding routes.

Travis, GRUSK’s founder and (along with his wife Rachel) principal organizer, has been riding bikes in the Spruce Knob area since well before the term “gravel bike” came into wide use. Though getting to fishing spots was the primary reason for his earliest cycling adventures in the area, a precursor to GRUSK came about at the invite-only New Year’s Eve Ride Up Spruce Knob in 2010.

Evolution of GRUSK

The idea for GRUSK itself was born on a birthday ride. Travis rode to the top of Spruce from Seneca Rocks with a good friend for their birthday, during which they schemed up a gravel event on Spruce. Shortly thereafter, another promoter failed to launch a proposed 3-day stage race on Spruce Knob. Travis offered to help pitch in, and before he knew it, he was planning the first GRUSK.

This year was the 10th running of GRUSK. Over the last decade, it has evolved and changed as the “gravel scene” has changed around it. GRUSK was run for years as the Gravel Race Up Spruce Knob, but the infusion of hypercompetitive, more road-race-like attitudes and the worry of racing on open roads with traffic and blind corners weighed heavily on Travis and Rachel. Eventually GRUSK evolved towards a granfondo-style event with competitive segments, to eventually the non-competitive fondo style it is now.

The shift in approach not only meant a safer event, but also a shift in resources away from prize purses and towards improving the experience of all riders. Travis tells me he fully expected the event to die once the competitive element was removed, but the year following the transition to non-competitive actually had a boost in ridership over prior years. I think I speak for the vast majority of GRUSK riders in saying that it’s one of the most exceptionally well-run aid station and rider logistical experiences of any event I have done.

The route itself has shifted over the last decade. As the bikepacking format gained popularity, longer and longer routes have been added to the trio of single-day distances. The route design has also been altered to improve rider safety by avoiding some of the sketchier road descents and high-traffic stretches. In earlier years the route summited Spruce Knob near the end of the day – however, both careless drivers in rented jeeps and thunderstorms are much more common on Spruce in the afternoon, so the summit was moved to earlier in the day.

I’ve ridden GRUSK five or six of the ten times it’s been run. I know substantial changes have been made over the years, but they’ve not impacted the character of the route enough for me to really notice. It’s a beautiful route. It’s challenging without being grueling. I’ve done the 50-mile version, the now-defunct 75-mile version, and the 89-mile version – always scaled to my level of fitness at the time – so no year stands out as particularly hard or easy. As a bike ride, GRUSK has been consistent and dependable, bordering on ritualistic. It’s a fixture in the yearly ride/race schedule for the team and me. But GRUSK is, and has always been, more than just a bike ride. It’s been a good excuse to get the increasingly geographically dispersed and busy-lifed gang together, see old friends, and throw down for a long weekend in the woods.

The Core of GRUSK

It’s all possible thanks to Travis, Rachel, and their small army of volunteers and local fire departments. Between the local bike shops that have supported the event with prizes, neutral aid, and even dry places for the bikepackers to rest, the local residents who wave and cheer us on throughout the ride, and the support of local leadership in working with GRUSK and its riders to fuel a growing outdoor tourism economy, GRUSK has been a catalyst of community building for a decade. I asked what running this event for the last decade has meant to Travis.

“Over the years, GRUSK has meant doing something bigger than yourself, building a community and showing the beauty of West Virginia to the cycling world beyond mountain biking. GRUSK has meant hard work, lots of long nights, and the usual blood, sweat, and tears event management brings. GRUSK has also meant thousands of smiles, dirty finish line hugs, campfire stories, and so many kind words from riders about the event. The results have been incredibly rewarding. I’ve strengthened friendships, forged new ones, and worked through differences in opinions to bring a quality event to every participant.”

Reflections at This Year’s GRUSK

GRUSK’s tenth year running was the perfect catalyst to draw together some communities of my own. Also celebrating tenth anniversaries this year are the bicycle club I co-founded with some of my best friends and DC’s Coffee Outside Ride series, which I’ve been attending since its inception in 2016. GRUSK 2026 falling on my 40th birthday this year meant that the group campout at Seneca Shadows was more than just a team affair – it brought together friends I’ve made through Coffee Outside, Great Eskape teammates, a ragtag group of other bike friends, Sarah, our dog Indie, and friends who’d be unlikely to sign up to ride up the side of a mountain.

Most, but not all, of us who camped together rode GRUSK. It was the impetus for all of this, after all. But the weekend was a lot more than a bike ride. We gathered around campfires, jumped into chilly swimming holes, cracked out our favorite camp stove recipes, marveled at fireflies, and joked and laughed deep into the night.

Gathering at GRUSK, and the decision to celebrate some big milestones there this year, laid bare some important reflections about the last decade. All the team rides, campfires, mugs of coffee, and front porch hangs offered more than a good time and memories. They connected people. I cherish the friendships I have made over the last ten years of this very bike-centric lifestyle. I am also immensely proud of the friendships these folks have made with each other at everything from events like GRUSK to semi-weekly coffee rides.

This community has really tied the last decade together, and I’m feeling upbeat about how it will grow, strengthen, and evolve.

As for GRUSK, rumors are that this may have been the last running of the event. I asked Travis after the event what the future holds for him, Rachel, and GRUSK. He said that the future was ambiguous.

“This may not be the last year of GRUSK, but it is the last year Rachel and I, along with our core group of friends, manage the day-to-day operations. It takes an immense amount of time and work to put on GRUSK every year, and the timing feels right to pass the torch over to someone with more time and energy to take the reins. We hope we can find the right person/company who will commit to keeping the spirit of GRUSK alive… We’re planning a small group tour to Italy in spring for the Strade Bianche and another small group tour to go watch and ride the routes for the first week of the Tour de France. There could be another gravel event in the future or maybe a gravel camp; we have lots of ideas, but who knows? We’re just going where our wheels lead us.”

The post Counting Milestones at GRUSK appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Reeb Cycles Teases Next-Generation Steel SST Prototype
entry.content:
Reeb Cycles is introducing the next generation of its award-winning SST steel 120 mm trail bike, featuring a redesigned chassis, updated geometry and improved suspension kinematics. The prototype will make its debut at the 2026 Sedona Mountain Bike Festival, November 6–8, where riders and media can get a first look at the refined platform and meet the team behind the bike…

Reeb SST

First introduced in 2022, and reviewed here at The Radavist in 2023, the SST blends the playful, rowdy character of Reeb’s steel hardtails with the capability and performance of a modern full-suspension trail bike. The 120 mm flex-stay platform combines custom steel tubing, innovative 3D-printed stainless steel components and proprietary suspension technology to deliver a responsive, efficient ride that’s equally comfortable crushing climbs, slapping berms and getting rowdy on technical descents.

Building on that foundation, Reeb has evolved the SST prototype geometry to improve stability and confidence on technical descents while maintaining its efficient climbing performance and playful handling. At the heart of the next-generation SST prototype is an updated 120 mm flex-stay suspension platform featuring revised kinematics designed to improve small-bump sensitivity, pedaling efficiency and overall suspension performance. These updates also expand tuning possibilities, including improved compatibility with coil shocks.

Steel SST Prototype Updates

The SST’s steel chassis also received engineering updates, including an additive-manufactured rocker pivot housing and enlarged bottom bracket cluster for improved alignment and a more cohesive, integrated design. A new bridged rocker linkage with a collet system delivers smoother, more consistent suspension performance, while redesigned hardware simplifies routine maintenance and makes the SST more approachable for riders who prefer turning their own wrenches. The rocker and suspension hardware are manufactured by Prosise Metal Works, led by longtime Reeb collaborator Adam Prosise.

Designed by the Reeb team and fabricated in-house in Longmont, Colorado, the next-generation SST prototype continues Reeb’s commitment to handmade steel frames, innovative engineering and building bikes that are as fun to ride as they are to look at. Reeb’s fabrication operations are now based at Hooptie Bike Lounge, bringing frame building, a full-service bike shop and a craft beer bar together under one roof.

Where To See It

Visit the Reeb Cycles booth at Sedona Mountain Bike Festival, November 6–8, to see the next-generation SST prototype, meet Jeff Lenosky and the Reeb team, and learn more about the bike’s development. Media are invited to stop by for interviews, prototype photography and a closer look at the new chassis, rocker and suspension hardware.

The next-generation SST is currently in development for 2027, sign up for updates with additional specifications, pricing and availability details at Reeb.

The post Reeb Cycles Teases Next-Generation Steel SST Prototype appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Prototype KYB Suspension Brings Moto Tech to the Trails
entry.content:
Known for their motorcycle race suspensions, Japanese brand KYB is expanding into four wheels with new kits for Toyota & Ford trucks and SUVs…and human-powered bikes, too!

Their debut products will be an inverted trail fork and coil-sprung rear shock. Like the MTB debut from Eibach, details are sparse here, but there’s a lot we can tell from looking at it.

For starters, it’s shown on a Marin Alpine Trail eMTB, which is a 160mm travel bike with 170mm fork. So, they’re starting with enduro travel ranges.

Second, the heavily shaped crown should keep the legs stiff. Interestingly, the uppers themselves are skinny compared to recent inverted forks from Cane Creek and Fox. So, they’re likely lighter, but… stiffness?

It’s also interesting that the legs clamp into the uppers, which could be great for serviceability. Damage one? Blow a damper? Just replace that side.

KYB’s moto forks use coil springs with speed-sensitive compression damping, and that’s included here, too. I couldn’t feel any knobs on the bottom of the legs, but there are two adjustments on the top of the right leg – one for compression, one for rebound.

On the left, there’s a single adjustment, however they couldn’t (or wouldn’t) say what it did. The fork uses a “coil spring with air support”, so it could be a fixed air spring with swappable coils and a preload adjustment to dial it in.

The lowers have rock guards and a thru axle that looks like it has a standard bolt holding it in rather than a typical thru axle bolt interface. The opposite side of the thru axle has an open end and it’s completely hollow all the way across, which makes its function even more of a mystery. But, it does clamp into both lower legs, so it’s some sort of floating design.

Despite the lack of firm details, they said the fork is pretty much done and ready for production. For the European market, they’re likely starting with aftermarket availability, and it was teased at Sea Otter Europe earlier this year, too. But for North America, their current plan is OE placements, and you can guess who might be an early bike brand partner…

The rear shock is a little behind in development, so what you see here may change before production. But the basics are all here.

Adjustable spring preload, likely dual compression (high and low speed) using the outer blue knob and inner bolt, and low-speed rebound on the bottom (red knob).

This bike is headed back to northern California (which is conveniently where Marin Bikes is HQ’d…) for testing after the SEMA Show we spotted it at. No word on pricing or availability, and there’s nothing on their website about them yet.

KYB.com

entry.title: absoluteBlack’s New TPU Road Tubes Come With Reusable Protective Packaging
entry.content:
You can add absoluteBlack to the growing number of brands selling lightweight TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane) tubes. But unlike the rest of the TPU tubes out there, absoluteBlack says its tubes are “Designed to be carried. Not just installed.” The Road TPU Tubes come in a 2-pack with 60mm aluminum valves and weigh a claimed 40.5 grams each. Perhaps more importantly, however, they come in reusable packaging to protect them from damage in your saddle bag, jersey pocket, in-frame storage, or hydration pack.

Reusable Packaging

TPU tubes have become popular with all types of cyclists for their low weight and compact size. But one thing that has plagued these lightweight wonders is the potential for damaging the somewhat delicate TPU material. Often, this damage occurs when carrying them, with sharp objects piercing or abrasion wearing holes in your spare tube. While this probably hasn’t happened to all of us, there are plenty of folks out there who have pulled out their emergency tube, only to find it already has a hole in it.

Most TPU tubes come in small cardboard boxes, which are then discarded, and the tube is stuffed into tight spaces alongside tools, or pulled frequently in and out of jersey pockets. absoluteBlack thinks there’s a better way, which is why its new TPU Road Tubes come in a reusable pouch to protect them from damage. The pouch is “made from a durable three-layer puncture- and abrasion-resistant laminate” and is resealable.

The protective pouch comes with two separate compartments, one for each tube in the 2-pack, and the divider in the center can be cut so the tubes can be carried separately. Unlike traditional tube packaging, the pouch is intended to stay with the tube, providing a layer of protection to hopefully avoid those “oh no, my spare tube already has a hole in it” moments.

The Tubes

absoluteBlack’s TPU tubes are made from transparent Thermoplastic Polyurethane. They feature 60mm full aluminum Presta valve stems with removable cores for a durable, serviceable connection that can stand up to the heat of the oh-so-popular electric mini-pumps. They’ve also included a “generously-sized TPU reinforcement cone” around the valve connection to bolster strength by the rim’s valve hole.

The new TPU tubes are designed for use with 700c road tires 25-30 mm in width. absoluteBlack says it went with a 28mm flat tube width and deliberately focused on this tire compatibility range, as this “approach minimizes unnecessary stretching, which can thin TPU walls and contribute to unreliable patch repairs — particularly when undersized ultralight tubes are used at the upper limits of their advertised tire ranges.” 

Specs

  • Tire compatibility: 700C / 25–30mm
  • Weight: 40.5g
  • Valve: 60mm aluminium Presta, removable core
  • Included: 2 TPU tubes, 2 repair patches, reusable dual-compartment protective pouch

Pricing and Availability

The new absoluteBlack TPU Tubes come in packs of two and retail for $29.99 USD / €26.95, which is competitive when compared to brands like Silca and Tubolito. They are available now directly from absoluteBlack.

absoluteblack.cc

entry.title: Video: EXPOSURE: Capturing Red Bull Rampage
entry.content:
Red Bull Rampage is arguably one of the most extreme events in all of outdoor sports, with the best freeride mountain bikers in the world taking on some of the wildest terrain on the planet. It’s truly a spectacle like no other. In its 25-year history, we’ve witnessed the evolution of big mountain freeride firsthand and a rate of progression that is almost unfathomable. While the riders deservedly get the spotlight, the photographers work tirelessly behind the scenes, putting in herculean efforts each year to capture the action and create the iconic imagery that always blows our minds. 

In Pelican’s documentary short, “EXPOSURE: Capturing Red Bull Rampage”, they turn the lens around on three of Rampage’s most experienced photographers: Christian Pondella (25 years), Paris Gore (13 years), and Bartek Wolinski (12 years). We’ve all seen the images, but we don’t see the 4 am starts, 40-pound packs, ridgeline scrambles, triple-digit heat, and late-night editing sessions. This short film gives us a behind-the-scenes look and a little taste of the hard work and dedication it takes to shoot Red Bull Rampage. Check it out.

entry.title: 32″ TOOT Racing Tritone Ti Gravel Burn Bike Shows TRed’s Rider-Focused Custom Concept
entry.content:
Not every new 32″ bike is simply riding a wave of me too, bigger wheel trends. This custom titanium TOOT aka TRed Tritone gravel bike built for Felix Ritzinger to race Gravel Burn is a perfect example of the Italian bike builder’s overarching custom concept.

Designed for a tall rider, looking to tackle long-distance, multi-stage gravel racing, it simply made the most sense to develop the bike around 32″ wheels for the highest performance. Enter the 32″ Toot Tritone

TOOT x TRed Tritone fully custom 32″ titanium gravel bike

Italian bike maker T°Red custom designs and builds each bike they create specifically for the rider and how they plan to ride. Their ADAPT (Adaptive Design Advanced Process Technologies) custom bike design process starts with a rider scan, virtual rider fit, and aerodynamics simulations to dial-in each bike for the individual rider. That’s the same process they use for amateur cyclists and pro riders alike.

Toot calls it a ‘digital twin’ of the rider that helps them perfectly fit and customize a bespoke bike to each cyclist. And it lets them visualize and optimize the final bike before it leaves the design stage.

Racing for clothing maker RH77, Ritzinger is more than 1.91m/ 6′-3″ tall, with especially long legs, and he often struggles to get an ideal fit on stock XL-sized bikes. So this ADPAT process helped Toot tweak a gravel race bike to his needs, and led to the conclusion that 32″ wheels would solve a lot of his particular fit & performance issues.

Is it TOOT, T°Red, TRed, even TiRed… then, Tritone or Triton?

To keep things a little bit confusing, T°Red has been the name of the company’s bike brand for more than a decade. And even that’s been written several different ways. But TOOT Engineering is and has been the name of the performance design & development team behind all TRed bikes and Toot-branded components. Toot is also the name used for their highest-level race bikes custom-built for professional cyclists, encompassing track, road, gravel, and even some cross-country. But even racers like Ritzinger use both TRed and Toot interchangeably.

As for the new ti gravel bike… Toot officially call it the Tritone, in their native Italian. But their site uses auto machine translation, so you’re as likely to see it listed as Triton on its English-language product page. So, we’ll try to stick with the original.

Why 32″ if not just to jump on the bandwagon?

TOOT Engineering explains that it essentially boils down to the simple geometry of a classic diamond-shaped bike frame for a tall rider (not handling geometry, just yet). In order to get the bar high and far enough above the bottom bracket for Ritzinger, a traditional 700c bike with a normal fork axle-to-crown length results in a tall headtube and a large open front triangle. That resulting larger-than-average distance between the down and top tubes, invariably means decreased frame stiffness, no matter the frame material.

So going to bigger wheels let Toot create a more compact frame that was stiffer and more responsive, while nailing Ritzinger’s fit. Small frames often end up too stiff, a real problem for comfort and grip on gravel. But the longer 32″ wheelbase here compensates

In fact, the reason Ritzinger (who’s RH77 team typically races on BMC bikes) came to TRed & Toot in the first place is that they previously built him a super-slammed Falcon track bike for the Berlin Six Days in 2025. That bike followed a similar philosophy of keeping the frame low and compact, with a rider-customized high & long cockpit (and wildly long seattube extension).

Ritzinger was psyched with that bike, saying, “I hadn’t felt since I was under 17: stiffness, reactivity, precision riding. With my height, my physique, I thought I’d never be able to feel them under my ass again.” So when it was time to build a gravel race bike for South African Gravel Burn, returning to TRed & Toot was a no-brainer.

Custom 32″ Ti frameset – Tech details

  • fully custom titanium gravel bike developed around the rider
  • all-new full carbon 32″ gravel fork developed by TOOT Racing, 445mm a-c & 110mm axle
  • 3D-printed titanium tube junctions & dropouts, plus hydroformed ti tubing
  • fully-integrated internal cable routing (wireless-only drivetrains)
  • slack real seattube angle to offer three saddle positions with 0 offset or forward-facing +10mm or +20mm curved seatposts
  • widely curved dropped seatstays for tire clearance and comfort
  • 64mm (32″ x 2.5″) max tire clearance
  • max 54T 1x chainring (with narrow 47.5mm chainline on 150mm road Q-factor cranks)
  • Boost axle spacing
  • UDH dropout
  • T47 86.5mm road-style threaded bottom bracket
  • integrated seatpost clamp
  • 3D-printed titanium band clamp for braze-on mount mini chain guide
  • handmade in Italy, in Montichiari in Lombardy

Unique 32″ gravel race bike build specs

  • Toot Marassha GR ultra-narrow 38.5cm outside, +35mm reach, +50mm stack aero carbon handlebar & Toot alloy stem
  • 9th Wave Sandstone SL32 LTD, 32″ x 52mm deep aero carbon wheels
  • 32 x 55mm Schwalbe G-One RX Pro (32×2.4″ Silca Protocol RCG-3 tires in photoshoot)
  • 44T 1x chainring paired to 10-52T Garbaruk cassette and SRAM Rival AXS Xplr

TOOT Tritone 32″ gravel bike – Options, pricing & availability

The trick to getting a 32″ titanium Tritone gravel bike is just reaching out to Toot. Each frame and complete bike they build is custom developed for each individual rider. Geometry, material, and stiffness characteristics are tuned to each rider, not a stock geometry chart or rider weight table.

A fully-customized replica of Ritzinger’s build will set you back approximately €11k. While Toot’s still-custom Club Edition complete build of the 32″ Tritone with a Rotor 1×13 groupset & M4 cockpit sells for €10,580.

As Toot describes their custom bike concept, “You don’t need to be a pro to ride like one. Every single rider who comes to us gets this exact same treatment and dedicated approach.” So, just get in touch to start building your own super bike – whether that’s a titanium, steel, or alloy bike, whatever discipline you ride, and whichever wheelsize makes the most sense for you!

performance.TOOTengineering.com

entry.title: Redshift Expands Awesome Mousetrap Pedal Adapter Range with SPD SL & LOOK Keo Versions for Road
entry.content:
There have been many different flat pedal adapters for clipless pedals to this point, but as the saying goes, ‘build a better mousetrap, and the world will beat a path to your door.’ Redshift took that expression literally and created their version of the ideal pedal adapter and called it the Mousetrap.

Starting with SPD pedals, Redshift unveiled their ingenious design. Tool-free, incredibly quick to install and uninstall, impossible to release accidentally, low profile, high grip, and easy to transport with magnets that hold the pair together. It really is a near-perfect design.

Now, that same design is porting over to road pedals with new versions for SPD-SL and LOOK Keo. Note that the SPD-SL version is also compatible with other SPD-SL-compatible pedals, including Garmin & Favero power meter pedals. The glass-filled nylon composite Mousetrap pedal adapters use a mechanical lock that snaps into the clipless pedal without the requirement to buy extra cleats.

Our sample of the SPD-SL version came in 2g less than claimed at 168g, while the LOOK Keo versions are a bit less at 160g per pair. Both offer a fairly large 80mm x 105mm platform that is just 10mm thick.

When fitted, the platform sits level with the top of the clipless mechanism and offers a surface that is grippy without being too painful if you manage to catch your shins.

Really, the only negative we can find is that the weight causes the pedal to rest upside down. But it’s very easy to flip over the platform when you start to pedal, since the front side of the pedal still rests higher than the rear.

Available in black/grey, purple/black, teal/pink, and blue/orange in both LOOK Keo and SPD-SL; pricing is set at $59.99 per set. However, Redshift is having an early Black Friday sale, which means you can get them right now for just $44.99 (25% off on nearly everything).

Redshift has also announced that a Crankbrothers-compatible version is next up, and is expected in 2027. You can sign up for their email list to be notified.

entry.title: Eibach Develops Lightweight, Precision-Tuned MTB Coil Springs
entry.content:
Eibach is a leader in performance car and off-road suspension, especially popular for track and desert racers. Soon, they want to bring that same performance to mountain bikers.

The new range of coil springs will be made in the USA, just like their automotive springs. But they’ll be sold as a kit with custom spring seats from German suspension performance brand Lorey.

For the springs, Eibach has two benchmarks: be the lightest in class, and offer the best tuning range. For weight, it’s a matter of using their decades of experience turning steel wire into springs. And they admit, it’s a goal, but that getting the performance right matters more than being the absolute lightest-weight coils on the market. Regardless, expect them to be among the lightest.

For tuning, they’re aiming for 20lb increments. Meaning, they’ll offer spring rates of 200lb/in, 220lb/in, 240lb/in, etc., up to 500lb/in or more to meet market demand.

Compare that to the standard 50lb increments from stock options by RockShox, Fox, and Cane Creek. Even current high-end aftermarket springs typically come in 25lb increments. Dropping that to 20lb increments gives you much finer tunability. A range of lengths will be available to fit popular shock stroke lengths, too.

For the perches, Lorey’s precision-machined spring seats thread onto popular shock bodies from Fox, Rockshox, etc. In this case, they’re custom-mated to Eibach’s springs for an exact fit, cradling the coil and keeping it rock solid top and bottom.

Beyond this info, details are sparse. There’s no set pricing or release date, but their reps told me they’re very close to production. Look for them (hopefully) in early 2027.

Eibach.com/MTB

entry.title: Redshift Introduces SPD-SL and Look Keo-Compatible Mousetrap
entry.content:
On the heels (or rather, on the toes) of Redshift’s popular Mousetrap SPD adaptors, the innovative Pennsylvania brand has just released two much-anticipated sequels. The new SPD-SL and Look Keo versions of the Redshift Mousetrap are now available, and they’re even on sale!

If you’re not familiar, the Redshift Mousetrap is a removable but secure platform that can snap in and out of your clipless pedals to effectively convert them to flats. You won’t need to suffer hot spots through your Vans slip-ons, or click-clack across the patio after riding to your friends’ barbecue in your road shoes.

  • Material: Glass-Filled Nylon (Composite)
  • Weight: 170g per pair (SPD-SL), 160g per pair (Look Keo), 176g per pair (SPD)
  • Dimensions: Generously sized 80mm x 105mm platform x 10mm thick (when
  • installed, sits level with top of clipless mechanism)
  • Colors:
    • Black/Gray, Purple/Black, Teal/Pink, and Blue/Orange
  • Compatibility:
    • NEW SPD-SL: Compatible with SPD-SL and most SPD-SL-compatible clipless pedals (including Garmin & Favero)
    • NEW LOOK Keo: Compatible with LOOK Keo clipless pedals
    • SPD: Compatible with SPD and most SPD-compatible clipless pedals
    • Coming soon: Crankbrothers compatible versions coming in 2027 – sign up here to be notified
  • Retail Price (MSRP):
    • $59.99 USD | £49.99 GPB | €59.99 EUR | $79.99 CAD | $99.99 AUD
    • 25% Off at Launch as part of Redshift’s Early Black Friday Sale
  • Available to order from the Redshift website, ship dates vary by region & SKU

The simple two-piece design locks in just like your cleat would, aided by an easy-to-access lever that eases entry and exit. The Look Keo and SPD-SL versions work essentially like the original SPD version, and share the same big-but-not-too-big 80 x 105mm platform. They’re just 10 mm thick, and a pair will securely snap together with embedded magnets to make for a pocket-sized package when not in use.

They’re also available in a handful of colors, ranging from quiet to loud. We think the teal / pink looks great in person, but you do you. Oh, and for those of you who run Crankbrothers pedals, you are not forgotten. Redshift revealed they’re working on an Eggbeater-style Mousetrap for 2027. But if you’ve got Look Keo, SPD, or SPD-SL, act now. They’re 25% off at the time of publishing this.

See more at Redshift

entry.title: State Bicycle Co’s 4130 Trail Now Comes in a Variety of Build Options
entry.content:
State Bicycle Co. has expanded its 4130 Trail platform from a single hardtail offering into a completely configurable platform. The 4130 Trail frame now builds two fundamentally different bikes: a 130 mm trail hardtail or a sub-28-pound rigid MTB—across two shifting systems, three front ends, three colorways, and a component upgrade path from wheels to dropper to handlebars…

New Finish: Hammered Tobacco Powdercoat

A textured powder coat rather than liquid paint — applied dry, oven-cured into a thicker, tougher shell. The hammered texture throws deep metallic flake in direct sun and breaks up the scuffs that read as bright scratches on a gloss frame. Available on both shifting systems and as a frameset.

4130 Trail Two Configurations

With the RockShox fork, the 4130 Trail is an underpriced trail hardtail: slack 65° head angle, 130mm up front, built for steep, technical ground. It fits either a rigid fork, and the front end drops 55–58mm. As the head angle steepens, the bottom bracket lowers, the wheelbase shortens, and the same frame becomes a fast, light all-terrain bike for dirt roads, doubletrack, bikepacking routes, and hardpack singletrack.

State is explicit that this is a different bike, not a trail bike with the squish removed — and that the distinction is the entire point of the platform.

Shifting Expectations

Cable. Raw Phosphate and Hammered Tobacco run Shimano Deore M6100 1×12—an 11–50T cassette paired with a 32T ring for 454% of range and a 0.64:1 climbing gear, plus the shift ramps and chain management of the tiers above. Sagebrush Green runs MicroShift XLE 1×11, 11–46T. Both are serviceable anywhere, by anyone, with parts on every shop wall.

Wireless. Every colorway is also available with SRAM Eagle Transmission AXS. There is no derailleur hanger — the S1000 clamps directly around the rear axle through the UDH dropout, referencing the frame instead of a sacrificial aluminum tab that bends every time the bike tips over. No limit screws. No indexing to chase across a season. Shifts complete under full power, standing, mid-climb, because the firmware knows where every tooth on the cassette sits and times the shift rather than just moving sideways.

520% of range from a 10–52T XS-1270 cassette — and unusually for Transmission, it mounts to a standard HG freehub, so there is no XD driver or new rear wheel to buy on top of the drivetrain. Battery and charger included.

All three fork options are available on both.

Run it 29/32er Mullet

The carbon rigid fork has been run with a 32 x 2.4″ tire — rare in a category whose main obstacle has been a near-total absence of forks with room for one. A 32-inch wheel stands taller than a 29, lifting the front end and slackening the head angle back out, which partly offsets the shorter axle-to-crown.

4130 Trail: TL;DR

We know you care most about two metrics: price and weight, so here ya go!

Pricing

  • Carbon rigid: $1,399.99 Shimano/Microshift, $1,899.99 SRAM AXS
  • Steel rigid: $1,199.99 Shimano/Microshift, $1,699.99 SRAM AXS
  • Suspension: $1,499.99 Shimano/Microshift, $1,999.99 SRAM AXS
  • No fork: $1,099.99 Shimano/Microshift, $1,599.99 SRAM AXS

Weight

  • Carbon rigid: Small 27 lb 13 oz, Medium 27 lb 14 oz, Large 28 lb 2 oz, X-Large 28 lb 5 oz
  • Steel rigid: Small 30 lb 7 oz, Medium 30 lb 8 oz, Large 30 lb 12 oz, X-Large 30 lb 15 oz
  • Suspension: Small 32 lb 3 oz, Medium 32 lb 4 oz, Large 32 lb 8 oz, X-Large 32 lb 11 oz

See more at State Bicycle Co.

entry.title: Evidence Engineering 12-in-1 Adjustable Gravity Stem
entry.content:
Evidence Engineering, a new company from Poland, has released its first product: an adjustable stem with 12 settings to dial in the perfect cockpit position on your trail, enduro, or downhill bike. Read below for all of the adjustable details. And yes, it reminds us of a Bionicle…

Evidence Engineering Adjustable Stem Quick Hits

  • Reach (Length) adjustability – 20 / 30 / 35 / 45 mm
  • Stack (Rise) adjustability – 33 / 45 mm
  • Handlebar clamp width adjustability – 58 / 70 mm
  • Handlebar diameter – 35 mm only
  • Steerer diameter – 11⁄8” (28.6 mm)
  • Steerer clamp height – 24 mm
  • Min. steerer insertion – 21 mm
  • Intended use – Trail / Enduro / Gravity / E-bikes – ASTM cat. 5
  • Max system weight (bike + rider + gear) – 130 kg
  • Made in Poland

Adjustments

This stem design features 6 possible combinations of reach and stack (Fig. F-K) and 2 clamping widths available (Fig. L, M). Pay attention to the markings on the side of the stem to find out your current reach and stack. There are 4 reach configurations: 20, 30, 35, 45 mm. The 20 and 30 mm reach options are available only when using a 45 mm stack setup. To adjust the reach, bolt the clamps to the base with different holes and rotate the base around the steerer tube if necessary. There are 2 stack (rise) options – 33 and 45 mm. To change the stack height, flip only the stem base upside down. There are 2 handlebar clamp width options: 58 and 70 mm (Fig. L, M). You can run either width, regardless of your reach and stack choice. To adjust the clamping width, swap the left and right handlebar clamps. Always check if the handlebar clamping zone is straight and wide enough (Fig. D, E). Many handlebars may not be compatible with the 70mm width setup, and there may be some handlebars that are not compatible with either width setup. Please contact Evidence Engineering if you have any concerns about the handlebar compatibility.

Join the second round of preorders at Evidence Engineering.
