entry.title: Ari Shafer Review: Deliciousness – Paul Kalifatidi
entry.content:
The Ari Shafer is a progressive gravel bike, but what does that really mean? Paul has been riding one for almost a year and has his thoughts on gravel bike biology, head tube angles, really long seatposts, and why you might actually like a race-centric gravel bike for your casual daily ride.

Ari Shafer Quick Hits

  • Named after the Shafer trail in Utah, not Ari Shaffir, the comedian.
  • Carbon frame only
  • 29×2.25” (700x58c) tire clearance
  • XS-XL sizing
  • Accommodates 3 water bottles: 2 inside main triangle, 1 on the bottom of the downtube
  • Additional mounting points on fork
  • 27.2 mm seatpost
  • Top tube bag mount
  • Downtube storage
  • UDH compatible
  • Compatible with 60mm suspension forks
  • 1x specific
  • Designed with 180mm rotors
  • Threaded BSA bottom bracket
  • Integrated headset cable routing
  • Can be set up with a mechanical dropper post, just not directly from Ari
  • Can accommodate full fenders
  • Internal dynamo routing on rigid fork
  • Price:
    • Frameset: $1,999
    • Complete builds from $2,999 to ~$10,500 (with build spec modifications)

Ari Shafer Overview

I’m not throwing shade, but sometimes it feels like the gravel scene tries to claim it invented off-road riding. Ari isn’t claiming they did either; I’m just starting to pick up on that notion when I read between the lines on my Instagram explore page. The original mountain bikes mostly rode terrain that is now firmly the realm of gravel bikes. Especially where I live, in Bellingham, WA, the average “gravel” ride would probably best be done on a cross-country mountain bike. Maybe it is time I put my money where my mouth is and put together a frighteningly light hardtail. Yet, I still find myself addicted to riding curly bar bikes with aggressively low front ends.

Why? I love them. I love how they look. I love how they ride. I love how they make the ride from my city home to the “backcountry” gravel trails feel sprightly and fast, more than a flat-bar bike. I don’t race bikes, and I don’t regularly or enthusiastically track my rides. This is a vibes-based opinion, and this review is entirely vibes-based.

Gravel Bike Evolution

The gravel bike phenotype has two distinct sides of the story, two converging branches on the evolutionary tree. One is gravel bikes that take design direction from mountain bikes. This branch includes bikes like the Kona LBF and Salsa Cutthroat. They inherit traits from mountain bikes, such as boost spacing, mountain bike head tube angles, and 100mm suspension forks. The other branch contains gravel bikes evolved from road bikes. They retain road-bike chainring clearance and aggressively low cockpits meant for high-speed efficiency, and narrower q-factors. This branch includes most gravel bikes, like the Specialized Crux, Manzanita Whippet, and barely, this here Ari Shafer. The Ari Shafer definitely evolved from the road-bike side of gravel, yet I think it sits firmly in the middle, trying to span both branches. Let’s talk about it.

What the Heck Is Progress?

The Ari Shafer is quite progressive, but what does that actually mean? A “progressive” bike design from ten years ago certainly doesn’t resemble one from today, which I guess is the whole point: we progress past what once was. In my opinion, the current “progressive” gravel bike in the year 2026 has these qualities: clearance for 55mm tires and a 48-tooth chainring, a headtube angle of 70 degrees or slacker, a large amount of exposed seatpost for comfort or a dropper post, an effective seat tube angle steeper than 73.5 degrees with a straight seatpost, no toe overlap, and non-boost hub and bottom bracket spacing. I’m not even requiring a suspension-corrected front end, but perhaps I should given my perspective after this review.

While my original description of the evolutionary branches of gravel bikes made them sound somewhat equal in length and shape, the reality is that the “road bike” branch is evolving closer and closer to the “mountain bike” branch, while that one seems content to evolve on its own. More mountain-bike-like gravel bikes will probably meet these requirements or diverge and become boost-spaced, drop-bar 29ers with wider tires and smaller chainrings.

Wow, bikes are silly.

Let’s briefly look at Evil bikes and what they did with the Chamois Hagar. Evil set the standard for what an ultra-progressive carbon gravel bike can be. The Chamois Hagar is clearly inspired by mountain bikes, it has a 66.6 degreed head tube angle, for example. Yet, it can only clear a 50mm tire, which immediately makes me think of it as somewhat derived from the road-bike side of things. Frankly, it’s such an oddity that it sits outside the evolutionary tree of gravel bikes, at least in my mind. It’s an outlier that hasn’t been matched.

Why do I bring it up? I think this Ari is more appealing to the masses. That said, I think Evil takes pride in not appealing to the masses. Ignoring looks, I think that the Ari Shafer’s seattube length works much better for a true gravel bike. The Evil Chamois Hagar has a large “mast” to support the seatpost, which some people find visually unappealing. It might help get the top tube lower and out of the way for pushing the bike away from the body during intense steering and aerial maneuvers, but that is not how 99% of riders are going to use the bike. The Chamois Hagar has a much slacker headtube angle, which makes bike/body separation more important, so I do see why the seattube is so low. That said, the people who can ride a Chamois Hagar like Ian Fey, the talented rider in most of the Chamois Hagar marketing material, are rare. I think that Ari’s design, which places the seattube collar only 10mm higher than Evil’s, is better visually and allows a larger front triangle for a frame bag or really large water bottle. Even with a dropper post, I don’t foresee leaning the bike over like a mountain bike in most use cases.

The Ari Shafer meets all of my demands for a “progressive” gravel bike. It easily clears a 55mm tire, is designed around a 60mm suspension fork, has a striking amount of seatpost, can clear a 52-tooth chainring, has a 68mm BB shell, and 142mm rear hub spacing. All of this adds up to one of the more interesting gravel bikes out there. The geometry is race-like, with a fairly low cockpit, which we will discuss in more detail below.

This is perfect for the “gravel” ride I do most often: a sub-two-hour sprint that takes me across Bellingham on asphalt, onto a gravel rail-to-trail, climbs a fire road, and descends on singletrack. I have found that bikes with taller stack heights feel far too upright for such an intense effort, and bikes with narrower tires just don’t feel suited to the off-road terrain. This is the best bike I have found for this ride, and maybe that is why I burned through a set of brake pads and a chain during the review period. Most review bikes go back to the company they came from without any replacement wear items, but I rode the Shafer so much I had to replace things. That says a lot.

Ari Shafer Geometry

At first glance, the Ari Shafer seems like a geometric oddity. In reality, it’s not too dissimilar from what most of us expect from a gravel bike. It’s a bit slacker, has a more exposed seatpost, and is a bit longer. The stem isn’t super short, so it still steers like most gravel bikes. I used the provided 70mm stem and had no desire for anything different. I’m going to say something controversial: 69 degrees is the best headtube angle for an off-road gravel bike.

I’ve ridden slacker, and the quick steering feel that makes riding flat terrain enjoyable somewhat disappears. I’ve ridden steeper, and things get a bit spicy too quickly off-road. Again, these are simply my opinions. If most of your riding is on typical gravel roads, flatter and less rocky, you’ll probably find this head tube angle more than enough for handling the rough stuff. I think this headtube angle also pairs better with the suspension fork; the travel of the fork more closely aligns with the angle of the fork.

I also appreciate the 74-degree seat tube angle. It makes long, fire road climbs more comfortable. Ari provides a zero setback seatpost (which, by the way, is simple and very well made), and with my 750mm saddle height, the effective seat tube angle comes out to ~73.5 degrees. That’s great for me.

The chainstays are short, which I like on pretty much all my bikes. Ari makes the chainstay length proportional across all sizes. A size small has a 425mm chainstay and a size XL has a 440mm chainstay. It’s shocking how few bikes do this; for example, I’m waiting for an Open Wide 2.0 to arrive in the mail, and all of the frame sizes have identical chainstay lengths. Is that bad? No, but it does mean that the different sizes will handle with more variety than the designers likely intended.

I want to briefly discuss the stack height. Unlike John and Spencer, who will argue that most people should be riding taller front ends, I much prefer being low. Even on a mountain bike, I detest having my handlebars much higher than my saddle height. I live for the climbs and intense efforts as much as I do a descent and a pleasant pedal, and find that I can do more of this with less stack. A good example is my own Northern Frameworks drop-bar MTB. It’s somewhat similar to the Ari in many ways, but one of the biggest differences is that the cockpit is much higher (619mm vs 585mm), a design element I chose to prioritize comfort on long rides over intense pedaling efforts. When I do take that bike on more “spirited” fast rides, I am constantly scrunched over the handlebars with bent arms, and I finish the ride with tired triceps. I find bikes with lower, more “race” cockpits suit my average ride better than the longer, slower ones I do less often. They’re more fun for the rides that I intend to be fun. The Ari has a certified “race-like” low front end. It’s not the lowest out there, but it certainly isn’t tall.

The Build Kit

Ari sent me the “Shafer Comp” build kit, which uses the SRAM Apex Eagle hydraulic drivetrain. I cannot say enough good things about this groupset; it’s affordable, capable, and comfortable. We used to have to rely on third-party modifications to combine mechanical 12-speed mountain bike gearing with drop bars, but SRAM released this and made those modifications unnecessary. It is also not reliant on SRAM’s direct mount system and can be equipped on bikes that do not have a UDH derailleur hanger interface. The hydraulic brake hoods are very comfortable, and the brakes are powerful. It’s a stellar drivetrain that I don’t think gets enough love, as it’s been overshadowed by electronic systems and the hangarless derailleurs.

The best part about every Shafer, regardless of the tier you choose, is that it can fit 180mm rotors. I cannot stress this enough: I hate small rotors. A large rotor adds marginal weight, while it provides immeasurable stopping power and longevity. I had an interesting discussion with my friend Erik Binggeser, who has been on a four-year North American bike tour. He uses 160mm rotors on his 200-ish-pound cargo bike with no issue. The difference: he doesn’t use his brakes much. Most of his riding is on roads where the natural angle of things controls his speed. That is not the case on my gravel terrain, where I am either constantly feathering the brake on singletrack or grabbing handfuls of it while approaching a downhill corner on a fire road. I cook 160mm rotors consistently. Ari, thanks for making a flat-mount off-road bike that fits 180mm rotors without any silliness.

I did opt for one upgrade to this build: I requested the Zipp 303 XPLR S Carbon wheelset. It’s deep, it’s wide, and I think it complements the rather svelte frame beautifully. Unfortunately, it did result in my least favorite riding characteristic: the cheap hub is really clanky. When coasting, the hub is relatively quiet, but a quick pedal stroke results in a loud clanging sound as the freehub engages. It’s a noticeably poor experience. The “SW” version of the wheelset comes with a nicer hub, and yes, it costs more. If I did it again, I’d splurge on that wheelset, but I don’t think you can get it with this affordable build kit. You have to spring for the more expensive “elite” build to option the nicest SW wheelset. Ari, please change that. The people deserve nice wheels with mechanical drivetrains.

On the subject of poor spec choices, let’s discuss the headset cable routing. I’m not saying headset cable routing is bad in general; I’m saying the way it was done on this bike with the provided cockpit components was poor. Ari sent me a bike that is on the more affordable side of the build spectrum. The cockpit features an aluminum handlebar and stem with external routing, but the cables must be routed through the headset. Over time, the cables twisted the headset and migrated counter-clockwise around the stem. I have no clue if this would cause some kind of issue down the line, as I consistently fixed it, but it was annoying and unsightly nonetheless. Couple that with the seemingly incorrect amount of rear brake cable, which formed a larger loop than the other cables, and I found myself consistently frustrated with the aesthetics and experience. I suspect that more expensive builds with integrated handlebars and stems would mitigate this issue. I think this is the clearest example of more affordable bikes having to compromise to appease the expensive side, and that upsets me.

Frame Details

Though I discuss some of these things elsewhere in the article, some frame details and features should be isolated in their own section. Firstly, the internal storage. This feature has become seemingly ubiquitous on carbon gravel bikes and mountain bikes, except for models targeting the ultra-light category. It is not a make-or-break for me. The Shafer’s downtube is rather large, and so I did end up putting a tube, pump, and multi-tool in it. The issue is that Ari doesn’t provide an organizer or sleeve to contain items and keep them from rattling against the frame. I wrapped the multi-tool and pump in a rag to get around this issue. Over time, I stopped using the storage option altogether and was content to store everything in my jersey pockets. Sometimes I put a bar or snack in there, but rarely. So yes, it’s there if you want it.

The door to the storage compartment is where the downtube bottle cage mounts. You can flip the door either way to change the bottle cage position. And yes, when riding with a full bottle on incredibly rough terrain, I did notice some rattling from the door. I’m not saying that this is a downside, because frankly, it was only noticeable when I hit stuff so rough that even my body and the rest of the bike complained. We’ll call this rattle the canary in the coal mine; if you hear it, you should probably be walking the bike anyways.

Speaking of water bottle cages, there are a number of places you can mount them: seattube, downtube, and bottom bracket. I guess you could also use the toptube mounts, but I think that’s a better place for a bag. Regardless, water storage should not be an issue on any of the sizes.

Frame Finish

To put it bluntly: this frame is freaking beautiful. I absolutely love the “rootbeer metallic” color. It looks good clean, it looks good covered in mud, and it has a wonderfully outgoing yet reserved character that is rare. The creamy logo text and other decals contrast beautifully with the base paint.  I kept calling it metallic chocolate, and yes, that’s where I got the word to capture my experience with this bike: deliciousness.

The back of the seattube has a few hidden details: coordinates and map tell you where you can take this bike, and after looking them up, I’m realizing there’s no terrain more fitting: the backcountry roads of Moab, Utah. Specifically, the map and coordinates plant you at the top of the Shafer Canyon overlook. Given that Ari is based in Utah, this is a no-brainer. All of their bikes are named after iconic peaks or riding locations in Utah.

There are some small things I would love to not have seen as part of the paintjob: the giant “M” denoting the size and some silly emblems above the downtube storage. I have no issue with a subtle, permanent size indicator on a bike, but I don’t like how Ari went about it. The first thing I tend to notice when eyeing someone’s bike is stickers left on from assembly, like the orange ones on brake rotors or various stickers that serve a purpose on the shop floor but none to the rider. The “S4” indicator on a Specialized is what comes to mind. That sticker can be removed, but the “M” on the Shafer is part of the paint. For the life of the bike, it always looked like I had neglected to remove the shop floor sticker and make it my own.

The same goes for the little emblems above the internal frame storage. Five months into owning the bike, I shouldn’t have to be reminded what I can store in the frame. The proprietary stem cap that integrates with the expansion plug on the rigid carbon fork is the cherry on top. I don’t understand these decisions, as they immediately make the bike feel more “corporate,” which I know DTC brands like Ari are trying to avoid.

Frame Compliance and Ride

Ari absolutely nailed the ride feel. The frame is quite stiff laterally but quite compliant vertically: efficient yet comfortable. It’s the most compliant carbon fiber bike that I recall riding. I won’t go as far to say that it is noodly, like over-cooked pasta, but it’s certainly not harsh and ultra-stuff like a racing road bike. It’s well tuned for rough gravel. For a brief comparison, I received the new Open Wide 2.o for review and that bike feels quite different. It’s stiffer, but even bigger tires soften that stiffness around the edges. I’ll report more on that in a few months when I’m well-versed on the Open.

The Ari Shafer has a lot of seatpost, which is amazing! Or rather, there is not a ton of seattube. This lets the seatpost act as a leaf spring, helping absorb vibration and bumps. The frame design contributes: dropped seatstays that join the seattube below the toptube and a very thin seattube cross-section near the bottom bracket help the entire frame flex under impact. The forgiving ride feel is noticeable.

The fork also plays a key role in the forgiving ride. The very slender, long blades (remember, it’s corrected for a 60mm suspension fork) allow a lot of flex. With the front wheel between my legs, I could twist the handlebars a lot without the wheel following. On trail, I never saw or felt this, and it didn’t contribute to inaccurate steering. The only time I ever noticed it was when inching down a super steep asphalt grade. I could feel the fork chatter under the force. At speed and in the usual riding scenario, I never encountered any issues and did feel that the fork was compliant and predictable. Funny enough, the suspension fork was actually stiffer (in regard to this twisting) than the rigid fork.

I loved riding this bike. On flats, it felt fast, efficient, and how I want a speedy bike to feel. Every moment hunkered over the handlebars and hiding from the wind was pleasant. The same goes for climbing: I pointed the bike uphill, and it went there. I think some of my fastest climbs have been on this bike as it felt perfectly poised to do so. The steep seattube angle and low front end put me in the perfect position for steep watts.

To suspend or not to suspend

When I received this bike, I had no intention of riding it with a suspension fork. Yet, after a few months, I figured I should try it. The Shafer is one of the few mainstream gravel bikes designed around the RockShox Rudy XL, 60mm fork. Curiosity got the best of me, and I contacted Ari for a squishy fork. Technically, I should state that the fork they sent is a pre-production prototype, but nothing about the ride quality or the fork’s finish would indicate that more prototyping needed to be done.

 

At the moment, I have two gravel suspension forks: the DT Swiss F-132 ONE and this RockShox Rudy XL. They have different characters. The DT Swiss is far more sensitive when in the open damping setting, almost too much for intense pedaling, but this is remedied by how easily it can be actuated with the handlebar-mounted lever. The RockShox is more heavily damped and much firmer even when fully open.

To my surprise, I actually preferred the Ari Shafer with the suspension fork. I typically ran the fork in its full open setting with zero complaint and only reached to lock it out when riding long stretches of asphalt. Off-road, it added just more comfort and control without having to drop the front tire to pressures that handled high-speed asphalt descents poorly. As expected, it made the bike more capable.

Yet, I don’t think that the rigid fork is a poor spec choice. Truthfully, I’d take both if that were an option. If you ride lots of singletrack, the suspension fork would be a thoughtful choice. If you’re mostly riding smoother gravel roads or doubletrack, I’d stick to the rigid fork.

What is it for?

To oversimplify, the Ari Shafer is a fantastic gravel bike. I applaud Ari for making such an adaptable bike; I rode a myriad of surfaces, angles, and terrains and rarely felt out of place. No, I never took it places where I’d want my trail bike, because I don’t think that is the point of this bike. I’m not claiming that the Shafer is a mountain bike for your average gravel rider; I’m claiming that it is a really good gravel bike for your average gravel rider.

It is also certainly not a gravel bike that behaves more like a road bike, at least not with 55mm tires. Sure, I pumped them up to 30psi and did a lot of road riding, but it didn’t feel like I was riding something like the Litespeed Toscano I’m reviewing at the same time. That bike has 45mm tires and toe overlap and feels like a road bike that pushed itself to ride gravel. The Ari is confidently capable at pretty burly gravel and smoother singletrack. The geometry is more stable and composed than any other gravel bike I had ridden, which is why I say it’s planted firmly between the two branches of the evolutionary tree that is the gravel bike. It has a low front end and sprightly road-bike underpinnings, yet its tire clearance and confident handling make it feel like a mountain bike.

TL;DR

The Ari Shafer ended up being one of my favorite gravel bikes. It fit perfectly into my universe where I consistently ride a wide variety of terrain types: singletrack, rail-to-trail, fire roads, and city streets. It’s progressive design pushes the envelope enough to be capable but is reserved enough to remain palatable. Ari clearly put a lot of care and time into designing this bike, and I doubt they’ll have to go back to the drawing board for a long time.

Pros

  • Progressive design is adaptable and capable without feeling eccentric
  • Frame is wonderfully compliant for off-road comfort
  • Delicious finish matches the attitude of the bike
  • 60mm suspension-corrected design further adds versatility
  • Affordable when compared to the carbon fiber gravel bike market

Cons

  • Cable routing is frustrating on the more budget cockpit spec
  • Parts of the finish feel too “department store”

See the Shafer at Ari Bikes.

The post Ari Shafer Review: Deliciousness appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Hest Foamy Review: Front Country Comfort – Paul Kalifatidi
entry.content:
Paul has spent countless nights sleeping in cars, and he’s got opinions. Those opinions eventually led him to Hest, a Seattle-based company specializing in modern bedroll mattresses. For the past many months, he’s been sleeping comfortably, and now he wants to tell you all about it.

Durable Decision

I imagine that most people who have ever used a sleeping pad have used an inflatable pad. It is the industry standard, and for good reasons: lightweight, packable, and customizable in its firmness. There are a myriad of inflatable pads out there at all price points. Some options are luxuriously plush and comfortable; some are bare-bones and pack as small as a bike bottle. Your mileage may vary as to how comfortable you find any sleeping pad. I have an ultralight Therm-a-Rest that I love for any adventure beyond the reach of a vehicle. My mother swears by her plush Big Agnes that strikes a middle ground between car camping and ultralight backcountry packability. But I have one gigantic gripe with all inflatable sleeping pads: they will, with use, leak and need to be patched.

Growing up, just about every summer weekend was spent camping at Devils Lake with my dad, my brother, and the Chicago Mountaineering Club. My dad is the kind of guy who likes a ridiculously firm mattress. At home, jumping on his side of the bed was a painful experience, as he quite literally had a sheet of plywood on top of the mattress and under the mattress cover. It might come as no surprise then that we did not use inflatable pads while camping and all of us exclusively used Therm-a-Rest Z-Lite foam pads. It wasn’t until I got into bike camping and backpacking, where packability became a concern, that I purchased an inflatable pad, and I’m still on the fence about them. I’ve owned a few over the years, and have always found them to leak and be frustrating. Even when I lived in a Honda Element for a summer, I used two thin foam sleeping pads instead of an inflatable pad or mattress.

Four years ago, I bought my KZJ95 Prado and immediately built a sleeping platform in it. I found an inflatable pad that perfectly fit the shape, and for a long time I loved that setup. And then, a leak. I loved that pad; I found it incredibly comfortable, but after falling asleep on an inflated pad, I would wake up an hour later and feel the hard, cold bed platform underneath me. No longer was good sleep reliable.

Before you jump down my throat about finding the leak and fixing it, trust me, I tried. Most of my possessions are patched and repaired; this sleeping pad was no different. I did find where the leak was, but it was underneath a layer of foam that I had to dig through. After many failed attempts to patch the hole, I used the pad to protect a bicycle that I was shipping, told the new owner they could use it as a dog bed or to use it again to protect a bike, and I switched to a Hest mattress.

Ultimately, the thing that made me reach out to Hest about reviewing their product was wanting a foolproof and leakproof landing pad after a long day of riding, running, or fishing.

Hest Foamy Overview

Camping should not be complicated. Whether you’re sleeping in the car, next to the car, or miles from any cars, you shouldn’t be missing out on sleep. I did not always sleep well when camping, but I have made small changes that have made a monumental difference to the quality of sleep that I get while on the go. Those being, switching from a mummy-style sleeping bag to a quilt when in the backcountry or a big blanket when car camping, and choosing reliability over packability. This article will pertain to reliability and comfort, as you cannot sleep well if you are waking up constantly to inflate a mattress.

The Hest Foamy is dead simple: it’s two densities of memory foam wrapped in a weather-resistant and washable cover. The bottom is covered in a durable and water-resistant PVC-like fabric, while the top, the part your body rests on, is a very comfortable and stretchy fabric. The mattress rolls up, has a carry handle, a small pocket for essentials, and can be attached to a neighboring pad to double the sleeping area. Boom. That’s basically it. There aren’t a ton of features to discuss, and yet, below are 1000 words about why I’ve come to love this piece of gear. Let’s get into it.

 

Hest Foamy Quick Hits

  • Foam core: Two layers of foam provide body contouring support and pressure-point relief. The temperature-resilient foam is designed to perform in cold conditions and is CertiPUR-US certified, meaning it has been made without harsh chemicals and with environmentally friendlier methods.
  • R-value 8.8: High insulation helps keep you warm in colder camping conditions.
  • Outdoor-ready construction: Waterproof, dirt-resistant materials and a waterproof lower fabric help protect you and the mattress from wet, muddy conditions.
  • Compact roll design: Rolls tightly for easy transport and storage, with an integrated compression harness to keep it securely packed. The compression harness doubles as a dry, flat surface for changing clothes when the mattress is unrolled.
  • Easy to carry: A durable built-in handle makes grab-and-go transport simple.
  • Removable, washable cover: Easily remove the cover and machine wash it when needed.
  • Convenient features: A built-in phone pocket keeps small essentials close, while side clips allow you to link mattresses for extra sleeping space.
  • 3 sizes:
    • Foamy Short 64” x 25” x 3.9” (reviewed)
    • Foamy 78″ x 25″ x 3.9”
    • Foamy Wide is 78″ x 30″ x 3.9”
  • $279-379 USD

About Hest

The name Hest is derived from Hestia, the Greek goddess of hearth and home. Hest’s driving goal is to make camping as comfortable as sleeping at home. I see this in the way that they approach their product category: front-country and car camping comfort.

Hest approached this product category differently than most of their competitors, which tend to be heritage camping brands. Those companies have taken their inflatable camping pads, initially meant to be light and packable, and made them larger and more comfortable to bring them back to the front-country. Hest took the at-home mattress idea and slimmed it down to a more packable form factor that I think better solves the comfort side of front-country camping. Removing the inflatable element comes with very minor drawbacks, with the added advantage of foolproof and durable reliability.

Choosing your Hest

There are a myriad of options if you peruse the Hest website. This is a review of two Foamy Short mattresses. When I was initially in discussion with Hest about this review, we were set on the Dually, their fold-in-half mattress meant for one or two people. At the last minute, I decided to switch to two Foamy mattresses instead of the single Dually for two reasons: the Foamy is more adaptable with its waterproof base fabric, and I don’t always need 50″ in width like on long trips where I have duffel bags and gear that occupy half of my sleeping platform.

In hindsight, I think I would have preferred the Dually in the Short size, as it would’ve worked in my Prado and I wouldn’t have experienced one issue that I’ll discuss below. I also did not find myself sleeping on the ground as much as I originally anticipated. But I’m not unhappy with the Foamy options, and I think they are more applicable to more people. Regardless, here’s a brief overview of their mattress options, which are all built using the same fundamental memory foam interior.

  • Foamy: waterproof base, single-person size that can be linked to another mattress, adaptable
  • Dually: folds in half for storage, wide enough for two people, less durable but not really meant to be used outside of a vehicle, comes in a multitude of sizes for RTTs, Rivians, GFC campers, etc.
  • Sleep System: an oddball hybrid option that combines the bread-and-butter Hest Mattress with an inflatable base pad. It’s aimed at frontcountry tent and car camping, but not really meant to be carried deep into the backcountry

Sweet Dreams

I sleep really well on this mattress. It is not a complicated product; there isn’t any trick that unlocks some new level of performance. The face fabric, even without a fitted sheet (which Hest does sell), is very comfortable, even on bare skin. Sometimes, when sleeping on an inflatable pad that feels rather plastic-like, it can get a little clammy. The face fabric and interior foam of the Hest solve this completely; I never felt sweaty because of the mattress. I also have not yet found the need to fully wash the covers. I’ve wiped them down heavily with a wet towel, but they still feel as good as the day I received them. The fabric is not as absorbent as cotton and doesn’t feel like it gets dirty as quickly. Regardless, the washable covers are a welcome change compared to having to soap and spray down my previous sleeping pad.

The Foamy is also quiet. There isn’t any crinkling when rolling around. Now that I’m writing this, I’m curious how often I’ve been unknowingly woken up by a crinkly inflatable pad. I can say that most nights on the Hest were uninterrupted sleeps from beginning to end. I felt well rested for whatever the next day had in store. Speaking of which, the small pockets at the head (or foot) of the mattress are secure and easy-to-access spots for my phone, alarm clock, and wallet. Those are all things that I like having in easy-to-reach and secure places that are also not super visible, should I forget to take them with me the next day.

The compression straps, which double as a welcome mat, have also proved handy. I do wish they were larger, but they are sufficiently big as a place to step when removing shoes. I would miss them if they didn’t exist.

It’s not all sweet dreams.

I do have a few small things I would change to the Foamy if given the opportunity, and indeed, I might bust out a needle and thread and do some experimenting. First on my list of fixes would be the joining mechanism to attach a neighboring pad. Though the two clips work, they do occasionally slide apart. The bigger issue is that they don’t tightly sandwich the two pads together. If you roll into the crack, it is noticeable. While I don’t think couples will have this issue so long as each partner sticks to their own pad, I did find it to be an occasional and minor annoyance when using both pads by myself, which was actually the most common configuration I used.

There are some other sleeping pads on the market that do a better job of this; they feature a closure mechanism in the middle, on the corners, and at all locations, a closure on the top layer and bottom layer. This prevents any gap from opening. The Hest Foamy just has two clips that meet halfway up the foam layer. I’m going to try stitching a layer of hook-and-loop closure to the bottom edge of the pad with a removable strip to prevent the pads from separating. I understand why that isn’t an OEM option, as I don’t think it would be the cleanest-looking solution.

I am 70″ tall and find the Foamy Short to be sufficiently long, as I don’t sleep fully extended like a fishing pole; I curl up a little bit like a human. Yet, I don’t fully understand why there is not a 72″ long Foamy option. The standard Foamy is 78″ long. The Foamy Short is 64″ long. The bed platform that I built in my Prado is 72″ long, or 6′. A Toyota Tacoma (somewhat of a litmus test for car/truck focused camping accessories) has a 5-foot or 6-foot bed length, neither of which matches a Hest Foamy very well. The Dually does come in a 72″x60″ size, but that wouldn’t fit in my Prado. Anyways, this isn’t an issue with the product as much as it is a product strategy decision that is beyond my pay grade and outside of my control.

My final gripe is purely subjective: I would love it if these were slightly firmer. I love a very firm mattress. While the plush feel of the Foamy is still very comfortable and helps me sleep like a baby, the conscious version of me that initially lays down always thinks: perhaps firmer? This is the biggest drawback of not having the customizable firmness of an inflatable pad.

Pillow Talk

I have not yet mentioned it and I absolutely should: the Hest Pillows are amazing. They sent me two for this review, and I didn’t think I would love them so much. They are made out of the same outer materials as the mattress but with a different construction. Instead of layers of foam, the filling is shredded foam. You can remove this filling to achieve whatever level of plumpness that your head desires. I did not remove any as I find the stock level to be perfectly comfortable.

The pillow can be turned inside out when not in use to keep it clean, so when it comes time to put your head on it, the interior becomes the outside, and it is the same face fabric as the surface of the mattress. The cover is also removable for washing, like the mattress. I wholeheartedly recommend these pillows, even if you already have a stellar mattress solution in your rig. I’ve even used them at home; I like them so much.

TL;DR

The Hest Foamy is a great solution for camping settings where packability is not a concern. The memory foam construction doesn’t deflate throughout the night but is supportive and comfortable. The face fabrics are durable and comfortable, and can be removed for washing. The pillows, made out of much of the same materials, are just as wonderful. Overall, if you are looking for a car camping setup, I highly recommend perusing the various mattress and pillow options from Hest.

Pros

  • Reliable Comfort that always supported a good night’s sleep
  • Easy-to-live-with features make ownership easy
  • Feels like a premium bedding option in a setting where most people might expect the bare bones

Cons

  • Pad connectors are finicky
  • The size option you most desire might not exist, but there are also tons to choose from
  • Price might dissuade some buyers

See all of the Hest products.

The post Hest Foamy Review: Front Country Comfort appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Silca Makes the Fastest Clog Charms
entry.content:
Silca spent two years on research, prototyping, and wind-tunnel testing to develop the world’s most aerodynamic pair of foam slip-in clogs. Here at The Radavist, we take aerodynamic efficiency seriously. It’s no laughing matter, so please read the important details about the titanium turbulators below.

Titanium Turbulator Quick Hits

  • Sold in packs of three
  • 12.3g of pure titanium speed
  • Manufactured at SILCA HQ, Indianapolis, Indiana.
  • $ 20.00

Aero Clogs

Silca takes marginal gains and performance seriously. After two years of relentless research, prototyping, and wind-tunnel testing, they have developed the most aerodynamic pair of foam slip-in clogs in the world. Leveraging the watt-saving technology of their Aero Socks, they utilized in-house additive manufacturing to build custom titanium turbulators. These are designed to enhance foam clog performance. The titanium turbulators introduce small vortices in the boundary layer that energize the flow and promote flow attachment further around the foot. To celebrate this engineering achievement, we are offering a 3-pack of Silca clog charms.

Each set of three includes one turbulator, one Silca wordmark, and one Silca shield logo.

And yes, sport mode is mandatory.

See the aero titanium turbulator clog charms at Silca.

entry.title: Gravel Adventure Field Guide Releases its New York Guidebook
entry.content:
Gravel Adventure Field Guide just announced its New York Guidebook. The Hudson Valley in New York is one of the most storied regions in the United States. What makes Ulster County a special gravel destination is a blend of rich American history, a pioneering art and environmental movement, a high-quality culinary scene, and dramatic natural landscapes. Plus, it’s located only 90 miles north of New York City. This Ulster County / Hudson Valley Gravel Adventure Field Guide highlights the communities of Kingston, New Paltz, and Woodstock…

A strong foundation and legacy around environmental conservation set the stage for Ulster County to offer some of the most exceptional and diverse gravel riding on the East Coast. The combination of rail trails, historic carriage roads, along with old wood roads and trails, accommodates all types of gravel riding. With over 600 miles of riding, the Ulster County Gravel Adventure Field Guide has something for old roadies or mountain bikers to appreciate.

Highlighting this Ulster County edition are routes that traverse the Shawangunk and Catskill Mountains. Riding out of the community of New Paltz, cyclists access the premier car-less gravel riding on Mohonk Preserve, Minnewaska State Park, and Mohonk House. Meanwhile, the Catskill Mountains offer up some challenging, yet rewarding, adventure riding options. An argument can be made that the Hudson Valley is the Shangri-La of East Coast gravel riding.

The close proximity to New York City and several major East Coast cities makes the Hudson Valley easily accessible for all gravel enthusiasts to explore. Grab a copy of the first Gravel Adventure Field Guide to discover all the great gravel routes and local insights to do an Ulster County visit right.

You can find the Ulster County-Catskills / Hudson Valley New York Gravel Adventure Field Guide at select bike shops listed on the Get One page. If residing outside the distribution zone, you can order one online.

entry.title: Video: One Year With The Trek CheckOUT – Travis Engel
entry.content:
The Trek CheckOUT full-suspension gravel bike has been out for a year now. Travis reviewed one at launch, but he still hasn’t given it back. So, he got on camera to share what he’s learned in the past twelve months. Hopefully it’ll get people riled up about it again.

Normally, I keep a review bike for about five or six weeks before sending it back to the brand. But I talked Trek into letting me hold onto the CheckOUT full-suspension gravel bike for a year. Partly because I wanted to see what kind of nonsense we might get up to, and partly because I just really really like it. Now that the year has come to an end, I’m a little emotional. I’m grateful for the experiences I’ve had on this bike, but I’m grieving that doesn’t seem to have spawned the revolution I hoped it would.

The review I wrote in September of 2025 goes into all the bike’s facts and figures, plus an account of a five-day trans-Rockies I took it on. It’s the best place to start if you’re looking for the “what,” “how,” and “why” behind the CheckOUT. But I wanted to put a more personal touch on my final thoughts on the CheckOUT. So, I decided to stand in front of a camera, and slightly diagonal to another camera, and pour my heart out about this weird machine.

entry.title: Scottish Mixtape Pt. 1
entry.content:
A self-supported mission to link 3 classic cycling routes and 3 peaks in Scotland.

In partnership with Arc’teryx, Moots Cycles, Tailfin, and Skratch Labs.

Words by KYLE RICHARDSON · Photos by THOMAS WOODSON, KYLE RICHARDSON


Exploring a place by bicycle works its way deep into your soul. Once you’ve traveled this way, it becomes your beacon and north star for how you want to explore the world. Taking in the landscape pedal stroke by pedal stroke, you start to learn the fabric of a place. Feeling the weather and terrain isn’t just one aspect of the outing; it becomes your identity and sole purpose for moving. The reward for moving your body all day through a place is knowledge and wisdom, things you can apply towards future trips and life in general.

Scotland is world-renowned for its rugged and beautiful landscape. Its people are hardened by the weather, but their desire for exploration and adventure in the hills is very much alive. There is a deep mystery about this place that is intriguing to me. The craggy tracks and alpine roads cutting through magnificent mountains planted a seed of curiosity. What would it be like to travel through this place simply? On bike and on foot, carving our way through this ancient country. Thus the Scottish Mixtape was born — a fully self-supported mission to link up 3 classic cycling routes and 3 peaks. From Scotland’s capital, Edinburgh, we traveled over the famous highlands, traversed the Cairngorms, and then down the Pictish trail, creating a big, diverse loop.

For the purposes of organization and to showcase this route, I will break the mixtape into 3 separate tracks, each corresponding to the 3 cycling routes we explored.

Filmmaker and photographer Thomas Woodson was alongside me for this Scottish adventure. This wouldn’t be a bike blog without digging into the bikes, and I will touch on setups a bit throughout. Thomas was riding his Moots MXC, and I was on the new Moots Womble, both bikes equipped with front forks and dropper posts for maximum shredding and efficiency. As always, feel free to drop a comment or email if you have more specific questions about setups, and I will include full bike check photos at the bottom. Sit back, grab a tea or a pint, and listen to the play-by-play from the Scottish Mixtape.

   

Track 1: Into the Highlands

Our bodies are stiﬀ and creaky. It’s really 3 am Colorado time as we depart our flight into Scotland's capital, Edinburgh. I think the biggest stressor for a trip like this surrounds traveling with a bike. This topic alone deserves its own blog and write-up. Needless to say, our bikes made it, and soon enough we were building our extremely capable mountain rigs in the crowded airport arrival terminal. Thomas must have snuck some coﬀee in somewhere, because by the time I was getting organized, he was ready to roll. Dang, time to get with it! I was distracted by the bright lights and stream of people passing by.

Handlebars, wheels — straighten it up - wait, tinker again, fix. Okay, is this right? Thomas! “I need help!” Good thing we make a great team. I have been adventuring with Thomas for a decade now. We have traveled to many countries together and mesh super well. Finding a partner that complements you and brings out your best self is a wonderful thing. Outside of being strong in the mountains and competent on technical terrain, Thomas is a logistical wizard and has an everlasting attitude to get things done no matter the circumstances. These are instrumental attributes on a trip with so much uncertainty and the unknown. We have a tight timeline. We need to be back in Edinburgh in 8 days to then catch our flight back to Colorado the following day. Okay, enough of this, time to hit the road!

Moots all built up at Edinburgh International Airport

In classic Scottish style, as we roll away from the hustle and bustle of the airport, the skies open up. The wind picks up in a fury, and we put on our rain gear. This would be the first of a long trip- a long process of navigating and handling the weather. Under my hood and amidst the rain, I crack a smile and let out a giddy laugh. This is why we are here. To experience the full spectrum of conditions and emotions of traveling through a new place. Our first day of riding would almost exclusively be on canal and bike paths; what a treat! One of my goals for this trip was to get oﬀ the main roads and into the magic of a place. And by magic, I mean all the sneaky little roads that take you to the heart of place rather than around it. As we worked our way towards Callander, we got to experience the canal boats and farm lifestyle that make up this part of the country. Riding through tunnels and lush forest, we sneak glances at quaint villages and ancient cobblestone paths. At one point during another wave of rain, we pass by a school. It was clearly lunch break, and all the teens were out walking towards their favorite hangouts. In the pouring rain, we noticed that no one was wearing raincoats. Huh. Are we doing this wrong? Rain and being wet is a way of life in Scotland; not much fuss about the weather. Go do your thing and get on with it!

By this point in the day, we had linked into the famous GBDURO (Great Britain Divide), a cycling route that covers the entire length of Great Britain. We would use this route to help carry us North. We traversed our first fields of Scottish livestock and enjoyed varied riding on all types of surfaces. Our bodies still on Colorado time, we visualized and dreamed about our first proper. Bopping and weaving around more farms, we could see our first stopping point of the night in Callander. A beautiful little village right on the edge of the highlands. We had booked a night at the Crown Inn, knowing that a real night's sleep in a bed would help set us up for a successful trip. Thomas and I love to play games, but when it comes to bikepacking, we generally adhere to a few basic rules and let the rest go with the flow. We see what the land and weather give us. This trip wasn’t about how hard and brutal can we make things; it's about the full-body and mind immersion into a landscape. We have our notepads out and want to learn and grow from this place. Students of the world traveling by bike.

One of the beautiful things about Scotland is how popular and welcoming the people are to bikes. People tour here on bikes, and it's not a new thing. You won’t get any strange or random looks. You will get chirps of encouragement and curiosity. The hotel staﬀ and BnB hosts will welcome your dirty bikes and bike shoes and have a safe place to store that stuﬀ, either in your room or a dedicated indoor bike shelter. I think this way of life helps cut the tension and edge that one can have while traveling in a new place, especially when your body is depleted after a hard day of pedaling. After sorting ourselves in our lodging, we slipped on our running shoes and headed out to the streets of Callander for some fish and chips. Thomas and I exchanged stories from the day as the native language and tongue echoed through the dining hall. Mates bantered about golf and what pint to drink next; we quietly observed our surroundings as our new reality for the next week set in. With our bellies full, we enjoyed some sunset light while strolling down the River Teith. It was a hectic and full-on first day in Scotland. Time to dry out our clothes and get some rest.

Moots arriving in Callander Day 1


Alarms chirping at 5:45 am, the hot water kettle starts bubbling, and we tear open our instant craft coﬀee from Idle Hands Roasting. The little morning treat that brought us energy and psyche every day. Thanks to Peter Jones for the full trip supply! Skies were grey and overcast, with mild temps. After hunting down some classic Scottish pastries and goodies down the street, it was time to set oﬀ. Our day would start oﬀ following the GBDURO to the small town of Killin, before branching oﬀ towards the mega-classic West Highland Way — (Scotland’s premier long-distance walking route, stretching 96 miles (154 km) from Milngavie (just north of Glasgow) to Fort William in the Scottish Highlands).

A misty collection of clouds started to form as we made our way north along bike paths, contouring lochs and villages. It felt special and unique to be on such fantastic bike infrastructure, tucked away in the woods. After a couple of hours of spinning, we reached a tiny pass, and the skies started to open up. As we stopped, we came to our first interaction with the famous Scottish midges. Tiny microscopic flies, coordinating in unison and buzzing towards their next victim. I could feel their wrath as we stopped to put on our rain jackets and pants. Maybe it's better if it's raining? At least then the midges subside. More to come on that later. As we buzzed down to the town of Killin, we had our first proper feeling of being completely saturated with water. My giddy smile and laugh from the day before started to flatten.

Thomas Woodson on film above Loch Lyon


In the town of Killin, we rushed towards the first cafe in sight. Was this a storm that would pass, or something that was hugging the mountains and would be around all day? Only time would tell. No use looking a weather app or forecast, it was unreliable and inaccurate. In classic Scottish style, we ordered a few breakfast teas and some toasties (basically a grilled cheese with a sweet chutney). Thomas and I slipped out of our wet cycling shoes and air-dried our feet discreetly under our table. As we were eating, a pair of cyclists showed up in similar fashion. Good reminder that this is totally normal and what we were doing wasn’t anything extraordinary. They were from Poland on a similar grand adventure (albeit on gravel bikes) out taking in the wonderful countryside.

For us, it is always encouraging and enjoyable to chat with folks along the way and feed oﬀ the energy of a place. Our new Polish cyclist friends seemed to have a determined edge, and we ended up sharing a similar route for a few miles. As we hit some steep grades, I think they started to grow jealous of our mountain bikes and gearing. As we soft-pedaled up our first real mountain pass, I was grateful for our setups and the terrain we were about to encounter. While never truly quitting, the rain turned more into a soft mist, which is far more favorable than a straight downpour. Our views were limited at the top of this pass, but I could tell we were on the cusp of getting into the good stuﬀ. Remote, wild, and properly in the highlands.

As we traveled around the south side of Loch Lyon, we rode premier double track. The kind of tracks I dreamed about, my inspiration for putting this whole trip together. Riding the right bikes, with the right person, everything was falling into place. Steep grassy hillsides, sheep, Highland Coos, countless river crossings- this section really had it all. Quintessential Scottish riding. Beams of sun would occasionally pop out and highlight a magnificent hillside. My giddy smile and laugh returned. Thomas was on the same page, and we hooted and hollered around each bend. Finally able to let loose and ride our mountain rigs with some flair. Being out in the wild, tucked in the mountains, felt like being home in Colorado. This is where Thomas and I thrive. At the end of this double track segment, we started a long downhill towards Kinglass Cottage and the West Highland Way. It was pretty obvious once we were on the WHW, as we immediately started passing thru-hikers. As we traversed the hillside, we set our sights on our next pitstop: Bridge of Orchy.

In classic logistical Thomas style, he had found a semi-secret stop for dinner, just a ways past Bridge of Orchy. He had made a call during lunch to set up a dinner reservation. We planned to stop in Orchy, grab a pint, then roll down the road for dinner plans. After dinner, we would continue on the WHW and find camp somewhere. I think trips like this require you to act fast and think on your toes. No one decision is ever that hyper critical, but make a decision and then go with it. I think having a good partner helps this process. Sometimes it's easy to get lured into a resupply or waste time. Finding the balance between riding the flow and making calculated decisions is the game. On this Day 2, we played our cards right and were rewarded with a fantastic day of quality and diverse riding. At dinner, we enjoyed one of our best meals. Sometimes best on a trip like this equals quantity, but at this fine establishment, we were treated with massive portions and delicious food. We even had a first tasting of some local whiskey. Felt rude not to sample!

Throughout the day, we had heard rumbles of evening and overnight torrential rain. Let me skip to the chase. Yup, that happened. We ended up riding maybe 3 miles to one of the few clusters of dense trees in the area. All of the Highlands is barren due to centuries of deforestation. Which means finding a good bivy site that is protected is tough. I think most locals would have laughed at our sleep setup, but I think I still stand behind it. Between us, we shared a flat tarp and ground sheet. Individually, we each had sleeping pads, bags, and bug nets. It appeared most people camped out in the open with proper enclosed tents. Hmmm. So we were oﬀ into the dense woods and mossy floor for a tucked-away bivy. I like feeling cozy even if it has its downsides. An exposed tent out in the open just feels wrong, especially on a night forecasting torrential rain and high winds.

Sleep was on and oﬀ. Out of the whole trip, this was one of the harder moments. The rain was persistent and loud against the Dyneema tarp. I also don’t want to gloss over the fact that just a couple of hours earlier, I was being eaten alive by midges. It was the Scottish gods (and maybe Thomas) seeking sweet revenge on my trip and idea. Making sure you never walk away unscathed, gathering a few lessons to learn along the way. In some aspects, the heavy rain eased my tension and pain. As we would come to find out later on Day 3, which proved to be one of the grandest and hardest day yet. Despite the rough night, we still had the energy and stoke to keep pushing. Waking up in the mist, Thomas and I remarked back and forth how intense that was.

morning wakeup ritual with Idle Hands Instant coﬀee


Moots on the West Highland Way


Awake and caﬀeinated by morning cold brew in a running soft flask, a few bites of something go into the body (not to mention the bites I was nursing on my body). We pack our wet bikes and gear inside fully waterproof Tailfin bike bags, proving their weight in gold. For me, I think it was seeing the sun that morning. It provided me the internal stoke and confidence to complete this trip. The light and scenery were otherworldly and magical. Entering the Glencoe valley was what dreams are made of. Giant peaks and ridges in all directions. We stopped for breakfast at one of the few ski resorts in Scotland, the famous Glencoe Hill. Full Scottish breakfast and coﬀee for me, please. The midge welts on my face and arms burned and itched. This felt like a warm trap to stay here all day, and I’m glad we were both motivated and stoked to keep the pace up.

Back on the bikes, feeling small. Coming around the corner, seeing Buachaille Etive Mòr (Stob Dearg) is a top 3 moment of the trip for me. This perfect pyramid, erupting out of the earth, was visually too perfect. How could something like this even exist? It was full steam ahead to our next objective, our first scramble of the trip, Curved Ridge. I first heard about this route when I saw an iconic photo of Kilian Jornet Burgada scrambling up Curved Ridge during his 2017 win at Glen Coe Skyline. Ever since then, it’s been on my tick list. One of the anchors of this project was to link 3 technically interesting running and scrambling routes in Scotland. Curved Ridge proved to be indeed a mega classic. As Thomas and I approached this massive pyramid of a peak, we could see a series of twisting ridges jutting up towards the summit. Clouds were swirling and rays of sun stabbed through the sky. It was now or never. As we approached the trailhead, the scale of this mountain started to introduce itself. We stashed our bikes against a climbing school hut, switched into our running kit, and set oﬀ. I’m always full of stoke and excitement when switching to running oﬀ the bike. The legs feel wonderful with a new motion, fresh to carry us up the peak.

Starting up the iconic Curved Ridge


Curved Ridge was everything you could ask for. Exposed, steep, airy, with wonderfully solid rock. As we ascended higher and higher into the clouds, the moves got more interesting. Culminating in a steep crux with plentiful holds and jams, Thomas and I motored our way up this aesthetic feature as a light mist set in. The view of the valley floor as we climbed up seemed mystically low and far away. As we reached the summit, the perspective we were rewarded with was hard to describe. That sweet satisfaction after biking for 2.5 days and lots of hills; the trip and vision were all coming together. After a few summit photos, the clouds swallowed us up, and the wind said hello. Okay, time to get oﬀ this thing! Running back down was a techy treat, practicing some quick footwork to navigate many a slippery rock and chunky talus. When it was all said and done, despite feeling like a full day's adventure, we were back at the bikes in 2 hours. Plenty more time for adventure and progression in the day.

Back into bike shoes, we grabbed our rigs and crossed the road. Next up was the most infamous section of the West Highland Way: Devils Staircase. From the summit of Stob Dearg, we could see the Staircase. Coming from Colorado, Thomas and I are accustomed to hike-a-bike (HAB). Some of our favorite local rides include HAB. I’m on record saying multiple times that all good adventure rides need to have some HAB. Despite the hype, Devils Staircase made us feel at home. No big deal really, maybe 30 minutes of pushing at the most? Come on! That is light work for us, even after a 2-hour run. The thing that challenged us really in this section was the weather. It was raining pretty hard for the rest of our day. Towards the bottom of the Staircase, Thomas had a rear tire slash while riding over one of the many water bars that line this climb. If my memory is correct, this was the only bike mechanical issue we encountered all trip. One of the benefits of doing a trip like this with a partner is that bike mechanicals and problems are so much easier to solve as a team, especially when the weather is bad. Couple plugs, add some air, back on the trail!

We made fun work of that climb, hiking with our heavy rigs past many thru-hikers. Showing them who is boss. At the top of the pass, we then proceeded to encounter our gnarliest true MTB terrain of the whole trip. Rowdy riding and chunky terrain. It was a brake-squealing, arm-pumping descent down to Kinlochleven. We were reminded once again that our bike choice was 10/10. I was thinking to myself that if I had been on my fully rigid ESC, I would have walked that entire descent. The trip would have been nearly impossible and stupid on that bike. Hardtail mountain bikes for the win!

In Kinlochleven, Thomas and I hit the local grocery store for some orange soda and a bag of chips. Something on the lighter side to fuel us over the next pass to Fort William. In some ways, I think we both thought our day was close to ending; little did we know we had some brutal climbing and weather to contest with. Oh, and some really rough and muddy tracks. The day was starting to add up. Waking up in our wet bivy spot just some hours earlier felt like a lifetime ago. Eventually we made our way up a steep mixed-surface climb and started a long gradual service road to a small pass that gave way towards Fort William. The riding here was tough and tedious. Our progress slowed, and our motivation waned. As we battled into a headwind, we eventually hit our last steep climb before ripping down to Fort William. Town was a bit of a blur for both of us. I remember stopping at a bike shop, and Thomas pleaded for a hose. Our bikes were filthy and covered in all types of mud and manure. The rain started and stopped. Thomas had booked us luxurious accommodations down the road that included a full sauna/steam situation. Felt like we had earned that, and with how the weather was acting and our current location, sleeping inside felt like a no-brainer. When I think back to planning and dreaming up this trip, it was a day like this that really lit the spark. Interesting riding, run/scramble up an incredible peak, get back on the bike and do it all again. It was only the night of Day 3; Thomas and I were getting our full value experience I was grateful for how it was panning out.

Stay tuned for Track 2: Cairngorm Traverse

Moots Womble (Kyle)


Moots MXC (Thomas)

entry.title: Pivot Announces Its New Road Bike: Pivot Pravia
entry.content:
Pivot Cycles introduces the all-new Pravia, a World Tour-inspired road bike engineered to deliver race-level speed, efficiency and handling in a position riders can sustain beyond the opening miles.

Pivot Pravia Quick Hits

  • Clearance:
    • 700x38mm 2x
    • 70x40mm 1X
    • Spec 700x32mm
  • Hidden fender mounts
  • UDH
  • Not compatible with mechanical groups
  • Front Derailleur mount fits upto 50t
    • Long FD mounts available for 52t+
  • Toolshed in-frame storage (two bags included)
  • Proprietary D shaped seatpost
  • T47 bottom bracket
  • Builds:
    • Team Red AXS $11,999.00
    • Pro Force AXS $8,499.00
    • Ride Rival AXS $5,999.00
    • Frameset $4,599.oo
  • Colors: Purple Prism, Stealth Black Gloss

Built to turn every watt into forward momentum, Pravia features a carbon frame engineered using Finite Element Analysis and Pivot’s Hollow Core Molding process. Modern tube shaping reduces drag, while Pro Tour-level bottom bracket stiffness delivers immediate acceleration and efficient power transfer. A custom tapered aero fork balances sprint-ready stiffness with compliance. Pivot’s proprietary Ride Tuning ensures every frame size receives its own tuned shapes and carbon layup, creating consistent ride quality and handling across the complete size range.

Pravia pairs that race-level stiffness and handling with geometry designed around real riders and the positions they can actually sustain. Because speed is not just about how aero you can get for five minutes. It is about how fast you can still ride after two, three or five hours. A proprietary D-shaped seatpost adds aerodynamic efficiency and tuned compliance, while clearance for up to 700x38c tires in 2x configurations and 700x40c in 1x gives riders more freedom to match the bike to the roads they ride. Integrated in-frame storage keeps ride essentials cleanly inside the frame, eliminating the need to strap bags or gear to the bike and helping maintain its aerodynamic profile.

Three race-ready builds, Team, Pro and Ride, bring the Pravia platform to riders with performance-focused specifications throughout the range. All builds feature carbon wheels and power meters, while the Team and Pro models receive an integrated one-piece bar and stem with the rider selecting their preferred size at the time of order. A frameset option is also available.

Find out more at Pivot.

entry.title: Prevelo Zulu One Review: A Real Mountain Bike for My Four-Year-Old – Miguel Ovalles
entry.content:
As Miguel’s kids grow older, he’s been intrigued by the kids’ bike options on the market, which led him to try the Prevelo Zulu One…

When Prevelo offered me a Zulu One for my oldest, Roman, I jumped on the opportunity. He had just turned three and wasn’t on a pedal bike yet, but he was shredding his balance bike, and I’d been dreaming of the day he could ride with me since before he could walk.

When he first saw the Zulu, he immediately pointed out that he was finally going to be able to keep up with me now. That was all the motivation he needed.

Roman is now four and a half, and the Zulu One has been ridden, crashed, dropped, pushed up hills, and generally treated the way a kid treats a bike. It’s still going strong, and after watching him learn on it, I think I understand why.

Prevelo Zulu One Quick Hits

  • Frame/fork: 6061 aluminum, low-CG trail geometry; bladed aluminum fork, 1⅛” aluminum steerer
  • Wheels/tires: 14″ aluminum, sealed-bearing hubs / Kenda Booster 14 x 2.2″
  • Brakes: Front + rear Promax DSK 940 hydraulic disc, kid-sized short-reach levers
  • Drivetrain: Singlespeed freewheel, 18t chainring / 10t cog, 3.765 gear ratio
  • Cranks: Aluminum 3-piece, 85mm, narrow 146mm Q-factor
  • Weight: 13.5 lb
  • Fits: 14–17″ inseam; saddle height 15.5″–25.2″ (ships with tall + short posts)
  • Price: $649

Learning to Pedal

The Zulu One comes with meaty Kenda Booster 14 x 2.2” tires, which I immediately loved. They’re wide, grippy, and have performed great on pretty much every surface Roman has ridden them on, dirt especially. It also comes with hydraulic disc brakes, which I thought was overkill on a 14-inch bike.

We’ll get to that.

The learning curve took a little longer than I expected, and honestly, most of that was my fault. Roman kept defaulting to his balance bike because he was so comfortable on it. He could shred on that thing, and he was having fun.

That’s the thing that balance bikes get right. Training wheels teach a kid to pedal, but never teach them to balance. Balance bikes completely changed that progression and start with the hard part. Roman already had the balance and the confidence; he just hadn’t found his pedal stroke.

When we went to Stillwater for the Mega MidSouth, something finally clicked. We stopped in at District Cycles, where Roman latched onto an old metal Trek tricycle that’s surely been long discontinued. He would not get off that thing, pedaling it into new bikes and shelves while I followed him to make sure he didn’t take anything out. After what felt like hours, I had a good feeling. He’d found the pedal motion.

Back home, we went outside to the walking trail that cuts through our neighborhood. Five minutes later, he went from tentative pedal strokes to full gas, singing and laughing to himself and having so much fun.

Credit to Prevelo here for the low bottom bracket. Roman could get his feet down easily, so he wasn’t afraid of falling. It gave him the confidence to actually ride the bike instead of worrying about what would happen if he lost his balance. Once the pedals made sense to him, he was gone.

A Real Mountain Bike

One of the things I like most about the Zulu One is that Prevelo didn’t just make a smaller version of an adult bike. It’s designed from the ground up around how kids actually ride.

The bike weighs 13.5 pounds, which is not nothing for a little kid, and weight matters when you’re learning. Kids fall a lot, and having a heavy bike fall on top of them can make an already frustrating experience even harder.

Roman also spends a lot of time pushing the bike up the steep hills around our neighborhood in Santa Fe. Even with the great gear ratio Prevelo gives the bike, there are some hills he just hasn’t conquered yet.

The lightweight alloy frame makes that experience much more pleasant.

He has the strength to move the bike around himself, pick it up when he falls, and push it up the hills without the bike completely overwhelming him.

Metal is the Way

As most of you know, I race metal bikes, and I want the same for my kids. So the first question I asked wasn’t really a question about this bike, but the one I ask about every bike: which metal?

Titanium was out in price, leaving steel and aluminum. Roman had a steel pedal bike that felt incredibly sturdy (I once watched a 40-year-old man ride that little bike around a shop with no problem), but that toughness came with weight.

For a kid just learning to ride, I think weight matters more than we sometimes realize.

The Zulu One’s alloy frame strikes a nice balance. It’s light enough for Roman to handle on his own but still feels like it performs like a proper bike rather than a toy. Its lightness hasn’t cost a thing in durability.

Low Bottom Bracket and Short Cranks

These aren’t things a four-year-old is going to tell you are important, but this is where you can really tell that Prevelo is a company focused on kids.

The low bottom bracket keeps him close to the ground and confident, while the short 85 mm cranks fit his legs and let him build a natural pedal stroke. Prevelo also uses a narrow Q-factor, which is something I don’t think gets enough attention on kids’ bikes.

Big brands tend to do the bare minimum when it comes to adapting adult parts down to little riders. Prevelo is a dedicated young-riders brand, and that shows in the details and when Roman rides. His pedal stroke is cleaner than a few pros I’ve watched on TV. ;)

Hydraulic Brakes on a Kids Bike

You don’t see hydraulic brakes on a 14-inch bike very often. I didn’t even notice it until a friend pointed it out.

I questioned if a four-year-old needed that much stopping power, and I definitely got brake-checked super hard during the first ten rides we did together.

The short levers are reach-adjustable, which means his little hands can actually reach and pull them. He now modulates them with a finesse that surprises me, metering his speed down steep stuff and when we’re crossing streets, I have the peace of mind that he can stop quickly if he needs to.

Maybe hydraulic brakes are overkill on a 14-inch kids bike, but after the last year with them, I’m not sure I’d want to go back.

Do Kids Need a 14-Inch Bike?

For as long as I can remember, the 16-inch bike has been the standard “first pedal bike” for kids. So why create a 14?

I honestly don’t know the history behind it, but I have a theory. Balance bikes have completely changed the way kids learn to ride. Kids, including mine, are ripping balance bikes on pump tracks at two years old. They learn to balance before even thinking about pedaling, and thus arrive at pedaling far earlier and smaller than they used to.

The 14-inch bike fills the gap between the balance bike and the traditional 16-inch first pedal bike for kids two to four years old who already know how to balance and are ready to start pedaling.

The Zulu One is small enough that the transition doesn’t feel intimidating. It wasn’t much bigger than the balance bike he already trusted, so getting on it didn’t feel like starting from scratch, but felt like the next step.

The Wheel Size

There is one downside to building a bike around a less-common wheel size: finding parts.

Fourteen-inch, 2.2” tubes are hard to find, and thorn-resistant ones are harder. We live in goathead country, so thorn-resistant tubes are preferred. Most of what I could find locally was for skinny 1.75” tires. Prevelo does sell replacement tubes, and at the time of writing this review, they are in stock. But that hasn’t always been the case, and they’re also not thorn-resistant.

Then there’s the valve. The bike comes with Presta valves, which I think is an odd choice for a kid’s bike. I set out to find a 14-inch, 2.25”, thorn-resistant tube with a Presta valve and almost lost my mind.

The fix. Eventually, I decided to stop looking for the perfect tube and change the bike instead. My local mechanic was very nonchalant about it. “Just make the holes bigger.”

So that’s what we did. We drilled out the valve holes to run Schrader valves, and suddenly my tube options opened up. We’ve been running thorn-resistant Schrader tubes ever since. They’re a bit small for those big tires, but so far they’ve held up really well, and after spending way too much time patching tubes, it was a simple fix that made the bike much easier to live with in New Mexico.

Is It Worth Twice the Price?

This is the real question. At (649$), THE Zulu One runs roughly double what a comparable first pedal bike from a big brand would (for example, a $300 Woom or Trek Precaliber). That’s a lot of money for something a kid outgrows.

I don’t know if I can say that the Zulu One is twice as good, but I do think the things Prevelo spends money on are the right ones for my kids: geometry designed for little ones, a low bottom bracket, short cranks and the narrow Q-factor, serious brakes, grippy tires, and a frame that can take the abuse.

Most importantly, Roman wants to ride it.

Prevelo Zulu One: The Verdict

I don’t think of the Prevelo Zulu One as a kids’ bike. It’s just a mountain bike that happens to be really small, which is exactly the point.

Roman went from a balance bike to full gas in an afternoon, with the Prevelo giving him that platform. His feet were down when he needed them, it was light enough for him to handle himself, the tires made him feel confident on the dirt, and the geometry was built for his body. The only real downside has been living with a 14-inch wheel in the land of goatheads, and even that had a relatively easy fix.

I would buy this bike again and again. Not because a four-year-old needs fancy components, but because a bike that fits a kid properly changes their entire experience of learning how to ride.

I ride bikes because of how the right bike can make me feel. After watching Roman crush our neighborhood trails, rip pump tracks, and laugh the entire time, I’m just glad I got to give him the same experience early.

See more at Prevelo.

The post Prevelo Zulu One Review: A Real Mountain Bike for My Four-Year-Old appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Hudski Dualist Adds Sram NX Complete and New Colors
entry.content:
Hudski has an all-new entry-level build kit utilizing SRAM’s NX group that makes the versatile Dualist ($2,199 complete) more accessible, alongside three new fresh frameset colors and a long-awaited restock of size large…

Hudski Bikes is expanding its Dualist lineup with the introduction of the new SRAM Dualist, a more accessible entry point into the brand’s versatile all-terrain platform. The build consists of a mix of NX and SX components, a Transx dropper, and tubeless-ready Vittoria Mexcal 29×2.35” tires. The release also brings two new frameset color options and the return of size large, which has been out of stock for several months.

Designed to make the Dualist experience available to more riders, the new SRAM build delivers the same thoughtfully engineered frame, progressive geometry, and all-terrain capability as the rest of the lineup at a more approachable price.

Built around Hudski’s philosophy that one bike should be capable of doing more, the Dualist blurs the lines between gravel, mountain, and everyday riding. Its mountain bike-inspired geometry, generous tire clearance, and durable construction create a platform that’s equally at home on dirt trails, gravel roads, and city streets. The new SRAM build retains the defining characteristics of the Dualist while offering a straightforward, dependable component package for riders looking to get into the Hudski lineup without compromising on the bike’s core capabilities.

Check out a full review of the Dualist in our Archives and be sure to read our Shop Visit to the Marin-based brand as well.

See more at Hudski.
