entry.title: The Circles Japan RAL Exposure is a 26″ Rim Brake ATB – John Watson
entry.content:
Cari and John stayed in Japan after the Bespoked Osaka show and have been hanging out with the Circles fam in Nagoya. While there, he documented the newest product from Circles’ in-house outdoor brand, Ride Alive, or RAL for short. The RAL Exposure is a 26″ steel rim brake ATB, designed for commuting and mixed terrain riding. Let’s check out this $500 frameset below!

Circles is a shop based in Nagoya, Japan. Ten years ago, I did an in-depth Shop Visit on the multi-faceted culture surrounding the bike shop, including its brands Sim Works and RAL, or Ride Alive. Since it’s both The Radavist’s and Circles’ 20th anniversary, boss man Shinya flew Cari and me out to document the Bespoked show and to check out what Circles has been up to over the past ten years.

The short answer is a lot. So much that you’ll have to wait to see the updates, but I wanted to share something special from RAL today.

RAL Exposure Quick Hits

  • ~$500 frameset (varies due to currency conversion)
  • Made in Taiwan by Maxway
  • Three Sizes: S, M, L
  • Rim brake only
  • Single-speed optimized, but modular dropout design allows for a derailleur hanger
  • Gray Card paint color
  • 26 x 2.6″ clearance
  • Fender mounts
  • 1 1/8″ steerer
  • BSA BB

Circles Customer

After a week of Bespoked Osaka coverage and all the high-end custom bikes from the show, it felt fitting to share a $500 frameset. Japanese bicycle commuting culture is primarily mamachari bikes. Cruisers with low saddles, baskets, racks, and a kid’s seat. Other than that, most people just ride their road or gravel bikes to work.

In the previous decade, vintage mountain bikes have become popular in Japan. Customers of Circles will build them into commuters and campers, designed to haul work items during the week and camping stuff on the weekends. An increasing number of Circles customers have gotten interested in the post-performance cycling space and have requested a more affordable bike than the Sim Works Doppo line.

The problem with vintage mountain bikes is they don’t fit a big tire, and it’s sometimes hard to find the right size for a rider. This prompted Shinya and Masashi from Circles and RAL to design a bicycle for entry-level riders, inspired by vintage mountain bikes.

Exposure Model

This new bike, dubbed the RAL Exposure, named after photography exposure, is a simple, 26″ wheeled, rim-braked, single-speed commuter, designed for fenders, racks, a 1 1/8″ steerer, but with clearance for 2.6″ tires. It comes in Gray Card grey, a template used to establish the correct white balance in photography, and has replaceable single-speed dropouts that can be adapted to use a derailleur hanger as well.

Most of the RAL Exposures being built by Circles are flat bar and single-speed, but they have built a few drop-bar bikes as well as a number of bikes with gears. To keep the price point low, the Exposure frame is made in Taiwan by Maxway, and it lacks any cable guides for a rear mech. These frames are more robust than the 1″ quill bikes of the 1980s and have clean, elegant lines. Shinya and Masashi’s eye for design shines through in such a simple chassis.

Ryoma’s RAL Exposure

I photographed Ryoma Nakamoto’s personal single-speed, flat bar Exposure as well as a drop-bar build spec for the Circles showroom floor. Ryoma is an engineer at Sim Works, but he started in the shipping and distribution department while he was in school.

He built his up for commuting – fenders coming now that the rainy season is here – with used components. He splurged on nice Sim Works Homage tires, custom Sim Works Standalone rims, laced to Deore hubs and Hunter Smooth Move handlebars. With a Sim Works Sim Heads headset.

Dirt Drop Exposure

For the drop-bar option, Circles poached a drivetrain from Masashi’s MB-1 and utilized a Velo Orange Cigne stem to get the bars nice and high, just like a legit dirt drop bike from the 1980s. The RAL H2O Saddle is a throwback to 1980s designs. A Rivendell Silver shifter is mounted to the drop bar clamp area to shift the mech. Because Circles wanted to keep the bike as simple and as affordable as possible, there are no cable guides for a derailleur, but you can use any number of aftermarket clamps or zip ties to run the cables.

Affordable but Not Heavy

What was most shocking to me was how light the frame is. I was expecting it to be a heavy bike, but it was surprisingly light. It comes in sub-5 lbs for the largest size, or around 2,240 grams for the frame and 1,110 g (2.4 lbs) for the fork. All for around $500 USD for a frame and fork.

Circles in Japan has these frames, which they will ship internationally, and Sim Works USA should be stocking them soon, too.

Arigato to Shinya, Masashi, Ryoma, and the Circles fam for having us in Nagoya! More to come…

Check out more at Circles.

The post The Circles Japan RAL Exposure is a 26″ Rim Brake ATB appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Garmin Bringing Edge 1060 Features to Older Units: Full Details!
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

When Garmin announced the Edge 1060, they noted that the majority of features would come to existing Edge x50 series devices (Edge 550/850/1050), as well as a handful of features going to older x40 series devices (Edge 540/840/1040/1040 Solar). Heck, even the Edge MTB gets new tricks too.

The good news is that we don’t have to wait long, at least for some of the new features. Garmin has already started rolling out a portion of the new features in public beta, and I’ve got an outline for all the remaining features and which devices are getting what.

Which Features Go To Which Units:

Now, in my Edge 1060 post I explain all the new features in a bit more detail, but in short, these are the key software features that can be ported back (voice features like voice control and voice messaging require a microphone, which simply isn’t in older Garmin Edge hardware). Here’s what we’re looking at:

Strava Live Segment Updates: This essentially has three components to it. The first is allowing for collapsible portions within the Strava Live Segment page (e.g., resizing the different chunks, or getting rid of certain ones). Next, you can now see competitor icons on the map & elevation profiles (e.g. KOM position). And finally – the biggie, you can now do Strava Live Segments on *any* route (previously it was just Strava Routes). [Coming to Edge x50 & Edge MTB in Q1 2027]

Structured Workout Page Updates: Seen above, this allows for collapsible portions of the workout page, just like with the Strava Live Segment page above. [Coming to Edge x50 & Edge MTB in Q1 2027]

Alternate Data Fields: This allows you to specify alternate/secondary data fields for any sensor data field, if that sensor isn’t available. For example, you have power data fields in your data pages, but then ride a bike without power, this will let you swap out that data field for anything else you want (e.g. calories). Same goes for navigation-related data fields (like distance to end of course) if not riding a course. [Now available to Edge x50 & Edge MTB in Q4 public beta]

GroupRide Advertising Capability: This will automatically prompt you to create a GroupRide if it detects other Garmin Edge devices near you at the start of a ride. Think of it like AirDrop contact sharing for the Peloton, except to start a group session. This feature is optionally enabled, but makes it silly-easy to start a GroupRide, versus the messier past. [Now available to Edge x40, Edge x50 & Edge MTB in Q4 public beta]

Hazards & Road Closures: This is an extension to the community reporting page for hazards (such as potholes and such) that now allows for reporting and seeing road closures. [Coming to Edge x40, Edge x50 & Edge MTB in Q1 2027]

Garmin Messenger Support: This will add support for the Edge unit to see messages coming in from Garmin Messenger, including even playing those messages back on devices with a proper speaker (Edge 850/1050). You can also send text messages from all units (including quick replies). Finally, it also allows your Edge unit to participate in Garmin Locate, which is vaguely like a FindMy feature. [Now available to Edge x50 & Edge MTB in Q4 public beta]

Garmin Link: If you have a Garmin wearable, this will make the heart rate broadcasting feature a bit more seamless – automatically starting that broadcast on your wearable (if enabled), rather than having to futz around and end up with either dual recordings or manually remembering each time. My wife will very much appreciate this (assuming she remembers to charge her watch). This is actually not yet on the Edge 1060. [Coming to Edge 1060, Edge x50 & Edge MTB in Q1 2027]

There are also two features coming via Garmin Connect to Edge x40/x50/1060/Edge Explore 3 users that aren’t dependent on firmware on the unit itself. These roll out Tuesday, November 3rd to all users. They are:

Android Google Maps Support: For Android users, you can now send a pin/shared location from Google Maps straight to your Edge (via Garmin Connect app). iPhone users have been able to do this for a long while with Apple Maps instead.

Garmin Coaching Challenger Plans: Historically, Garmin coach cycling plans have required a power meter, these do not. They are going to all Edge x40/x50/MTB/etc users.

When it comes to a few features not going back to existing units, it’s essentially one bucket of map-specific features. I’ve broken them down as follows (I’ve covered both of these in my Edge 1060 post, and also show them in the video above towards the back half of the video):

Course hazard and closures preview page: When you load up a course on the unit, this shows expected hazards and road closures on the course page, like below.

Route Options (for routing): When creating a route on the unit (either point-to-point, or round-trip), this will add a small elevation profile at the top, as well as calculate the estimated time, and show total ascent and distance (all in tiny consolidated screen).

Up Ahead POI: This shows nearby/upcoming points of interest (POI) on your planned route as you ride, within the two categories you specify (e.g., cafes, or toilets, or a bunch of others). Further, there’s also a general page to see nearby/nearest POI even without a route loaded.

FreeFlow Routing: This offers routes that have less stop & go bits (e.g., fewer traffic lights or other traffic-induced slowness).

QWERTY Keyboard & Predictive Text: This adds a new Qwerty keyboard option, as well as type-ahead predictive text when doing things like typing an address into the unit.

Ride Readiness Checklist Page: This is a bit of a redesigned UI element that shows a checklist of things to ensure are how you want them, like sensor status and more.

Carbon Savings: This will show your carbon savings from a bike commute/ride. It is not a calculator to determine how much of your savings you need for that new carbon bike.

Got all that? Good.

Going Forward:

Both the Edge 1060 launch and the Garmin Fenix 9 launch represent a clear turning point for Garmin in how they deal with older unit software updates. Prior to these launches, Garmin generally speaking left behind the prior generation units. In the case of the Edge 1050 two years ago, Garmin did do a better job at bringing features of the x40 series for quite some time (because they felt as though the Edge 1040 Solar was still a cohesive part of their longer-battery life offerings).

In the case of both the Fenix 9 and the Edge 1060, the rough line in the sand here appears to be tied to mapping and navigation-related features. In the case of the Fenix 9, this was because Garmin said a new processor and increased RAM were needed for the new mapping engine. They didn’t say that was the case here, but appeared to sorta meet halfway on things for x50 users. For x40 users, there are a few quality-of-life enhancements. For competitive context, Wahoo has essentially ditched all non-V3 bike computers for new features since launching those. COROS just launched the Dura 2 last week, and the future of the Dura 1 software updates seems somewhat mixed (my gut says it’ll be similar to what Garmin is doing here).

Either way, it’s good to see this shift in thinking – and I hope it continues to other product groups.

Thanks for reading!

entry.title: Readers’ Rides: Kyle from Outer Shell’s Pop Punk Mall Goth Indy Fab
entry.content:
Hot Topic. Eyeliner. Checkerboard. Kyle from Outer Shell pulled together one sweet Indy Fab with a goth girl theme straight from the mall for this week’s Readers’ Rides…

When I saw the stars on this bike, I had stars in my eyes. The black-to-grey fade and spooky font are so cool and brought me back to growing up at the mall in 7th grade.

We all wanted to look cool cause that made us feel cool. I guess I was a poser, but now as an adult, I think that’s just totally fine. I mean, is it really that bad to want to look cool? I think a lot of people still want that, but we’re told it’s shallow, frivolous – and to ‘grow up’. Maybe being true to yourself is just acknowledging you want to look cool. So, is being a poser actually not being a poser??? Just encouraging others out there – don’t be afraid to accessorize, glamourize, and romanticize.

This bike is an ode to the early 2000’s – Avril Lavigne, Blink 182, Spirit Halloween, mall goths and black nail polish.

A little more detail about the bike. It was custom-made for a person who I think has loved it for a very long time. I bought it second-hand. It was probably made in the late 90s, given the quill stem and groupset. It’s mostly a CX bike, but with touring add-ons like triple bottle cages, fender mounts, and front and rear rack mounts.

The 3×9 drivetrain works great. It’s affordable and gives me a better gear range than anything I can buy today. I had Paul Components build me brake levers to match the black and silver finish of the XT group. Also, Tyler from BTCHN’ bikes built me some awesome Ti handlebars based on a mood board I sent him. It’s anodized with Goosebumps-inspired drips and scene queen-inspired checkers. Wow.

The front rack and bag combination were big considerations as well. I’ve been wanting this carry system for my daily commute, so I might have built an entirely new bike around it. I DO like to build bikes based on the bags they go with… You may notice the extra adapter plate on the rack. That’s part of our new Fidlock Tote attachment system I’ve been prototyping. Of course, I had to have matching straps on the bag and a custom hand-stitched leather doll from Pretty Popular Studio.

For the top tube pad, I used a polished nickel zipper with DIY distressed canvas. I discovered you can separate out the warp of the fabric and cut them out, leaving the weft strands still attached. A little sandpaper and it looks just like pants from Hot Topic! To top it off, I also made a custom tiny tie and added some studded bracelets.

Yes, my bike has an outfit that isn’t practical. Bikes don’t have to be, and neither do you.

Build Spec

  • Frame: Independent Fabrications CX/Touring Custom
  • Wheelset: Sun Rhyno Lite with Deore XT M750
  • Handlebar: BTCHN’ Ti FlatBar 16 with Custom Anodizing
  • Bar Ends: HEX Components
  • Stem: Nitto Dynamic 11
  • Grips: ODI Cult x Vans Waffle
  • Seatpost: SunTour XC Comp
  • Saddle: Selle Italia Flite with Anodized Ti Rails
  • Groupset: Deore XT M750 3×9
  • Brake Levers: Paul Canti
  • Brakes: Paul Minimoto
  • Pedals: MKS Gamma
  • Tires: Panaracer Urban Max
  • Rack: Rat King RIP
  • Bag: Outer Shell Fidlock Tote
  • Bracelets: Hot Topic
  • Top Tube Pad: Outer Shell Custom
  • Tie: Outer Shell Custom

 

 

We’d like to thank all of you who submitted Readers Rides builds to be shared here at The Radavist. The response has been incredible, and we have so many to share over the next few months. Feel free to submit your bike, listing details, components, and other information. You can also include a portrait of yourself with your bike and your Instagram account! Please shoot landscape-orientation photos, not portrait. Thanks!

The post Readers’ Rides: Kyle from Outer Shell’s Pop Punk Mall Goth Indy Fab appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Introducing the Velo Orange Gravel Crankarms & Chainrings: Classic Style Meet Modern Gravel

Let’s be honest; contemporary gravel cranksets have gotten a bit… intense. Between aggressive angular lines, massive graphics, and proprietary interface standards that seem to change every season, finding a clean, classic-looking crankset for a modern gravel or touring build has felt like an uphill battle.

Velo Orange Gravel Crankarms Quick Hits

  • Q-Factor: 176mm using using a 118mm bottom bracket spindle

And let’s be honest; contemporary gravel cranksets have gotten a bit… intense. Between aggressive angular lines, massive graphics, and proprietary interface standards that seem to change every season, finding a clean, classic-looking crankset for a modern gravel or touring build has felt like an uphill battle.

For 2x Range Seekers

Pair our 110bcd Outer Chainrings (40t to 46t) with our 74bcd Inner Chainrings (24t to 30t) to create true sub-compact gearing. Up front, the outer rings feature ramped and pinned shift profiles for crisp under-load front shifting, while the inner rings give you the low-torque bail-out gears you actually need when grinding up steep, loose grade with gear. We suggest sticking with a 16t ring difference – that’s for optimal shifting.

For 1x Simplicity

Mount our 110bcd Narrow-Wide Chainrings (38t to 44t) directly to the outer position using the outer hardware. The alternating tooth profile locks onto your chain to keep everything secure through rough washboards and doubletrack chatter without needing a chain guide.

entry.title: Zwift Plus Explained: Zwift Video Routes & Zwift Coach Hands-On
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

Roughly six months after acquiring Rouvy, Zwift is starting to do things with it. Or at least, starting to emulate it. In this case, Zwift is rolling out a two-component premium tier called Zwift Plus, which includes both an adaptive coaching feature and a new video routes function. Those video routes are like Rouvy, but…umm…not Rouvy.

Instead, they’re completely newly shot routes in ‘iconic cycling locations’, yet with the social aspect of Zwift riding built atop it. Zwift says all of this began before they acquired Rouvy, hence everything not being Rouvy at all. But we’re getting ahead of ourselves.

In terms of pricing, the new Zwift Plus is $29.99/€29.99/£26.99 per month (instead of the existing $19/month), and there are annual plans that are $299 (instead of $199/year). Existing Zwift stays, and as we saw this past Monday, continues to get big expansions. This is purely focused on the new Zwift Coach and Zwift Video Routes pieces.

In any case, I’ve been riding it the past few weeks, so let’s dive into things.

Zwift Video Routes:

Firstly, no, this is not Rouvy merged into Zwift. It’s so much not Rouvy that Zwift literally went out and filmed every one of these routes by themselves, with their own team and their own equipment. One could (and probably should) have a solid debate about the logic in doing that, but nonetheless, they are indeed different videos…even if the places/locations near 100% overlap.

Zwift says their intent is to keep the company/videos/etc. separate. Rouvy keeps being Rouvy, and Zwift keeps being Zwift. By having a more curated selection, Zwift says it “maintains the social density Zwift is known for”. Further, all the routes are lap-able, though at launch there’s no support for meet-ups or organized events. However, it sounds like both are “fast-follows”, meaning they’re expected to launch quickly.

What Zwift is aiming for here is a more curated selection of routes, meeting a certain quality bar (both in terms of resolution, but also avoiding various road furniture, etc.), and then a continual drumbeat of new route drops every month (ideally looking at 5-10 routes per month). Further, the routes here tend to be a bit shorter (all but one can be completed in an hour), though all also support looping back to the start for continual riding. And of course, all of them will ‘feel’ like being in Zwift, as Zwift overlays various things onto the roads/etc. (which Zwift says they started working on before they acquired Rouvy).

In any case, to select a Zwift Video Route, you’ll choose ‘Routes’ at the top, and then use the gigantic Toggle to switch to video routes.

Once toggled, here’s what you see:

There are a few more routes if you scroll down; here’s what else there is – 21 routes in total today, covering 385km of roads:

As you can see above, there’s a good variety in this starter pack, covering Europe, the US, and South Africa. They say they wanted to aim for “cycling icons” in terms of routes, and I’d generally agree with that. These routes are the definition of that.

If I hover over a route, I’ll see the elevation profile:

And then if I click it, I’ll see basically the same thing but with a short one-sentence description. I do feel like these descriptions could use a bit more love.

Nonetheless, once you’ve decided on where to route, you’ll simply tap ‘Start Ride’, and you’ll be brought to the starting area (just ahead of the start banners). For some routes, they have more of a start corral, and others don’t.

At this point, you’ll just pedal like normal. You’ll notice that there’s plenty of augmented reality bits, just like in Rouvy. For example, arches/banners for Sprint/KOM finishes, bits on the road, and even occasional Zwift vans.

You’ll even see rider shadows on the boards too (just like you do in Rouvy):

Here you can see the green painting on the road surface, plus the boards, plus the Zwift van:

They’ve done a seemingly creative job at occasionally using these augmented reality bits to hide or conceal things like construction, some sketchy car situations, and more. It’s super well done. That orange van you see ahead is actually an augmented reality Zwift van. And only at the very last second did I realize it wasn’t real traffic.

Likewise, I didn’t even notice that this van here waiting to cross this bridge was an augmented reality Zwift van, until I was capturing these screenshots from my recorded rides:

Now, there are different quality levels you can choose for the video streaming portion. Which is *different* than the resolution of the Zwift app on your display. In other words, you could choose 1080p video routes, but then have a 4K resolution from Zwift (which would be things like the metrics displayed/etc). I found 1080p on a MacBook totally fine in terms of resolution, but if I were on a bigger screen, I’d choose the higher resolution video streams:

It’ll do some initial buffering at the beginning, but as I found out on one ride where I tried to do 4K streaming, the hopscotch internet connection I had to where my bikes are in a shed-like place didn’t quite work out. If you go beyond the buffer, you get orange roads:

The Zwift game and other people and all the rest still work; you just lose the route video until it catches up. Meaning the whole thing doesn’t stop from a riding perspective. You can keep on riding just fine.

In terms of riding with other people, most of that works as expected. There are some minor quirks. For example, steering around others seems a bit wonky at times. Or rather, just the automatic steering around others doesn’t seem as fluid/normal as I’m used to in Zwift. Sometimes there are hard and random swerves. However, they do a really good job of effectively ‘fencing’ portions of the road when there’s oncoming traffic, so you can’t have your avatar get hit by a car. Both Shane and I seemed to have the same idea here, trying to steer into this car, but you couldn’t. The ‘viable steering area’ was reduced as the car neared (as I was on the left edge of the road until shortly beforehand).

Likewise, when riders go far ahead of you, their avatar properly gets smaller and slowly fades away at normal human vision distances. All of this feels spot-on.

However, one thing that isn’t super ideal is that you’re always plowing through someone’s ass.

The fade effect is perfectly fine, but rather, it’s the issue that they filmed this to be roughly the same level as you would have your head on a bicycle (which makes sense). But that means when you add all these extra riders, you end up just looking at a lot of people’s butts all the time. An effect that’s gonna be even bigger when you have bigger packs. Whereas in normal Zwift, the camera angle is higher, so you’re not in butt-cam mode.

Meanwhile, you can do HUD-free mode (where you get rid of all the metrics), though not in ERG/structured workout mode. But for regular riding you can:

Now, when you reach the end of the route, it’ll simply ‘loop’ back to the start. You’ll basically teleport back for just continual riding over and over again. It would be cool to be able to ‘stack’ routes together, akin to what Peloton does for workouts (where you basically add things to a queue, and it just iterates through them without forcing you back to a menu). Here you can see me being looped back to the beginning of the route (note the time at 50-minutes, but starting me back at the beginning of the route):

Meanwhile, shifting topics entirely, you’ve got structured workouts. These worked exactly as you’d expect in regular Zwift, but now with Video Routes with your structured workouts overlaid. I did a few structured workouts this way without any issue.

This is where you start to get into some of the obvious differences to Rouvy, in that Rouvy has a gazillion courses, but also caters to specific race routes – such as Ironman routes and more. So this is where there’s still a solid gap there in that Zwift is targeting cycling icons, whereas Rouvy is targeting basically everything, including race/event routes. So if a coach wanted to create a structured workout (e.g. a race plan) on a specific race route, you’re lacking those routes in Zwift.

Here you can see just a tiny sliver of those categories in Rouvy:

And again, looking at the quality of certain routes, those on Zwift just seem higher, if I compare them side-by-side. Whether it be the weather conditions (e.g., sunny on Zwift vs. sometimes grey/overcast on Rouvy). A good example is Sa Calobra, which both platforms have. Zwift is a blue-bird sunny day, while Rouvy has two variants, one solidly overcast and one with some clouds. But even then, the video quality on Zwift is clearly higher – both in resolution and in general clarity. To be super clear: Rouvy isn’t bad here by any means, but Zwift feels sharp.

It does feel like Zwift is likely doing some color grading, which makes them all pop a bit more. More on that down below, though, in the Zwift Video Routes shooting behind-the-scenes section.

Which again, I’m definitely not crapping on Rouvy’s routes. Rouvy has a *far* bigger library of routes here. It’s not even remotely close. And in order to have such a massive library, you often need to make trade-offs. You can’t sit around an extra few days to wait for perfect weather conditions. Whereas Zwift has said they’ll re-film multiple times, and then pick the best one. They’re choosing a slightly premium quality experience, which you may or may not care about.

Either way, on the whole I’d say that Zwift’s implementation here is super well done, and makes it feel very Zwift-like, despite being outdoor videos.

Zwift Coach:

Next up there are the new Zwift Coach pieces. It’d probably be easy to say this is just another customized AI coaching platform, and to a certain extent that’d be true. Perhaps I’ve become jaded with the never-ending attempts at AI coaching that almost always suck. However, this actually isn’t leveraging AI for the coaching specifically, which probably makes it more interesting to me.

Instead, it’s leveraging work from one of the creators behind BestBikeSplit, to assign also-human made workouts to athletes using existing models they have on choosing the right workout intensity and duration based on a given athlete’s historical data. Where AI comes into it is simply for assigning which Zwift ‘thing’ to do (e.g., which Zwift route, Video Route, structured workout, Pacer Group, etc.) to fulfill that training load/intensity/duration requirement. It uses AI to look at components like whether or not you’ve done that route before, if you tend to do more routes than structured workouts, and so on.

But first, to get started, you’ll fill out a bit of an onboarding questionnaire with your goals. You can have different targets, including specific races on specific days at specific lengths. All of this is relatively straightforward, to be honest:

From there, you’ll see in your companion app (and on the Zwift main app) your upcoming schedule. This schedule is dynamic and responsive to other things you do off-plan. For example, yesterday I ignored the schedule and did about an hour of riding with DesFit & GPLama. Some of that was chill, and some of that was…unchill. As a result, when I opened things up today, it offered to adapt my schedule a bit. Specifically, it cut out some of my weekend riding to allow for more recovery before an interval run on Saturday:

One quirky thing here though, is that while I have TrainerRoad connected to my account (which then pushes a workout of the day each day based on my training load), that can’t be temporarily disabled when I have a Zwift plan. Though at the same time, Zwift says those planned workouts are ignored by Zwift Coach, unless I actually do one. Then they get accounted for.

As you can see above, when it comes to things that Zwift will prescribe, it’s actually not just structured workouts. It can be anything. You can see it’s telling me to just go ride for an hour today on the California Roll route. Other days it’s a structured workout. But it can also give me a Pacer Group to go follow, or a Video Route. Eventually it sounds like outdoor ride options are in the cards too, but not today.

You’ll see the planned workout shown in Zwift when you open it up, with the little robot head next to it:

In terms of doing the workouts, it’s just like doing any other structured workout (if you were assigned a structured workout). There’s no difference there once you start that workout (you can select what route to do, or a video route in my case). Here’s a workout it had me do:

Then, after the workout, it’ll give some brief comments in the Zwift Companion app to check out:

As you might expect, it’s a bit hard for me to judge any workout/training plan system without spending months with it. And given I’ve only spent a week or so with it, it’d be far too early. Plus, I find testing training plans tends to work best when you actually give it a specific race goal, and then let life get in the way. Thus far though, as I’ve ignored it roughly half the time, it’s zigged and zagged appropriately to try and keep the ship on course. That’s a good start.

Zwift Video Routes Tech Tidbits:

As always, I’m curious about some of the tech behind the tech. This isn’t a super long section, but there are some things I thought were interesting when it came to how they filmed the Zwift Video Routes.

First up, as noted above, they have a team that travels around and shoots these. They aren’t using some fancy car, these all just look like random rental cars. Instead, they have a suction cup-mounted system they travel with that just pops onto the car:

That system looks like they’re using:

– Two GoPro Hero 13 Black cameras
– Neewer CA013 suction cup mounts (three of them)
– Custom rig/cross-bar for mounting the camera
– Two V-mount battery packs
– A few 3D-printed camera mounting brackets
– Extra straps for stability/safety (seen below going horizontal, or above going vertical)

Each of those suction cups supports 110LBS/50KG of weight. Here you can see the rig out on the road, with all the straps, and a slightly different battery placement (my guess is this has evolved over time):

And again here:

Meanwhile, inside the car they’ve got a few things going on. You’ll see two tablets (upper) at left with feeds from each of the cameras. They’re shooting at 4K/120fPS in the ‘Wide’ profile. They’ve then got a Hammerhead Karoo 3 that’s recording the ride, from which they’d leverage the GPS track & barometric altimeter data later to create the route. And then you can see the course down below on the laptop with RideWithGPS pulled up.

All of this seems pretty logical to me. In the above photo, it looks like they were trying a variant with the cameras out wide for two different perspectives. All of the other BTS shots they sent had them close together. While there are reasons you’d use dual cameras for 3D-type video later, I can’t imagine that’s the case here. That’s been tried and failed countless times for all sorts of reasons (mainly sweat kills most headsets).

Instead, I suspect the reason is much simpler here: It costs a lot to reshoot things, whereas a GoPro costs $400 once, and you can ensure you’ve got a backup. Even if it’s because a bee landed on the camera lens:

Speaking of which, they often reshoot things. They said for Sa Calobra they reshot it 5 times. However, not to piece it together, but to find the single continuous take that had the least problematic things in it. Other takes could be ‘ruined’ by vehicles/drivers doing weird things, unexpected checkpoints…or just sheep and cows. Both of these are actual outtakes from Zwift Video attempts:

Zwift says all of them are continuous shots, noting:

“We don’t currently splice different sections of footage together – we want the highest quality continuous footage only as a bar for high quality for this product. So there does end up being lots of footage on the cutting room floor that cannot be used.”

In terms of the speed they were shot, Zwift says they had a bit of a model for gradient and then matched that to a certain speed. Meaning, they didn’t have a car driving at 20MPH/30KPH up at 10% grade. Instead, the car would slow down as much as viable for steeper hills, and then try to match cyclist speeds on other grades (such as going downhill).

The closer you can get the original footage to a real cyclist’s speeds, the better, as all other things seen in the video (passing cars, people, other real-world cyclists in the video), will feel ‘right’. Otherwise, they leverage the footage being shot at 120FPS in order to speed up/slow down the footage in real time as you ride it.

Anyway, I thought all the above was kinda interesting. I’ve seen lots of filming rigs over 15+ years of watching companies shoot various real-world style videos. Many have used motorcycles, since that tends to give other drivers a bit more flexibility. But conversely, using cars tends to force other vehicles ‘further’ away from the camera, which results in a safer-feeling video when you ride it on your computer. Some companies also shoot it on regular bicycles, which can work out, but is really hard to get right/perfect for long stretches. And many companies will splice video together from multiple attempts to deal with road randomness. So it’s kinda interesting that Zwift is aiming for the ‘one-shot-wonder’ approach here.

Going Forward:

In an era of ever-expanding subscription costs and AI-driven coaching things, I suppose it’s only time before Zwift was going to jump in on it. Though, I didn’t exactly expect Zwift to ‘combine Rouvy without actually combining Rouvy’. Nonetheless, here we are, where it’ll cost you an extra $10/month (or an extra $100/year). For folks who wanted occasional video access akin to Rouvy, but didn’t quite want to pay that much extra atop their Zwift subscription, this probably makes sense.

But first, looking at Zwift Coach, this is largely what I expected Zwift to eventually do. Though admittedly, I thought they’d do it a decade ago, either through partnerships with Xert or TrainerRoad. But what they’ve put forth here is roughly in line with what most other platforms offer in terms of adaptive cycling training plans. The key difference is giving you more than just a structured workout, but rather lots of options to get that training load in (regular rides, video routes, etc.). That’s unique in this space.

Meanwhile, looking at the Video Routes, it’s clear they spent some time ensuring that *all* of the routes met their given quality bar. This kinda reminds me of what FulGaz was aiming for back in the day. Certainly, there are many high-quality videos on Rouvy, but Rouvy’s goal was always more variety (thousands of routes) with sometimes varying quality. Here on Zwift Routes, it’s more curation over quantity. Still, one has to look at this and struggle to wonder how this all plays out for Rouvy in a few years. By Zwift’s own hopes, they want to have at least 100 routes within a year, still a fraction of Rouvy’s 6,000 routes. Nonetheless, the fact that Zwift didn’t use Rouvy people to film these routes says a lot (either organizationally/directionally, or just Zwift’s long-known penchant for spending money).

That said, as a consumer, setting aside branding, if Zwift ends up having all the same features and routes as Rouvy, do we actually care where it ends up? It’s an uncomfortable question to ask, but certainly one I’d imagine Zwift is pondering.

Anyway, in the meantime, if you want to spend an extra $10 for routes and coaching, go forth. While I don’t tend to be a video routes person most of the time, I will say the way Zwift has executed these makes them feel premium, and also feel like Zwift, and thus, makes the experience seem more akin to what I tend to gravitate to. But again, to each their own. I’m on the fence about whether I’ll upgrade my membership.

With that – thanks for reading!

entry.title: Fitbit Edge In-Depth Review: Worth the Upgrade?
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

The Fitbit Edge could most easily be called the Fitbit Charge 7, but sometimes switching things up is a good refresh for companies and brands, and so here we are. In many ways, the Fitbit Edge will feel very familiar to Fitbit Charge users, yet it’ll concurrently feel very much like a recent Google Pixel Watch. That’s both good and bad. There are a lot of good things coming from the Pixel Watch 5 & Fitbit Air that have landed here. Yet equally, having used it the past few weeks, there are a number of smaller things that aren’t quite what we had on the very popular Fitbit Charge series.

Speaking of which, both my wife and I have been using Fitbit Edge units over this last while on all of our workouts. Runs, rides, hikes, walks, gym stuff, and everything in between. With that, let’s dive into what’s new, and then all my daily and workout usage experiences.

What’s New:

The Fitbit Edge is the next version of the Fitbit Charge 6, which came out in 2023. Here’s how it’s different:

– Increased screen/display by 46% (has 1.34” display)
– Case thickness is 11.5mm
– Added physical side button that actually clicks (previous was just a touch area)
– Added altimeter (for stair tracking, as well as elevation tracking)
– Added automatic workout detection (now supports 100 sports)
– Increased supported manual workout profiles to 50 workout profiles
– Made user-replaceable/serviceable battery (the first Fitbit-branded product to do so)
– GPS accuracy improvement claimed at 40% more accurate (via new GPS chipset, and new aluminum case design)
– Switched to a more modern user interface, matching the Pixel Watch 5 series
– Added structured workout support
– Added support for dual usage with Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air (e.g., switching back and forth seamlessly)
– Added fast charging (5 minutes gets you 1 day of usage)
– Removed Google Pay (NFC Contactless payments)
– Removed EDA Scan feature (but does have continuous stress monitoring in the background)
– Changed the band attachment mechanism (old Fitbit habits die hard)
– Switched the charger to the same charger as the Fitbit Air (hey, at least they picked something else they already had this time)
– Added a bunch of band accessory types
– Price increased to $179 (officially the Charge 6 was $159 previously, but realistically it sat between $99 and $129 virtually all the time)
– Also a Stephen Curry model at $219 (US, Canada, EMEA)

In terms of some other general specs, just for recap purposes:

– Same claimed 7-day battery life
– Still has heart rate broadcasting feature via Bluetooth (though it can be a bit funky in terms of compatibility)
– Still has music control of your phone’s music (no onboard music storage)
– Still has Google Maps turn-by-turn directions (with phone)
– Still has smartphone notifications (more integration on Android than iOS)
– Still has full sleep tracking
– Still has continuous heart rate monitoring (background and workout)
– Still supports high & low heart rate alerts
– Supports the Google Health Guardian features announced a few months ago
– You can do quick replies on Android, though not on iOS devices
– Has FDA/EU approved medical ECG functionality, including background Afib detection
– Includes skin temperature sensor
– Supports Steps, Distance, Active Zone Minutes, VO2Max, Floor/elevation, Cardio Load, and many more metrics
– Two sizes of bands (see specs below)
– Water resistance level is 5ATM, and IP68 for dust protection

So that covers the piles of new stuff, and some of the bits that were there before. But there are still numerous color schemes/models to choose from.

Model Options & Detailed Specs:

The Fitbit Air case comes in 5 different colorways, and then with that, a huge slate of band options. Starting off with the core options you can buy, they are as follows:

– Matte Black Aluminum case / Obsidian Active Band
– Polished Silver Aluminum case / Fog Active Band
– Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Olive Active Band
– Champagne Gold case / Canyon Active Band
– Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Stephen Curry Special Edition

From there, you’ve got the following band types/options:

– Active Band
– Active Sport band
– Metal Link band
– Magnet band
– Performance Loop

Now, for most of our testing (my wife and I), we’ve been wearing the relatively basic/default Active band, which works perfectly fine and is easy to adjust/etc.

Still, we both wore other bands as well. Yesterday we had a fancy afternoon thing to go to, and swapped out to the Metal Link band. Hers was the champagne gold, and mine the brushed silver. Obviously neither quite perfectly matched with the models we had, but…well…that’s the models we had:

My only complaint here is that I found the clasp release button could actually get reasonably easily pressed. Ironically, it didn’t happen all day during most of the day, and then towards the end of the day, it was triggering constantly. My wife didn’t have this issue, so….yeah.

I’ve also worn the Active Sport band a bit, though I didn’t honestly find it all that meaningfully different than the Active band, in terms of sport wearability.

And finally, I have the Magnet Band, which is super cool and just snaps tight/shut.

Finally, looking at the tech specs, here’s a whole slate of things that may or may not be interesting to you:

– Display is 1.34”/34mm AMOLED display, supporting an always-on configuration
– Display supports adjustable brightness
– Bluetooth 5.4
– Processor: Ambiq AP5 MCU
– GPS chipset supports GPS+Galileo in US, and GPS+Galileo+GLONASS+BeiDou+QZSS outside of US
– Onboard memory: 64MB NOR flash memory, 7 days of detailed motion data (minute intervals), 30 days of daily totals, heart rate at 2-second intervals
– Internal sensors: Altimeter, Accelerometer, Gyroscope, Red and infrared sensors for oxygen saturation (SpO2), Multipurpose electrical sensors compatible with ECG app, Photoplethysmography (PPG) optical heart rate sensor, Ambient light sensor, Far-field skin temperature sensor
– Battery is 65mAh
– Fully end-user replaceable battery
– Charging speed: 5 minutes of fast charging for 1 day of battery life, or 100% in 90 minutes
– Requires iOS 16.4 or newer, and Android 11 or newer
– Fitbit Edge Weight: 17.7g without band
– Fitbit Edge Dimensions: 39.22 x 25.56 mm
– Fitbit Edge Height/Thickness: 11.58mm
– Case is made from 100% recycled aluminum
– Active band: Silicone with “soft-touch coating”
– Active Band Sizing: Small fits wrists 130-170mm around, Large fits 170-210mm around
– Stephen Curry band: “Recycled polyester yarns with water-repellent coating and stainless steel lugs, as well as a raised interior print for increased airflow.”
– Stephen Curry band sizing (US): Small fits wrists 135-170mm around, Large fits 170-210mm around
– Stephen Curry band sizing (EU/Canada): Single-size fits wrists 150-195mm around
– Water resistance: 5ATM/50 meters
– Dust immersion resistance: IP68

Phew, got all that? Good, let’s roll right into the basics of the unit day to day.

The Daily Usage Basics:

In this section, I’ll go through all the daily usage basics of the Fitbit Edge, like activity/step tracking, sleep tracking, and general health bits. Then after this I’ll cover workout pieces.

First up is interacting with the device. The Fitbit Edge gained a physical button on the right side, which quickly opens the apps menu, for things like accessing the alarms, ECG, exercise, media controls, and weather. Previously on the Fitbit Charge 6, this was a touch-sensitive area, but not a clicking button:

The button is great, and I’ve been super happy with it. Note that at present, long-pressing it doesn’t do anything.

Instead, for most other interactions, you’ll use the touchscreen, which allows you to swipe left/right/up/down, and tap it for what you need. Of course, the first thing you’ll see is your watch face:

You can customize these in the Google Health App, allowing you to save multiple watch faces to the Fitbit Edge for quick swapping between them. You can customize each of the complications (data bits) on the watch face, as well as the coloring. There’s roughly a dozen watch faces to choose from:

You can swipe down anytime to access the controls menu. This includes things like the flashlight, do-not-disturb mode, heart rate broadcasting, and more. I’ll cover some of these in more depth throughout the review.

Instead, if we swipe from the right, we’ll get the quick start menu for workouts, allowing us to access the most recent sport profiles:

Swipe again, and we’ve got a high-level overview of the Focus Metrics panel:

This one (above) is kinda odd, though, in that you have to tap into it again to get to a longer list of focus metrics:

However, the oddest part here is that you can’t tap any of these metrics to see more details on-device. For example, want to see what time it thinks you went to sleep or woke up? Can’t do that here. Have to go to the phone. Want to see why your Readiness Score is what it is? Can’t do that here. Have to go to the phone.

In discussions with Google/Fitbit, they seem to hint that changes are coming here in this area. I sure hope so, as this seems pretty half-finished at best.

In any case, as you keep swiping through these to the left/right, you’ll essentially see other data metrics for stuff I already showed in the Focus Metrics. For example, swipe again, and you’ll see the very small sleep tidbits. You can’t tap into this, though, for any additional details beyond what you see below:

Same goes for heart metrics:

And then there’s weather, showing current weather in your area, and then another page for quick access to the timers:

And finally, there’s another page for media controls. There is no music storage on the Fitbit Edge, which seems logical/fine to me. However, what’s less logical is the lack of NFC/payment support. This was in the Fitbit Charge 6 and has been in countless cheaper Fitbit devices over the years, yet it’s not here. Given Google doesn’t support the higher-end Pixel Watch series on iOS, this means there’s really no option for iOS users to use a Google device if they want contactless payments. And as both Google and Apple know well, very few people are going to change phone platforms merely to support a wearable. That ship sailed long, long ago.

Google did provide a bit of color as to why they cut the contactless payment support, saying:

“Fitbit Edge does not offer NFC for payments. It was not widely used by our Charge 6 users – in fact, less than 1% used the feature on Charge 6 – so we prioritized other top features such as adding a sleek design, altimeter and week long battery.” – Andy Abramson (Head of Product at Google Health)

And to be fair, I wouldn’t necessarily disagree with that line of thinking, though ultimately, I still think the lack of iOS option for higher-end Google wearables is really the core issue here.

In any case, since we can’t see many details on the screen itself beyond core metrics, a lot of that is shifted to your phone and the Google Health app (the Fitbit app is dead; long live the Fitbit app!). Here you can see your summary at the top for the day, in terms of steps, readiness scores, sleep, and cardio load for the week. This is all free. However, anytime you see lots of descriptive text, that’ll be part of Google’s Premium subscription. In other words, the data is free, but the wordy analysis requires a subscription.

Looking at my sleep metrics, for example from last night, those look accurate and have been consistently accurate over the last few weeks. The only one that caused many wearables to stumble was yesterday’s daylight saving time change, which seemed to truncate an hour of sleep. However, otherwise the times I woke up and went to sleep have been spot-on.

Note that I don’t compare accuracy of sleep stages/phases, as that’s simply not an accurate metric. In a best-case setting for so-called gold-standard devices, those basically top out in the mid-80% accuracy range, which is pretty poor for a gold-standard device to compare against. Thus, I’m not going to mislead you here.

Instead, I will get annoyed at one sleep-related thing that Google/Fitbit lacks on the Fitbit Edge, which is automatic sleep mode toggles. Specifically, while you can set up sleep schedules and do-not-disturb schedules, that actually won’t prevent the screen from illuminating all crazy-pants in the middle of the night (or, perhaps lack of pants in the middle of the night). Instead, anytime the sheets or you brush the screen, it’ll light up. Same goes for raise-to-wake. Which is both annoying and a long-solved problem on wearables.

Instead, you need to tap the bed icon each night to force it into sleep mode. That by itself isn’t actually as annoying to me as remembering again in the morning to un-tap that bed icon, so that things like raise-to-wake actually work. Again, like the other details piece, I get the impression there’s a fast-follow to enable this on the Fitbit Edge, but it does feel like the Google/Fitbit team is just a bit behind on getting this device fully baked.

In any case, beyond that, within the Google Health app you’ve also got the Health Status panel, which shows your trending metrics over the course of longer time periods:

There does appear to be a bug here in that my Blood Oxygen levels have been updating nightly, both on the Fitbit Edge since putting it on, as well as for months on other devices, but since wearing the Fitbit Edge, it’s stopped trending for me. This is a minor nit for me, though it does make my metrics ‘4 out of 5’, instead of ‘5 out of 5’.

When it comes to text notifications, note that you’ll see those come in on the device, though on iOS you’ll be unable to respond to them. But you can read them and clear them:

Finally, in terms of charging, you’ve got the same charger as the Fitbit Air, so kudos to the Google/Fitbit team for managing to keep the same charger for more than one product. I can only assume they had a grand celebration for finally unlocking that accomplishment, complete with Haribo gummy bears and rosé wine. Well deserved.

Indeed, you can fast-charge silly-quick to get you through the day/night. And in terms of battery life, if you leave it with the default gesture-based display, it seems to be on trend for the week-long battery life. However, I quickly changed it to always-on display, and that pulls things back real-quick to basically two days of battery life. Again, all dependent on how much GPS-outside workout time you have. With that, let’s talk sweaty stuff.

Sports & Workouts:

The Fitbit Edge takes virtually all of the best features from the recently launched screenless Fitbit Air (which is basically a Whoop competitor), and rolls them into the Fitbit Edge. This means that you’ve got equal parts manual activity/workout controls, as well as the ability to just totally ignore the unit on your wrist, and know that it’ll track things behind the scenes automatically. Both my wife and I have done both. Sometimes manually starting a workout, and other times just letting it figure it out.

Starting off with the manual side, to begin a workout you’ll tap either from the watch face (if the complication is enabled), or just swipe once from the right to the sport menu:

Here you can choose from your most recently used sports, or one of the ones in the list. On the manual workout profile side, here are the workout profiles that are supported on the Fitbit Edge. Note these are a subset of the automatic detection list, which is around 100 activities (see following this):

Manually Selectable Sport Profiles

Aerobics
Badminton
Baseball
Basketball
Bike
Bootcamp
Boxing
Canoeing
Circuit training
Core training
Cricket
Cross-country ski
CrossFit
Dancing
Elliptical
Field hockey
Football
Golf
HIIT
Hike
Indoor climbing
Kayaking
Kickboxing
Martial arts
Mountain bike
Open swim
Outdoor workout
Paddleboarding
Padel
Pickleball
Pilates
Pool swim
Powerlifting
Rollerblading
Rowing machine
Rugby
Run
Skating
Skiing
Snowboarding
Soccer
Spinning
Sport
Stair climber
Strength training
Surfing
Swim
Tennis
Treadmill run
Walk
Weightlifting
Weights
Workout
Yoga

I definitely appreciate having all of these profiles available on-device, rather than just a very basic set. Which I suppose is the general trend in watches/wearables the last year or two: More workout profile options is better.

Once you’ve selected a sport profile, there are a few options you can choose, such as any targets or goals like distance, pace (high/low), calories, etc.

Additionally, there’s the option for GPS usage. This allows you to leverage GPS internal to the Fitbit Edge, or to use it from your phone. The choice is honestly pretty simple: Which device’s battery do you want to burn? By default, even when you toggle GPS on for an activity (like a run), it’ll default to using your phone’s GPS (via Bluetooth).

However, within the settings of the Google Health app, you can choose to instead use the device’s GPS. By default, it’ll be on ‘Dynamic’, which Google has confirmed actually translates to “use the phone unless the phone isn’t there”.

In my case, as seen above, I switched to ‘Built-in’. This is the configuration I mostly used it within. In my testing, I’d burn the Fitbit Edge battery at about 15%/hour, for outdoor GPS workouts with the screen in always-on display.

However, if you want to save some battery, in gesture-based mode, I got a fair bit longer. Basically twice as much for this 5-hour ride in the mountains, burning at roughly 8%/hour:

In the above example, the battery started at 90%, though it ended at 50%.

Speaking of which, the Google Health app does support mirroring of data from the Fitbit Edge to your phone, if you want to use it as a bike computer or just generally see your workout data metrics on your phone in real time. This isn’t super detailed, nor does it show as much data as on the device itself, but it’s an option for the core bits.

Still, circling all the way back to the start of the workout, you’ll see your GPS status icon at the top:

Once you start, you’ll see your data details across a few different data pages:

That said, quirkily, you can’t change/modify any of the data pages from a sports standpoint. They are what they are.

Nonetheless, all of this works reasonably well within a workout, and I had no issues there in terms of general usage. For things like rain during workouts, this made the screen pretty tough to use for swipes specifically; that was also true of other wearables I was testing at the time.

Once you’ve completed your workout, you’ll see summary data of the workout:

And then over on the Google Health app, you can see more details of it:

One of the metrics you’ve probably noticed a few times is the ‘Cardio Load’. This is essentially your training load, and it resets every week. You accumulate Cardio Load during workouts, and roughly speaking, you get more Cardio Load the higher your heart rate is. So, on an easy walk with no meaningfully raised heart rate, you might accumulate just 0 or 1 cardio load. Yet a flat-out balls-to-the-wall 5KM run might score a few hundred units of cardio load. You can see this on the Fitbit Edge itself after a workout, as well as in summary stats.

Your goal dynamically changes each week, based on your personal historical data, as well as any goals that you might have configured in the Google Coach features (those are Premium features).

Otherwise, you can simply see how it compares to your historical data within the Google Health app:

Next, as mentioned, you can push a structured workout to the Fitbit Edge. This is a notable upgrade from the Fitbit Charge 6, which didn’t support structured workouts. However, it’s a little bit different than on a Pixel Watch, where you select it on the watch. Here, you’ll need to select it from within the Google Health app. This can be workouts that Google has created for you, or ones you create yourself:

Then, you’ll choose to start it from the phone, rather than on the Fitbit Edge. All of the instructions will be on your phone, not on the Fitbit Edge. The Edge is basically just recording and showing your general data. The phone is where everything is explained. This is perfectly logical for indoor/gym/yoga/etc. workouts, but it’s kinda wonky for an interval workout outside, where you need to keep checking your phone for what you should be doing. I’m not a huge fan of this implementation, especially if you’re a runner.

Finally, and semi-unrelated, if you are indoors and want to broadcast your heart rate to other devices, you can do so with the heart rate broadcast option by swiping down from the top and activating the heart rate broadcast icon. An example here would be pairing it to a Peloton Bike to use as a heart rate sensor/strap:

Note that Fitbit’s implementation doesn’t actually follow the Secure Bluetooth pairing standard, so it won’t really work with everything else out there unless they specifically partnered with Fitbit. For example, it works with Peloton and Zwift, but not with a Garmin Edge bike computer (sadly, the two Edges can’t chat). Sigh.

Of course, everything I’ve talked about thus far is about manually starting workouts and basically interacting with your Fitbit Edge. But the other way to do workouts is just to do them, and not even touch the Fitbit Edge (of course, still wear it). That then leverages Automatic Workout Detection, which is pulled from the Fitbit Air launched earlier this year.

Within that realm, there are basically two different ways the Fitbit Edge will detect workouts. The first set of workout types are ones it “really knows” and should get right each time. Whereas the second set are ones it takes a flyer on, based on historical data, and hopes for the best with an educated guess. Here’s the first set:

Core Automatically Detected sports without any context:

Outdoor Walk
Outdoor Run
Outdoor Bike
Stationary Bike
Elliptical

‘Activity’ (generic – periods of sustained elevated HR)

Then this next set requires some sort of historical context, as well as previous confirmations of the activity in the app. In other words, if it knows that you mow the lawn every Saturday morning, and then do hoeing on Saturday evening, it’ll likely detect those automatically each weekend if it feels the movement patterns are similar enough to your past hoeing activities:

I do want to point out that I’d love to have been a fly on the wall in conference rooms at Google when they debated putting the ‘Hoeing’ activity type in there.

While I cannot attest to the Hoeing activity accuracy levels, I can say that when it comes to other things it detected, it had no problems for me or my wife, in terms of detecting walks, hikes, and indoor cycling rides. When you do these activities, it’ll show up very similar, but slightly different than a regular activity. First, there won’t be any GPS tracks associated with it (even if outdoors). It doesn’t automatically turn that on. But second, you can actually change the times if it truncates something incorrectly.

While Fitbit had some basic automatic detection in the Charge 6, it’s nowhere near what they’re doing now with the Fitbit Edge. So this is definitely a bit of a step up.

With that, let’s take a look at the workout accuracy of both heart rate and GPS.

Accuracy:

The prior-gen Fitbit Charge 6 was known as a hot mess of a dumpster fire when it came to heart rate and GPS accuracy. As a user, you basically had two options: You could loosen up the band and get decent GPS accuracy, but nonsense heart rate accuracy. Or, you could tighten the band and get no usable GPS track at all, but good heart rate accuracy. Choosing both was simply not an option, due to a design that put the GPS antenna on the underside edges of the Charge 6.

One of the big things called out by Google with the Fitbit Edge is addressing that issue. The question is, does it?

Let’s start off with an indoor trainer ride. This one isn’t too hard, with some moderate but not crazy intervals. Here we can see that it really struggled at the beginning, for no obvious reason. It wasn’t until the main set started that it locked on.

I’m a bit surprised by this, as this should have been easy-town. That said, once it started the workout, it was largely fine.

Next, looking at heart rate on a bit under a 45-minute outdoor ride (mostly pavement,  tiny bit of gravel towards the end), we can see it struggles a bit at the beginning. To be fair, this was downhill on this first section, which many wearables will struggle starting with. By around the 10-minute marker, I’ve stabilized on flat ground, and you can see it largely trends OK, until round the 35-minute marker, where it struggles a little bit.

If we look at the GPS tracks on this, at a high level it looks very similar to the Garmin Edge 1060 and COROS Dura 2 I had on my handlebars then:

If we zoom in to a fast descent section, the Fitbit Edge (using built-in GPS), actually manages to stick on this road better than the $550 COROS Dura 2.

Though, on this much slower 20% grade climb, the Fitbit Edge wobbled a bit more than the others. It’s interesting that the section it wobbled (just below the pools), is actually the portion I had to get off the bike for a few seconds, as the recent rainstorms had basically washed away a portion of this gravel road, making brief impassable sections when trying to go up.

Lastly, if we look at the elevation profile on this, using the barometric altimeter inside the unit, it was quite close here, within just a couple of meters most of the time:

Looking at another ride, this one a 90-minute ride that was a mix of road and gravel, you can see things are…umm… a bit mixed when it comes to heart rate. Though, the Suunto Run 2 also struggled here on heart rate. Yes, you can see things ‘roughly trended’ in the right way, but overall this is a bit prickly.

On the GPS side of things, overall it was pretty good, occasionally slightly offset a meter or two from the other units when I’d do some lower-speed swerves, but still a *massive* improvement over the Fitbit Charge 6, which wouldn’t track GPS to save its life.

But you can see places like these straightaways here; it’s spot-on with the other GPS units, including $800 bike computers:

Finally, looking at a run from today, this is a simple 5KM run through both trails and pavement, split roughly evenly. Here’s the heart rate side first. This looks reasonably good. A few minor quibbles, but overall pretty solid despite being up/down on steep terrain; things are good here.

And then looking at the GPS, here’s the wide look at things:

Looking closely at some parts in the trees, and a bit of a ravine, it’s not meaningfully different than the $1,199 Garmin Fenix 9 Pro inReach model, or the $399 Suunto Run 2.

Same goes for this section here. Virtually indistinguishable.

Overall, this is a massive upgrade over the Fitbit Charge 6 for both heart rate and GPS. With the Charge 6, you had to ‘choose one’ of the two to be accurate. Here, the GPS is more than good enough for most things, and the heart rate is OK (though not great). The unit lacks the size/space to put in Google’s much better optical HR sensor found in the Pixel Watch 5, so instead it leans on a smaller sensor that fits into this case. Still, I suspect for most people interested in this device for probably more casual workout tracking, this is probably good enough.

(Note: All of the charts in these accuracy portions were created using the DCR Analyzer tool. It allows you to compare power meters/trainers, heart rate, cadence, speed/pace, running power, GPS tracks, and plenty more. You can use it as well for your own gadget comparisons; more details here.)

Final Thoughts:

For the vast majority of users, the Fitbit Edge will be a notable upgrade over the Fitbit Charge 6. Or definitely a Fitbit Charge 5. The GPS & heart rate situation is vastly improved, the user interface is cleaner and easier to understand, and I think the majority of the Google Health app is an improvement (though obviously, there are still some folks that prefer the older Fitbit app, especially if you don’t plan on being a Premium subscriber).

That said, while none of the issues I ran into were major blockers, it definitely lacks a bit of software finishing polish around the edges. Specifically, things like not having the automatic sleep mode for the display, not being able to tap into any of the metrics on the unit itself for more details, and then not being able to customize workout data pages. The way Google implemented these seems like they had grander/deeper plans, but eventually cut their losses for a holiday season launch. It sounds like some things are planned for firmware updates down the road.

Still, for a sub-$180 device targeted more at wellness than hardcore athletes, it largely fits the bill for tracking and analyzing your daily workouts, your daily health/sleep, and doing so in a tidy form factor that’s easy to understand. Having the automatic workout detection is super handy for when you don’t want to fuss with the screen, and yet it’ll properly track everything behind the scenes.

With that, thanks for reading!
