entry.title: Tech Tidbits: Withings Adds $100/year Apple Health sync Fee, and Omata is Back!
entry.content:
Amidst what might end up being one of the more ‘robust’ weeks of the year in terms of new product announcements, I wanted to briefly mention/cover two items I thought were interesting.

Let’s get right into it, cause I’ve gotta get back outside capturing data!

Withings Adds $100/year Apple Health Fee:

I’m putting this solidly in the category of ‘Wait…what?’. In short, Withings, the maker of the original WiFi weight scale, and generally speaking one of the best bets for a mainstream weight scale, has decided that if you want to update your weight in Apple Health, it’s gonna cost you $99/year going forward. This ‘feature’ will now be rolled into their Withings+, which offers a bunch of other features that most weight scale purchasers simply don’t need.

In response to the backlash, Withings noted that:

A) This won’t apply to existing users, only new users from Oct 13th, 2026
B) That you can export your data to CSV or PDF, for free, as well as other 3rd-party sync integrations, which are free

The problem with CSV/PDF is that it’s virtually useless to end users. There is no standard ‘weight data format’. For the most part, anytime a company skips using an industry standard fitness format and instead says “Oh, we can export as CSV”, that’s a solid red flag for me. Sure, on the surface it sounds good. But in practice it’s just annoying AF.

The kicker is, Withings probably thought they were being clever here by announcing this before the holiday purchasing period, to capture new revenue there. And there’s no product in the sports tech landscape that seems more predictable in sales/discounts than Withings connected scales. Like clockwork around Black Friday, every…single…year.

Except the thing is, they screwed up and announced this annoying change too close to Black Friday. Now, it wouldn’t surprise me to see many tech sites out there that will caveat their Withings Black Friday deals. I certainly will. Which will drive users to the boatloads of even cheaper random connected scales that do nothing more than measure weight.

And as I’ve proven many times over, when it comes to basic weight measurement, even the cheapest scales on the market get it correct. Inversely, when it comes to body fat and BMI measurement, virtually no fancy scales are getting that right. Thus, if you just want weight, Withings is saying: “buy the cheaper competitor scales”.

After all, this connected scale here costs $20, has an astonishing 40,000 units per month sold on Amazon (I don’t think I’ve ever seen any electronic product that high before), and has 4.7/5.0 ratings. And of course, Apple Health integration is free (along with Google, Fitbit, etc.).

The same goes for this $34 travel weight scale that I use. It’s tiny, fits easily in the bottom of my suitcase without weighing much (~2 pounds/1kg), but still syncs to Apple Health and everything else on the planet. And the accuracy is spot-on with all the expensive scales I’ve tested.

Point being, Withings has long been the premium-priced scale with a few more bells and whistles, but moves like this will quickly alienate future buyers.

Omata is Back?

Silca has announced the acquisition of Omata and, with it, resumed sales of an updated Omata bike computer.

For those not familiar, nearly a decade ago I unboxed the Omata bike computer (photo above). It never ended up having a full review, as there was delay after delay in getting the software ready. And eventually, it fell by the wayside.

The gist of the Omata is that it’s a watch/gauge style bike commuter that simplifies things to just what you see on the display. Behind the scenes, it’s still recording extra data to review later and/or upload to Strava. Internally, it has GPS as well as Bluetooth & ANT+. So it can connect to power meters and heart rate sensors.

But in terms of what you see during the ride? Just three metrics:

– Distance
– Speed
– Ascent
– Time

It uses analog hands to do this, which are made in partnership with Seiko. Oh,  they’ve upgraded the charging to USB-C, which gets it about 17 hours of battery life.

The company says, though, that this batch is a “limited re-release” of the unit, though they don’t really say how limited that is. Unlike Withings above though, they do support industry-standard .FIT files, and can sync to various platforms/apps like most other bike computers. Note, though, that they are iOS-only, however, and don’t have an Android app.

The price is $800, which is obviously the most expensive bike computer on the market. You choose between two versions of it, seen below (Imperial and Metric):

You can head over to Silca’s site to enter your credit card.

While I think it looks really pretty on a shelf with other bike-themed things, it’s just not super practical out on the road for me. I want details like power and other metrics. But of course, there are plenty of people who prefer a more ‘minimalist’ experience – yet still want at least the core/basic metrics seen above.

—

With that – thanks for reading!

entry.title: Suunto Race 3S In-Depth Review: A Pricey Upgrade
entry.content:
Suunto has just announced the new Suunto Race 3S, a small-form-factor watch that believes it needs a big-form-factor price increase. On top of that, Suunto has also launched a new subscription service, Suunto AI Coach, where new Suunto App features are being funneled into. I’ve been using the Suunto Race 3S over the last few weeks, and in this review I’ll dive into how it all works, and whether Suunto can justify the price.

The new Suunto Race 3S includes a brighter display, more storage, and some software feature updates that the existing Race S didn’t get this past summer. This isn’t really a major change from the previous model, but nonetheless these updates are appreciated. It also features upgraded materials, shifting from a stainless steel bezel to a titanium bezel.

In any case, I’ve been putting it through its paces over the last little bit, across all sorts of activities to see how it holds up, and how it compares to other newly announced watches from the last few weeks.

With that, let’s dive right into it!

What’s New:

Now, as you probably know, the Suunto Race 3S is an upgrade to the existing Suunto Race S. There was no Suunto Race 2S, and equally confusingly, there is no larger Suunto Race 3 companion at this point. When I asked about the Suunto Race 3 elephant in the room, Suunto simply said a variant of ‘No comment’. Thus, that elephant will stay with us for now, joining other elephants I’ll talk about later.

Of course, when you look at changes vs. the original Suunto Race S, that watch continued to get meaningful firmware updates until this past April. So I’ll ignore all of those things and focus on the new stuff otherwise (software and hardware).

Starting off with the hardware changes:

– Upgraded peak display brightness from 1,000 nits to 2,000 nits
– Upgraded lens cover material from Gorilla Glass to Sapphire Crystal glass
– Updated bezel material from stainless steel to titanium
– Upgraded optical heart rate sensor
– Faster processor (Apollo 510)
– Increased GPS time from 30 hours to 38 hours (dual-frequency), 45 hours (single-frequency)
– Increased smartwatch daily battery life from 9 days to 12 days
– Increased internal storage from 32GB to 64GB
– Added support for offline music playback (MP3 files, no streaming services)
– Increased number of SuuntoPlus apps in a single profile from 2 to 3
– Slightly increased official case size from 45mm to 46mm
– Decreased weight from 60g to 56g
– Increased retail price from $349USD to $599USD (and 349EUR to 499EUR)

Do note that while you might see NFC listed on some spec sheets, that’s only applicable for the China market. There’s no contactless payment integration elsewhere. Unfortunately, like the music streaming services piece, those industry gates closed a decade ago.

Then there are a few new software features, mainly ones that rolled out on the Suunto Race 2 this past summer:

– Added Tide Widget
– Expanded map labels (road names, water, mountain peaks)
– Added Ascent as an exercise target

Finally, Suunto has noted that there’s a new ‘Race Planner’ feature coming later this year to the Suunto Race 3S, though it’s not there at launch. Here’s a quick blurb on that:

This sounds super interesting, and so I’m keen to see how this works. Especially the pieces looking at weather. For example, does that also look at your historical training weather (e.g., if you train in cold temps, but then arrive at a hot-temp race day). And, best of all, it doesn’t require Suunto AI Coach.

Finally, when it comes to model colors, here are those three options – purple, white, and black:

With that, let’s get into the box.

In the box:

This section is pretty straightforward. Above is the Suunto Race 3S box, following the same design as other recent Suunto watches.

Below are the contents of said box:

You’ve got the band/strap, the pod (separated from the band), the braided charging cable, and some paper stuff.

The charging cable follows other recent Suunto models, and is magnetic and much better than the one that came with the original Suunto S model, which I found would often become misaligned.

In any case, you simply embark on a 10-15-second IKEA assembly project to attach the standard band straps to the watch pod, and you’re off and running.

The Basics:

In this section, I’m going to look at some of the basics of the watch, including daily usage such as activity tracking, sleep, etc. As well as pieces like responsiveness and general usability.

The Suunto Race 3S has a three-button layout, as well as a touchscreen. You can mostly use either touch or buttons for navigating around the user interface. The upper right button accesses the sport menu, the middle Digital Crown allows access to pinned widgets during smartwatch use (and of course scrolls up/down), and the bottom button acts as a back/escape button.

The left side has no buttons. Meanwhile, the touchscreen is a 2,000-nit display that’s perfectly viewable in both bright sunny conditions or shade conditions. I live on a Mediterranean island, and I’ve had no issues viewing the display in any scenarios out on the trails. Oh, for fun, here are three watches side-by-side: Suunto Race S, Suunto Race 2, and Suunto Race 3S

That said, it can’t be left unstated that virtually all watches released in 2026 are using 3,000-nit panels. The COROS Pace 4 Pro released a few weeks ago is using a 3,500-nit display (which is also larger), and atop that, the more-capable watch is $150 cheaper. To be super clear here, I have no issue with seeing the display at all. Period, hard-stop. However, we can’t ignore the fact that Suunto is putting in kinda old tech but with over-the-top premium prices. To me, the ‘savings’ on this display panel should be reflected in the price. It’s clearly not.

The only minor ‘nit’-picking I’d have with the display is that their power-saving algorithms seem a little bit aggressive at times, quickly dimming the panel within a few seconds of wrist-raise. Again, the display is still visible, but this could use a bit of work.

Speaking of brightness, note that for whatever weird reason, there’s no physical LED flashlight like there is in the Suunto Vertical 2 watch (which is priced the same at $599). You still have a screen-based flashlight, but obviously that’s not the same.

Perhaps given Suunto’s lawsuit with Garmin concerning the topic, they got a bit skittish. Either way, it’s a bit of a bummer.

In any case, scrolling down into the widgets, you’ve got a customizable set of quick-access data bits. I will note that if you watch the video, you’ll see it’s more laggy here than the older Suunto Race S – despite the claims of a faster processor. This is such a good example of why processor specs mean absolutely nothing in most devices. You can have the fastest processor in the world, but if the firmware/operating system isn’t optimized for it, it’ll still be slower than an optimized processor. Again, check out the above video for that.

As for those widgets, they all work just as before. Aside from the new Tides one, there’s nothing new here. You can tap into any given smaller widget in this list to open up details about that topic, such as steps, sleep, weather, etc.

When it comes to things like sleep tracking, the times I went to sleep and woke up have largely been correct here, usually matching the other wearables within a few minutes. The same goes for the HRV status values. I don’t compare sleep phases/stages, because doing so is peak faux-science. The best-case reference devices you can use to do so are only about 80% accurate, which isn’t all that great (and again, that’s a best-case scenario in perfect lab conditions). Thus, we’d never compare a heart rate sensor to a chest strap that was wrong 20% of the time. Therefore, I’m not gonna do it here either.

Meanwhile, most of the data around heart rate-driven metrics comes from the new optical heart rate sensor seen on the bottom. As I’ll show you within the accuracy section, this heart rate sensor is a huge jump up over the previous Suunto Race S sensor, which wasn’t super awesome.

Speaking of other internal-ish things, the unit now has 64GB of internal storage, which is ostensibly mostly for offline music (yes, it’s also for maps, but Suunto’s maps are so well optimized that you simply don’t need anywhere near that much storage…more on that in the next section).

Now, with Suunto’s offline music playback, it requires you to transfer MP3 files via USB cable to the device. There are no offline streaming services (e.g., Spotify/etc), and that’s simply not going to happen anytime soon. Those industry gates closed nearly a decade ago now, and the only way Suunto would gain access to them is by going back to WearOS. Nonetheless, if you’re one of 12 people who are still transferring your owned/“borrowed” MP3 files to your watch via cable, you can do that here. You’ll pair up any Bluetooth audio device (e.g., headphones) to the watch, and off you go. It all worked pretty easily for me, and you can also load in playlists as well.

Finally, when it comes to smartphone notifications, you’ll get the basic text and emoji from your phone.

Ok, with all that sorted, let’s get into the sports bits.

Sports Usage & Mapping:

Next up, we’ve got all things sports, including mapping and navigation.

To access a sport mode, you’ll tap the upper right button, which opens up the workout panel. Here it’ll automatically open your last sport mode, and start searching for GPS (if outside), as well as get heart rate lock. Further, if you’ve got paired sensors (like cycling sensors or an external heart rate sensor), it’ll pair to those too.

You can change the sport mode to one of a boatload of other sport modes in the list:

Back on that main page though, you can select to load a course (within Navigation), as well as select/load SuuntoPlus apps. The Suunto Race 3S supports up to three concurrent enabled SuuntoPlus apps within a given sport profile (you can have additional apps loaded but not enabled). In addition, you can also load up ‘Guides’, which would include things like structured workouts. However, you can only load two apps + one concurrent guide, if using guides.

Finally, there are also the exercise options, where you can tweak various display, map, and other target settings. For example, the Suunto Race 3S added the ability to set an Ascent target (similar to how you might set a calorie or distance target). This came in a firmware update for other newer Suunto watches this summer, but the existing Suunto Race S was skipped.

In any case, circling back, I’m gonna add a course to navigate for my trail run. So I’ll select that back in the Navigation/Routes area:

In terms of maps, the Suunto Race 3S doesn’t have any maps pre-loaded, though they are easily downloadable via WiFi from Suunto. You simply go into the app and choose the regions you want. Here are some random sizes to get a feel for things:

Since I’m here, one thing I really wish Suunto would sort out is their app to watch syncing/configuration situation. For years it’s been that as soon as the watch thinks you want to tweak something, it starts syncing, which in turn prohibits you from actually tweaking the thing until it’s done, taking forever to do that. It’s just very 1990s-modal style. I can’t think of a single other wearable device that still has that restriction left. And more critically, there’s no way to cancel the app from syncing once it starts. That’d at least half-way solve it.

It’s in this area of the app that you’d modify things like the data fields/pages of your sport modes, add new SuuntoPlus apps, create interval workouts, and more. Of course, like in the past, you still can’t modify default sports profiles; you have to create a new custom one if you want to tweak something. And it needs to sync a bunch back and forth too. These are the types of actual useful things I wished Suunto would focus on, rather than adding offline MP3 music support that virtually nobody will use.

With that all sorted, synced, and re-synced, we’re ready to start our workout. Off I go for a run. While running, I’ll of course see my data pages as configured:

From a navigation standpoint, I’ll get a little chirp and then an on-screen notification when a turn comes up. And then if I miss a turn, I’ll get a notification about that too, such as this:

Otherwise, the route shows as expected, and in terms of the responsiveness of the map, it’s a double-edged sword. For rotation, things were instant, and I didn’t experience any black square tiles. You can see this in the video.

But for zooming in/out, there was always at least a second or two of black square tiles. Ironically, a runner friend was with me as I was sitting there filming this, and not being familiar with Suunto watches, he was a bit surprised and asked “Is that normal?”

And ultimately, different companies handle things in different ways. For Garmin, when it slow-map renders, it has a fuzzy look or other color-matching tiles (or shows a tile at a higher zoom level first, before enumerating the detailed tile). Most other companies do the same. But in Suunto’s case, they’re just showing black tiles, which looks a bit sloppy.

Even more so, because I’d also notice these tiles as I run, if I had the map screen just open. Meaning, visible at a glance on my wrist even when not fully raised. Again, we can have an academic debate on slow-map-loading differences (more detail vs less detail, etc.), but I think we can all agree that the black tiles just look rough.

In any case, you’ll also be able to see your progress on the elevation and climbs, both for the full course, and then specific climbs as you trip them:

All of this worked perfectly fine. After the workout, you’ll get a summary of your workout as expected on the watch:

And then likewise you’ll see the additional detail within the Suunto App:

Assuming you have your account connected to one of Suunto’s boatload of partners (e.g., Strava, TrainingPeaks, etc.), it’ll automatically push that data off to those platforms. Again, all of that worked without issue for me.

So then, let’s talk about the accuracy of that data.

Accuracy of Heart Rate & GPS:

The new Suunto Race 3S has a new optical heart rate sensor compared to the existing Suunto Race S. Suunto says this new sensor has six LEDs and four photodetectors behind 2.5D curved sensor glass. No matter what it has behind it, I’ll just state things up front: It’s really darn good in my testing.

I’ll also cover the GNSS/GPS side of things, as well as battery and elevation bits down below. But the GNSS piece hasn’t changed here, so we’ll keep that efficient.

Let’s start off with this slightly hilly run I did. It started off with a long and occasionally steep descent, before some flats, and then going all the way back up again. As a reminder, hills (going down), can often be challenging for optical HR sensors. Still, the Suunto nailed it here. I’ve got zero complaints.

Next, we’ve got a 90-minute long trail run across plenty of varied terrain (steep stuff, shallow stuff, rocking spicy stuff, etc.). And again, overall very good.

About the only thing I could nitpick here is this section for about 20 seconds, where it’s off by about 3-5bpm. That’s nothing in a 98-minute long workout. Again, really good job here.

Here’s another trail run from yesterday. Setting aside whatever happened with the chest strap at the 28-minute marker for a few seconds, things here were quite good as well. Again, there’s virtually nothing to be upset about, and this also included some steep ups/downs.

Next, just for fun, check out this shorter morning gravel ride thing I did a few days ago. I was taking photos and such on this ride of a few different devices. So lots of stop-and-go. Lots of pretty spicy typical Mallorca gravel chunk (most would call it MTB material). And yet, it absolutely nails this. Like, really solid job while cycling.

Now, I’m going to continue to test this sensor, but switch over to the new Suunto Run 2 sensor over the coming weeks, so stay tuned for that. I don’t expect a difference though. Either way, this represents a major improvement for Suunto over past sensors.

Meanwhile, on the GPS side, let’s quickly run through some of these. Here’s that city run from a few nights ago. At a high level, obviously all look pretty good.

Meanwhile, in the actual city/downtown parts with tall buildings, none of the units did amazing. None were bad, but across the board (Garmin, Suunto, Apple), all of them were ‘blah’ accuracy-wise. I’m not quite sure why.

You can see this here as well. Again, nothing was crazy-bad, but all four units took turns crashing through buildings slightly, cutting corners, and generally acting like the drunk tourists that fill this area.

That said, as soon as I left the buildings behind, it was perfectly fine on the rest of the run:

Moving along, looking at yesterday’s trail run, which includes cliffs, ravines, trees, etc., things at a high level look good:

I could quibble about each unit being a few meters offset at different parts of the route. Here the Fenix 9 Pro briefly goes across the road, then the COROS and Suunto do the same some 20 seconds later.

Still, we’re talking less than a 5-meter difference in most cases, such as this here:

Or going around this gate for cars. The Garmin & Suunto were most correct here; the COROS went a bit more lazily around it.

Anyway, this is the pattern over and over again – basically all these units were spot on across runs, rides, etc. I’ve got some actual swim tests to do this weekend (I’ve spent a bunch of time in the water swimming with it, but wasn’t doing accuracy testing).

As for looking at the elevation, no major concerns on any of my activities. Here’s that 90-minute trail run:

This is the one I showed the other day in the Garmin MARQ Gen3 review, where for some reason both Garmin units started sliding downwards while I stood and took some photos (27min marker). Garmin’s already digging into it, as it’s likely firmware-related if two different units do it. I will say there’s a little bit of separation early on in the above that seems a bit odd between the Suunto/COROS and the Apple/Garmin watches. Though those all eventually bundled back up together again.

As for the battery bits, here’s the official battery chart:

Looking at my battery life in always-on display, with roughly 60-90mins of GPS time per day, I’m closer to about 5ish days, maybe a touch bit more, but a little shy of the 7-day above (which is spec’d as 60mins per day, versus my times a bit higher). Also, my routes had navigation enabled, which would draw more battery.

Speaking of which, looking at that 98-minute trail run, you can see it burned about 5%, putting me on a 28-hour battery estimate in dual-frequency/multiband mode. This is a touch bit lower than the always-on specs above, but again remember I did have navigation enabled, which draws more battery.

Also, kudos to Suunto for including battery data in their .FIT files (Garmin, Wahoo, and others do so, though unfortunately COROS does not).

In any case, in terms of all my accuracy bits, I’m good across the board here; I’ve got no concerns in any category. Again, for the heart rate sensor side, this is a big upgrade.

Suunto AI Coach Subscription:

Next, Suunto has announced a new Suunto AI Coach subscription feature, which let’s you use your current and historical Suunto data to get race planning information and tons more. This feature is launching on/with the Suunto Race 3S, though it is expected to go to other watch user bases. It’s currently fully on the app itself, as there’s no on-device component.

Suunto has a pretty good 10-minute video that explains the boatload of features that exist there.

<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

My one (kinda big) quibble here is that Suunto Race 3S users get 3 months free to the service, yet Suunto hasn’t defined what said service will actually cost once that free trial ends. And somehow that rubs me the wrong way. Perhaps it’s because my inbox is filled with AI vibe-coded slop apps that often attempt to hook you into the platform before eventually charging you down the road. In this case, Suunto is clear they’ll be charging you eventually, but aren’t saying what that is. Thus, once you get hooked on it, you’ll feel compelled to start paying for it.

Now mind you, what Suunto is offering certainly seems a heck of a lot more compelling than what Amazfit, Garmin, and others are doing. It doesn’t seem as deep as what Fitbit/Google are doing, but again, we don’t know Suunto’s pricing yet. Suunto says that part of the reason they haven’t decided pricing is because they want to see what people actually use, and get feedback. Which is fair enough, but still seems like something they could have done before they launched it.

Now, despite my annoyance with Suunto’s AI Coach rollout, I will give them all the credit in the world that they’ve also announced a new Suunto MCP that’ll be free for all Suunto users. This joins COROS in offering such a thing for free. I have a feeling we’re going to see similar announcements in the near future from others. Note that in the case of Suunto’s MCP, the details are thin at this point, other than it’ll be free, and it’ll exist. Still, I take both of those for the moment.

Wrap-Up:

Suunto has had a string of solid product launches over the last couple of years, paired with frequent and meaningful firmware/feature updates on the app side. And good expansion on the developer side. They’ve been on a roll across the board. But I struggle to put the Suunto Race 3S in that category of wins. This watch feels…off.

To begin, the biggest issue is the price. At $599USD/499EUR, it’s more than a 70% USD price increase over the launch price of the Suunto Race S just two years ago. And it’s not like they’ve drastically changed the hardware. Sure, it has a brighter 2,000-nit display panel, but that panel is what other companies were putting in their watches two years ago, not the 3,000-3,500-nit panels that companies are putting in watches in 2026. Further, while they increased the storage from 32GB to 64GB, it doesn’t really serve any meaningful purpose. Suunto’s maps are tiny in size, and easily fit within even just 16GB of space. And while in theory the extra space is for music playback, the reality is virtually nobody is downloading MP3s to their watches in 2026 (since Suunto doesn’t support offline music from any streaming service). Plus, where are the other hardware features that other companies are putting in their watches for half the price (e.g., flashlights, voice, microphone & proper speaker, etc.)?

After a string of wins, I think Suunto missed the boat on this one. It feels both overpriced, and kinda seems like it’s just a collection of leftover hardware parts, rather than representing the start of a new Race 3 series generation of watches. Perhaps if it was priced at $399 or at most $449, I’d feel differently. But with the just-released COROS Pace 4 Pro being at $449, that’s a very tough spot for Suunto to be competing in with the specs they have in the Race 3S.

With that, thanks for reading.

entry.title: More Wild Horses Than Cars
entry.content:
Thirty riders, eighty-eight miles, and the quiet fall backcountry of Routt County. Rapha x Moots Brevet, a fall gravel ride out of Steamboat Springs, Colorado.

Words by Richard Jara · Photos by Keegan Ashton, Nate Bradley


Friday

The factory is winding down on a Friday evening. The welding torches are off, and tubing sits racked along the walls in the miter shop. Evening light shines through settling into the corners. On the Friday before the Brevet, the shop floor filled with riders who had driven in, most of them from Boulder and the Front Range. We started the night with a tour, a look into the process behind a handbuilt titanium gravel bike, and a look back at Moots' history as we celebrate our 45th anniversary. Then we shared food and drinks to fuel up for Saturday's ride.

A brevet isn't a race. No clock, no podium, no free socks. There's the route, the people on it with you, and the experience shared after a hard day.

This day asked a lot.

Saturday morning. Thirty riders gather outside the Moots factory for the start.


The Climb

Wolf Mountain to Sand Mountain. The loop strings together some of our favorite roads and surfaces, from champagne gravel to rocky, rooted two-track over the divide.

The Route · 87.6 mi · 8,416 ft of climbing

Ride it yourself: Wolf Mountain x Sand Mountain on Ride with GPS →

The loop leaves the valley quickly, turning onto dirt county roads and winding through Mystic to the base of Wolf Mountain. If you weren't committed to the full route this was your chance to cut the route shorter. Long fence lines, grazing cows, and the quiet chill of morning. Golden, sunburnt hills in every direction, with dark pines along the high ridges, and off to the north sits the watershed divide we'd be crossing hours later. Recent rains had packed the dirt firm. We couldn't have asked for a better window.

More wild horses than cars. Somewhere in California Park, Routt National Forest

The climbing doesn't let up. It builds steadily through the first half, mile after mile, until the high point near mile fifty. By then the group had strung out across the route.

Nate Bradley putting the new Routt through its paces. Meet the new Routt →


Sand Mountain

The descent off Sand Mountain was, in Torin Lackmann's words, "chonky" loose, rocky, and a little above everyone's comfort zone. At the bottom, a pop-up aid station was waiting. Huge thanks to Gina, Keegan, and Indy for being there with food, water, and good spirits for a lot of tired souls.

Food, water, and good spirits at the bottom of Sand Mountain.


Home

From there, thirty miles and about 2,000 feet of climbing stood between us and the finish, most of it trending downhill. After Sand Mountain, the final stretch felt well earned, smooth champagne gravel over long, rolling hills, with the valley and Steamboat slowly coming back into view.

"The absolute fall ride of my dreams. Has to be my favorite single day out of the year. So pretty. So fun. So flowy. All. Time."

— Torin Lackmann, Rapha Boulder

Thirty riders rolled out that morning. They rolled back in dusty, cooked, and grinning. Post-ride beers waiting.

"Although there were a couple of hard, dark moments, everyone seemed to have an amazing ride. One rider told us back at the shop that afternoon it was the best gravel ride he'd ever done, hands down. We're truly lucky to have terrain like this right outside our front door. It validates why we make the bikes we do."

— Nate Bradley, Moots

We build bikes like the new Routt for days like this. Long days, rough roads, and every side of the map to explore.

Thanks to Rapha Boulder for making the trip to our corner of Colorado and making the roads we know by heart feel new again, and to all thirty of you for riding them with us.

Want to ride it yourself? Here's the route.

See you out there.

entry.title: One of One: The Vamoots CRD × Mavic x Campagnolo
entry.content:
Every so often a build comes along that only happens once. This is one of those.

When we were deciding what special project to bring to MADE 2026 in Portland, we kept landing on the same answer. Road. So that is what we built: a one-of-one Vamoots CRD, painted for this collaboration, built with Mavic and Campagnolo. It debuted at the show, and it is the only one we will make.

Handcrafted in Steamboat Springs, the way we have always done it since 1981.

The story

We have been welding titanium by hand in Steamboat for decades. Mavic has been building wheels for over a century. Campagnolo has been shaping road groupsets in Italy for generations. This bike puts all three on one frame, shaping the purest expression of the craft. Road.

The finish is where this one lives. A soft sea-foam green over the front triangle fades to white, with pinstripe detailing running through it. Get the light on it right and the paint stops behaving like paint. Fine flake sits suspended in the clear coat, and for a second, the right light catches it like the surface is still wet. The matching Moots seat post leaves a band of raw titanium exposed, and the Enve one-piece cockpit and fork are painted to match. Chris King's Jade finish on the headset, hubs, and lockrings ties it all together. The Jade Chris King surface is matte, but the color isn't flat, it shifts slightly depending on the light and the angle you're looking from. No two glances land the same. We designed the finish in-house for this frame, one of one.

The build

The Vamoots CRD sits at the top of our road line. It starts with our double-butted RSL titanium tubeset and runs a fully integrated cockpit, so the lines stay clean and the cables stay out of sight.

  • Frame: Vamoots CRD, 54cm, RSL double-butted titanium tubeset
  • Wheels: Mavic Comete 55/65
  • Groupset: Campagnolo Super Record 13, 2x13, 55/39T, 11-36
  • Finish: one-off MADE 2026 custom paint
  • Highlights: 3D-printed dropouts, Fully integrated, T47 bottom bracket, 32c tire clearance

See the full spec

The only one

Give us a blank canvas and one bike to make, and this is the result. Our best road platform, the best parts our partners build, and a finish that exists exactly once. An ode to the road, from a shop that has always loved it. Made to last.

There is only one, and this is it. The bike you have been looking at is the one for sale. See the full build and make it yours.

More from MADE 2026

The Vamoots CRD wasn't the only thing we brought to Portland. If you missed the show, here's the rest of what was on the floor:

  • The limited-edition "Phase" finish on the new Womble — the etched-and-anodized fade that ended up stealing the show. The Radavist has the finish story and a full gallery.
  • The new Routt — our reworked gravel platform, built around bigger rubber and a 3D-printed yoke, shown as a prototype. More to come soon. BIKEPACKING walked through it.
  • The new all road - one bike for smooth road, broken pavement, and the gravel shortcut, with clearance up to 42c. Shown a a prototype, more to come.
  • The 32" prototypes — two big-wheel hardtails we're still testing, including the Scrambler 32. Also in BIKEPACKING's builder rundown.

The conversations, the rides, the stoke, that's why we do this. Events like MADE are never just about the bikes, they're about the people who show up for them. Thank you for being a part of it.

We'll be back on the road later this year. Find us at Bespoked Japan in Osaka, October 23 to 25, and Rouleur Live in London this November.

Until next time.

Suggested links:

  • Womble → https://theradavist.com/2026-made-bike-show-06
  • Routt → https://bikepacking.com/bikes/bikes-and-builders-of-made-2026-part-5/
  • 32" prototypes / Scrambler 32 → https://bikepacking.com/bikes/bikes-and-builders-of-made-2026-part-5/ (same piece), or the video: https://bikepacking.com/plog/made-2026-video-part-4/

entry.title: MEET THE MAKER: KELSEY HUTCHINSON
entry.content:
From Fashion to Frames

Kelsey’s path to Moots began far from a welding bench. After stepping away from a career in fashion journalism in New York City, she returned to her hometown of Omaha, Nebraska, looking for something more hands-on. A job at a local bike and coffee shop sparked a growing interest in cycling, but everything changed after visiting Co-Motion Cycles in Oregon. Watching a frame being welded made the direction clear. Two days later, she quit her classes and enrolled in welding school with one goal in mind: to build bicycle frames.

Betting on the Craft

Welding school in the Midwest focused on structural welding, not bikes. The idea of becoming a framebuilder earned skeptical looks and advice about taking a long, traditional path. Moots saw her focus and commitment and hired her before she even graduated.

“I went to welding school with the sole purpose of building bicycle frames.”

The Reality of Building a Moots

While Moots bikes travel the world, Kelsey works within an intentionally small team of makers behind the scenes. Every frame is built by hand, with pride taken in each step of the process and the details that define a Moots.

Challenges and Wins

Most bike welds are smooth curves, which makes the occasional straight-line weld surprisingly difficult. For Kelsey, welding binders onto steerer blanks can be the most challenging. The most satisfying moments come when everything lines up, especially nailing the drive-side front triangle welds.

No Compromises

Kelsey credits much of her growth to the people around her. Teammates who have been welding for years continue to push her to refine her craft and show up striving for that extra one percent. For her, “No Compromises” means honoring the trust riders place in Moots by delivering nothing short of perfect.

Forever Bikes

Bikes are memory makers. Even if a bike eventually changes hands, the rides, adventures, and everyday moments tied to it stay with the rider. Knowing she had a hand in creating something that meaningful is what keeps Kelsey invested in every weld.

Why Titanium

Steel is fine. Aluminum is less forgiving. Titanium is different. Smooth, precise, and endlessly satisfying to weld, it’s the material that keeps her inspired at the bench.

Life Beyond the Bench

Kelsey rides a Routt 45, RCS, Womble, and a Routt CRD. Outside the shop, she stays active year-round with workouts, dance classes, boot packing with her dogs in the winter, and riding or gardening when the snow melts. Her go-to coffee is a light roast with a splash of cream, unless she’s feeling sassy, then it’s a cortado. While others tune into music, she listens to true crime podcasts.

 

The People

Ask Kelsey her favorite part of Moots, and the answer is simple: the people. The factory feels like family, and that sense of trust runs deep. Being asked by a coworker to weld their frame is still one of the highest honors.

Dream Ride

If she could take any Moots anywhere, she knows exactly where she’d go. Spain, on two wheels, is high on the list.

entry.title: San Francisco Bay Area Loop by Thomas Woodson
entry.content:
The San Francisco Bay Area, despite its massive population, holds an equally massive amount of protected land: networks of multi-use trails and campgrounds stitched throughout. You trade remoteness for convenience, but this kind of variety is something I love to fold into my bikepacking goals. Plentiful food, quality sleep, hard-charging downhills—elements worth remembering the next time you’re really out there and feeling a bit thrashed.

My introduction to the area was the SF Peninsula Traverse, a route I used to start a weeklong ride from San Francisco Airport to Los Angeles Airport in 2019. In 2024, Adam Sklar showed me around some of the Marin and Fairfax classics. I’ve been fascinated by the sheer number of options ever since, to the point that my Gaia GPS maps are now borderline too cluttered to navigate.

Looking for ways to combine the SF Peninsula Traverse with the Bay Area Triple Crossover led us to Bikepack the Bay—a 265-mile, +27,000ft route that we trimmed slightly to fit more comfortably into a three-day window with limited December daylight.

Day 1 covered 64 miles and +5,600ft from Sklar’s shop in the Mission District, following the SF Peninsula Traverse through Half Moon Bay, climbing into the redwoods (at night), and dropping into a Palo Alto hotel. The route starts urban, slowly dissolving into crumbling abandoned roads through the hills, coastline bike paths, and finally a lush, pine-needle climb that’s absolutely grueling. From Skyline Road, the Kings Mountain Road descent—ridden in the dark—was the best road descent of my life. Dynamo-illuminated reflectors twisted through the redwoods like the ultimate video game.

Day 2 began with a long bridge and shoreline crossing, then followed nearly the entire skyline from Fremont to Richmond along the Bay Area Ridge Trail (decently signed).  77 miles and +7,700ft. Spending the entire day on bike paths, wide dirt roads, and ripping singletrack was hard to believe given the proximity to millions of people. Fifty-two-tooth cassettes and the absence of camping gear were especially welcome for just how steep every climb was on this stretch.

Day 3 opened with another bridge traverse and 67 miles of +7,300ft along ridge top fire roads to Lagunitas—the only resupply point—before a final push along Bolinas Ridge, around Tam, and across the Golden Gate back into San Francisco. Once again, a full day without really touching a road. We skipped the Headlands trails as sunset approached, but there are plenty of options to explore there.

The varied, ever-changing terrain kept us engaged. The urban offered a reprieve from the steeps; the steeps, a reprieve from the urban. Staying in cheap hotels felt like a luxury—less luggage, more riding. Kyle is typically the route master when we’re out together, but I believe I showed him some things to change his perspectives this time around. The Bay Area is about to be one of our winter classics.

Tips
– Navigation is constant. A head unit is essential, and having the tracks on your phone as backup is smart. Trail closures around the Baylands in Palo Alto before the bridge crossing added a few miles of backtracking
– The Richmond Bridge closes the bike lane during the week but offers a free shuttle bus in its place. If you want to ride it, check schedules and plan a weekend crossing
– Keeping a variety of Bay Area routes saved allows for easy on-the-fly modifications or side quests
– SFO Airport offers luggage storage and a bike stand if you want to start and finish the loop there

Incredible resources:
SF Peninsula Traverse – https://bikepacking.com/routes/sf-peninsula-traverse/
Bay Area Triple Crossover – https://bikepacking.com/routes/bay-area-triple-crossover/
Bay Area Ridge Trail – https://ridgetrail.org/
Bikepack the Bay – https://www.bikepackthebay.com/

--- 

Thomas Woodson is a Colorado-based photographer and Moots ambassador known for capturing long days, quiet moments, and the kind of riding that rewards curiosity over convenience. He currently rides a dropbar MXC in our Groundswell finish, a setup well suited to the mixed terrain and exploratory routes that shape his work.

entry.title: Winter Desert Miles
entry.content:
When the temperatures drop and the mountains start to get capped with snow, many of us in the mountains start looking south. As winter settles into the high country and riding up high fades, the desert opens up. Cooler days, fewer crowds, and long stretches of quiet make late fall and early winter the right time to ride White Rim. It’s not about speed or numbers—it’s about choosing the season, committing to the miles, and finding space before winter fully takes hold. Richard takes us on his adventure on the White Rim outside of the famed Moab, Utah. 

I just got back from eight days in the desert.

Already checking the weather for the next warm window, planning how I’m going to keep riding through winter, something I’ve always abandoned for skiing. Living in the mountains, you share an unspoken bond with winter. It’s a fortunate place with easy access to snow and the outdoors. I’ve skied resort and earned my uphill turns for the last nine years, but lately the chairlift scene feels played out. So when opening weekend and the first storm of the year rolled through, I did the opposite and headed west, away from the noise. Offseason in Moab.

Bike choice: Routt CRD. 34mm road slicks mounted. 44mm Mezcals in the truck for when dirt was good

One bike. Keep it simple. 

Day one: blue sky above the red rock canyons, fresh snow on the La Sals. No wind, just stillness in the cold desert air. Cold start that never really warmed up, but I was out there riding, and that was the plan. River Road to Castle Valley, then out and back to Arches National Park. One hundred scenic miles, and 7k. Easily one of the best road rides in the country. Had to bail into the truck near the end, blast the heaters, and warm up. Then back outside to finish it. Glad I did. 

I fell into a rhythm for the next three days. Wake up, coffee, pick a direction, go ride, try not to freeze. Hit all the Moab road classics: 313 out to Island in the Sky, Potash Road, the Canyon Path, Arches, Upper Colorado River Scenic Byway to Dewey Bridge. Missed the window for La Sal Mountain Loop Road, but that was okay. 

The views in the Moab desert are magnificent, whether you're on pavement or deep in the desert. I was chasing another route. By the end of the week, after the cold front cleared, it became clear that conditions in Canyonlands would be dry enough. Saturday would be the day. Forecast in the 50s. White Rim.

White Rim is a one-hundred-mile route through the Island in the Sky district of Canyonlands National Park. First rode it in December 2019, but I keep coming back to check in. It's become a benchmark. A testing ground. An escape. Just hard enough. Just remote enough. But this wasn't about PRs or pushing numbers. This was about chasing desert miles and the low winter sun. About being out there and just riding.

Texted Andrew on Friday. “White Rim tomorrow?”

“Yeah, I'm in.”

Quick logistics: 8am start, Mineral Bottom/313 intersection, counter-clockwise. Day permits sorted. Self-supported, everything we needed on the bikes. Keep it simple.  Andrew runs a custom bikepacking gear company with his wife Katie, out of an off-grid workshop at the foot of the La Sal Mountains. We first connected on the Colorado Trail back in 2019. It's always good to reconnect with racing friends, and to ride with someone who gets the appeal of long days, minimal setups, and backcountry routes. I’ve taken a lot of inspiration from the way Andrew approaches cycling and racing. Most of the ride was a conversation about gear, bikes, and what’s next on the list. By then, we had already approached the final climb up Schafer Trail, the sun had gone down, and we rolled the final 8ish miles by headlamp. A full day on the pedals, no major mechanical issues, and good conditions. Hard to ask for more.  

On the way back to the mountains, I stopped and camped on 18rd in Fruita, spun the legs out once more around the Colorado National Monument, another Colorado classic. Back to winter, for now. 

https://www.strava.com/athletes/6042499

 - Richard

entry.title: MEET THE MAKER: ERIC HINDES
entry.content:
25 Years of Craft, Curiosity, and Getting It Right

Some people find their way to bike building through formal paths. Others through obsession. For Eric Hindes, it started at home and it stuck.

Eric has been part of the Moots team for 25 years. Today, he programs and runs multiple CNC machines, helps shape how we manufacture frames and components in-house, and carries decades of institutional knowledge across the production floor. But like many great bike builders, his story starts long before his first day at Moots.

A Family Affair and a Pile of Magazines

Eric’s entry into bikes came courtesy of his dad. Mountain biking was new, exciting, and everywhere in the pages of Fat Tire Flyer, Mountain Bike, Dirt Rag, and Bike. Those magazines introduced Eric (and his family) to the early pioneers of the sport: Charlie Cunningham, Joe Breeze, Kent Eriksen and sparked something deeper than riding.

That curiosity led to building bikes. Building bikes led to becoming an “annoying shop rat.” And that, eventually, led to working in bike shops and for a local frame builder. Moots came next and the rest is a quarter-century of titanium history.

What Riders Might Not Realize

There’s a perception that building bikes, especially titanium bikes, is all sparks and welds. Eric is quick to point out that the real work often happens quietly, methodically, and obsessively.

Titanium demands cleanliness and precision. Once a Moots frame has gone through reaming, facing, and hand finishing, it’s essentially done. No paint. No heat treatment. No residue to clean out. No mold artifacts. What you see is the structure itself: pure, honest, ride-ready titanium.

The Challenge and the Reward

Like any craft, framebuilding has its hard moments. But the most satisfying part? Knowing the job was done right.

Eric came up during a time when the Finish Department was just him and Caleb. They forced themselves to slow down when needed, to redo work when it wasn’t perfect, and to always think about the rider on the other end someone who had invested serious time, money, and trust into choosing a Moots.

“Don’t let them down,” he says. That mindset hasn’t changed.

How the Craft Has Evolved

When Eric started, much of his week was spent bead blasting frames. At the time, Moots had a single CNC machine and it wasn’t even set up.

Today, the shop runs four CNCs that Eric programs and operates, producing everything from frame parts to stems, seatposts, and fixtures. Nearly everything you see on the production floor is made in-house. (And yes, he admits he occasionally bribes Bryce and Richard to help with bead blasting.)

The tools have evolved. The standards have gone up. The expectation to do it right has remained exactly the same.

“No Compromises,” Minus the Bumper Sticker

Ask Eric what “No Compromises” means, and you’ll get a laugh before a real answer.

It’s not about slogans. It’s about doing things the right way even when it’s slower, harder, or less convenient. It’s about respecting the rider who chose a Moots and making sure every decision honors that commitment.

The Bikes and the Moments That Matter

Eric currently rides a Womble, a Routt 45, and a Forager. He’s helped build bikes for legendary cyclists like Andy Hampsten and Ruthie Matthes, and even athletes outside the sport, like Reggie Miller.

But the moments that stick most don’t involve famous names.

They happen at Ranch Rally. On group rides. In conversations with riders who are genuinely stoked about their bikes: how they ride, how they feel, and where they’ve taken them.

That’s the payoff.

Life Beyond the Shop

After work, Eric’s ideal recovery involves standing in a cold river with a fly rod. Reality often looks like picking up his kid, running errands, or making sure the “crazy dog” gets some exercise.

His coffee routine is simple: Moccamaster in the morning, and he’s set. Though when the mood strikes, he won’t say no to a vanilla oat-milk latte...even if it costs nine bucks.

The shop soundtrack? A mix that includes Dag Nasty, Spoon, Dinosaur Jr., Wire, and Archers of Loaf.

Dream Rides

If Eric could take a Moots anywhere, the list is long: bikepacking and fly fishing in Japan, an overnighter with the family, or a “dumb” fat-bike adventure in Alaska.

Wherever it is, the bike will be built the same way with intention, care, and zero compromises.

entry.title: MEET THE MAKER: RICHARD JARA
entry.content:
The Creative Force Behind California Dreamin’ & the Topo Scrambler

Every special edition finish that leaves our factory carries a story and this one belongs to Richard Jara, the artist and visionary behind both our California Dreamin’ and Topo Scrambler designs.

This year, a cycling injury kept Richard off the bike for three months.
Instead of slowing down, he turned all of that restless, ride-longing energy into design.
The result: two finishes infused with movement, meaning, and miles.

With over a decade of self-propelled exploration from racing the Tour Divide, to logging more than 2,000 miles on the Colorado Trail, to countless long days spent exploring the backroads of Routt County Richard’s work is rooted in place, experience, and the culture of adventure.

For the Scrambler’s topo finish, he leaned into that connection even deeper. Inside the Moots factory hangs a giant topo map of Routt County the same map we gather around after weekends out, tracing lines, sharing stories, and planning the next ride. Those lines became the foundation of the design: a tribute to terrain, movement, and the freedom of deciding where the trail will take you next.

“I wanted this bike to evoke a sense of exploration,” Richard says. “My hope is that it becomes an outlet for adventure every time you load it up and head out.”

From setback to artwork, from map lines to titanium. Richard’s finishes are more than paint. They’re reminders that the ride always finds its way back.

entry.title: Sandstone and the Scrambler
entry.content:
Reflections on an adventure through Bears Ears National Monument by Kyle Richardson

———

Dropping down the backside of Elephant Hill into the Needles District, Canyonlands National Park feels meaningful and distinct. It feels remote. There is something gratifying about loading your bike with food for a couple of days and 7 liters of water, and then pointing towards remote and quiet country. This feeling only arises when you know you are about to be in the good stuff. Confidence is there because you have everything you need on your bike, even some comfort items, plus the knowledge of managing and repairing your bike. The excitement for adventure is brewing.

It was fitting for this adventure to be riding the new Moots adventure bike, the Scrambler. Firstly, I cut my teeth and made some notoriety for myself scrambling around in the Flatirons and peaks above Boulder, CO. For me, scrambling is one of the peak forms of movement. It's the blurry line between running and climbing. It's an all-engaging and encompassing way to move in the mountains. In the world of bikes, scrambling encompasses taking your bike to those remote and unique places. Seeking out mixed terrain rides that demand all of your attention and skills. Secondly, it was a bit of a scramble to pull off this adventure. From the side quest to acquire the bike in Steamboat Springs, to squeezing this midweek adventure into a few days and hectic schedules, to riding a brand new bike without any prior knowledge or time to really dial in the bags or setup. I think spontaneity and adventure embody the spirit of the Scrambler. A true adventure bike that you can rely on, but also a bike that will push you out of your comfort zone. Okay, back to the adventure.

Bears Ears is a culturally significant and delicate zone. You feel the importance and beauty while riding through these amazing landscapes. Bears Ears is massive, over 1.36 million acres. For this loop, we focus on the interior of the national monument. Over the course of 2.5 days and 153 miles, we rode through 3 distinct zones. The Needles, Elk Ridge, and the Abajo Mountains. One of the most incredible aspects of this route is the change of elevation. From 6,000ft up to 10,000ft and back, each tier of the route is unique and distinct. Each time you climb or descend to a new level, you are rewarded with a brand new landscape with new flora and fauna. From the sagebrush and cottonwoods of Indian Creek, up to the aspen and ponderosa forest of Elk Ridge. This constant changing of environments makes this route intoxicating and exciting.


The roads and terrain around Bears Ears are rugged to say the least. Rocky, sandy, and bumpy.  The Scrambler was equipped with a 100 mm Sid fork. In previous years on this route, I have always ridden a fully rigid bike. To no surprise, this iteration with some squish was a delight. Previous sections that were trying and tough, now became rideable and actually enjoyable. The bike's geometry was designed to carry weight well and was a dream on this route. All Moots bikes are beautiful, but I will let the photos speak for themselves. This bike was blinged out and shining among the desert sandstone.

The stars shine brighter when you are in a remote country, tired after a long day of biking. Food and water taste better after hauling them around rugged roads. Climbing from Ruin Park up to Elk Ridge is a fascinating and magnificent climb, one of my favorite climbs in the whole world. This route has many secrets and side quests. Malt shakes and burgers in Blanding are things worth pedaling far for. Circumnavigating beautiful country and sleeping out, it all makes for a memorable adventure. From the desert floor to the high alpine, you see it all in a condensed period of time. This adventure was a good reminder to always seize the opportunity to get outside and ride. It’s always worth it. If you want to see the route, send me an email at kylerichardson.atx@gmail.com or a DM on Instagram @kylerichardson.

entry.title: From Residency to Routt RSL: A Ride Worth the Reward
entry.content:
Photo by Ethan Herrold

 

For some, a bike is just a tool. For others, it’s a milestone—a symbol of where they’ve been, and where they’re going. After completing medical residency, Dr. Emily gifted herself something extraordinary: a handcrafted titanium machine built for freedom, self-care, and serious fun. In this Q&A, we dive into why she chose the Routt RSL, how the custom build came together, and why this bike—equal parts art and performance—continues to inspire her both on the trail and in the clinic.

 

What originally drew you to Moots? Was it the craftsmanship, the ride feel, the titanium, or something else?

I learned about Moots from Alpha Bicycle Studio and fell in love with the high quality, their Colorado heritage, and the art like details on their bikes. I wanted a sturdy bike that was comfortable, beautiful and well-crafted.

 

Why did you pick the Routt RSL?

I chose Routt RS as I wanted a fast, fun and playful gravel bike that could tackle over biking on single track but still be agile enough for riding on the road. 

 

How did you decide on the finish or anodization? Are there any details of the bike you are obsessed with?

I chose the Stanley finish as I am an artist. I love the color and detail, especially on the chain stay. I also love Estes Park and the Stanley hotel; we go annually and always come to the Stanley. 

 

Did you customize the build? Did you build this with a local shop, if so, which?

I customized the build with Alpha Bicycle Studio in Littleton. They completed a bike fit prior to the build, recommended sizes and coordinated with me on each aspect of the build.

 

 

Any standout adventures, races, or moments that made you think, “This is why I bought this bike”?

I race Foco Fondo yearly and completed the blue course at SBT GRVL last year. The bike always turns heads, but I really love the bike on gnarly gravel descents where I feel comfortable, fast and confident that my Moots can handle it all.

 

What does riding a Moots mean to you?

Moots means expert craftsmanship that blends function and fun. 

  

If you had to describe your bike in three words, what would they be? 

I describe my bike as a piece of art, reliable and a beast! 

Photo by Ethan Herrold

I purchased my Moots after finishing medical residency, the bike represents an ultimate self-care gift and the beginning of freedom to enjoy outside hobbies. I now work as a primary care physician and medical director. I use my moots to clear my head after long days caring for patients. I often bond with patients on cycling and always push for patients to get outside and move!

entry.title: Precision, Passion, and the Pursuit of the Perfect Ride
entry.content:
For George, the journey to Moots didn’t start with a marketing campaign or a showroom test ride—it began with a moment in his own repair stand. A Moots rolled in for service, and what caught his eye wasn’t flashy paint or radical geometry, but something far more rare: absolute precision. The welds, the fit, the finish—it was flawless. From that moment on, he knew one day he’d own a Moots.

Fast forward, and George is now the proud rider of a custom Vamoots CRD finished in our stunning Groundswell anodizing, built with meticulous attention to every component. It’s a bike born from months of careful part selection, dialed for road speed, comfort, and long-haul confidence.

But for George, riding a Moots is more than performance. It’s freedom. It’s connection. It’s the feeling you get when craftsmanship, community, and capability come together in a way few brands can offer. And this summer, George and his CRD are taking on the Tour de Stations, a 1000km bikepacking race across Switzerland with over 21,000 meters of climbing. In his words: “It’s sure to push me and my bike to the limits—but hey, that’s what it’s all about.”

Let’s dive into George’s story—from the spark of inspiration to the ride of a lifetime.

1. What drew me to Moots… 

It’s a collection of things really. The first time I saw a Moots was actually in my repair stand for a service - at the time I noticed the weld quality and the overall fit and finish of the bike was absolutely perfect. From then on it was always going to be the case that I would buy one.

2. Why did I pick the Vamoots CRD?

Being primarily a road rider, I prioritise speed, lightweight and comfort over long rides as well as having the rigidity needed when putting the hammer down! Having previously had a Trek Madone, I would say I was a little worried that it perhaps wouldn’t quite have the same level of performance or edge riding at speed - but having done plenty of solo 100 milers over 22 mph avg and having completed many a chaingang, I can say with confidence that box has been ticked. It could be due to the precision of the frame and how aligned everything is, or it could be that maybe aero isn’t everything and that rider comfort and fit play the biggest part to speed… who knows! The geometry is also probably the best I’ve ridden, providing a level of telepathy to the steering that while apexing a corner no other bike has given me, the feedback the frame gives you means you have absolute confidence in the line choice you take. It’s almost magic. No joke.

Bottom line - I can say with confidence the reason why I picked this frame over anything else was probably the best decision I’ve made in terms of bike purchases.

3. How did I decide on finish?

Having ridden an Apex designed Routt CRD, I knew that having the frame anodised for me was the right choice - I quite like gold and deep purple/almost petrol colours, so Groundswell for me was the right choice and oh wow what a finish it is. When the sun hits it right, wow oh wow…

4. Did I customise the build?

Short answer, absolutely!

Long answer, I took months finding parts for this bike, be it handlebars, bottom bracket (even down to the titanium bearing covers), cranks, seatpost… it was a long process but one that when I put everything together just worked and felt absolutely brilliant. I have a few different wheel sets for it of varying depths, each serving their purpose.

5. Any standout rides or adventures?

The first ride obviously was the one with the most excitement and anticipation, having waited a month or two for the frame and then subsequently building it up… That feeling still hasn’t really faded… Every single time I look at it I still think wow that’s a nice bike… I’m lucky to have this.

The main event I’m doing on it this year is the Tour de Stations 1000km bike packing race, which you have to complete within 5 days. Over 21000 meters of climbing on some of the best cycling roads Switzerland has to offer. It’s sure to push me and my bike to the limits! But hey, that’s what it’s all about!

6. What does riding a Moots mean to me?

To answer that question, you first have to ask what does riding a bike mean to me. And to that I say Freedom. The ability to wake up at 5am and ride wherever the road takes you, to cover counties, countries or continents. Riding a bike gives you the ability to go wherever, whenever which is part of the reason we do it, right?

But why on a Moots? Well, having ridden some of the world’s best bikes from the likes of Trek, Specialized and Giant. You start to look less at just the tech specs listed on a website, the weight of a frame, the aerodynamics. And more on the craftsmanship, precision and also the team of people that weld and finish the frames and the passion that they share for what they do. It’s that which I appreciate more and more. To be able to message the owner of Moots and say “Hey, when I come to Steamboat do you fancy going on a bike ride” and to get a response “Hey George, sure - let’s do it”. You don’t get that sort of response from many companies. But you do from Moots.

So yes, I ride a bike for freedom, but I ride a Moots for the little things, things that over time you begin to appreciate more and more. And the team behind that, it all matters.

7. Three words to describe your bike. 

Precise, comfortable, understated - just how it should be.

8. Tell us about your build! 

  • Vamoots CRD Custom Geo Groundswell 53cm
  • SRAM Red AXS E1 Groupset
  • Reserve 42/49 or Reserve 52/63 or Cadex Max 40 depending on conditions
  • 5Dev Road/Gravel Ti Cranks in DLC Black
  • ENVE AR One Piece Bars 38cm 130mm stem
  • Gemini Alsak Seatpost with Fizik Argo 00 Adaptive
  • Enduro XD15 T47 BB (DUB) with Titanium Dust Covers
  • Titanium bolt kit from Better Bolts
  • Moots Ti Cages (coming soon)!

entry.title: Inside Our Traka Adventure with Artu and the Routt CRD
entry.content:
We’ve had a longstanding relationship now with Artu Adventure Club, a truly special place outside of Girona nestled in the hills.  You couldn’t find a more perfect escape for your cycling adventures in this part of Europe, so when Artu rang and asked if Moots wanted to come be part of the Traka experience, well, it didn’t take long to change plans and make the bookings.

The Traka has built quite the reputation as the premier gravel race in Europe and having participated in gravel events all over the US, I figured it was prime time to give it a go in the heart of Girona which has been all the buzz for gravel riding. With almost 4,000 riders participating and distances ranging from 100K to 560K, this event has something for everyone. Despite it being early season, I chose the 200K as I like long distances and because the team had built up a special Routt CRD for the season I was dying to show off to my mates at Artu.  With Zipp 303 wheels and the new SRAM Red Drivetrain, this bike is truly amazing.  Add to that the new California Dreamin finish, and the bike is a stunning beauty to say the least.  Without question it was a head turner throughout the day.

As you get older you know what you like and roughing it isn’t exactly in the cards most days.  That’s where Artu comes in as they take amazing care of you every part of the day.  From meals curated to the needs of a cyclist, guides who tee up the best routes and the serenity and beauty of the surroundings, you can get away from the busyness of a city and simply relax and ride your bike.  Having visited here a few times before, I find the best way to enjoy Artu is to just be there with no agenda that doesn’t involve the bike.

The event itself was a load of fun and the experience didn’t disappoint.  We had perfect weather on the day of the 200K with a cool start and warmer temps throughout with plenty of sunshine.  With almost 9K feet of climbing on primarily gravel surfaces, it isn’t easy either, but seems the organizers worked hard to find the best tracks in the region offering challenging climbs yet amazing views.  There were lots of twists/turns and singletrack sections that allowed you to avoid any traffic on these open roads and the crew supporting racers were everywhere to make sure you didn’t get off course as even the Wahoo can be tricky at times.  The aid stations were perfect and you really could roll this course without much needed on your own beyond the requirements to get to that first aid station.  Nothing was too technical and overall, just a phenomenal ride.  It was clear the race organizers had a little fun on the participants behalf though, as near the finish when you could see town and knew you were close, they took you up a nasty little hill that was best served on a mountain bike.  I’m sure that was solely to crush some spirits and to get the beautiful shots of riders pushing their bike, but they weren’t getting that from me on this day as I had heard to leave some gas in the tank for that part and was able to clean the climb.

It felt great to finish and then even better to be whisked away shortly thereafter by Aga, our lovely host at Artu, where I could then get a shower and celebrate with friends.  They dialed up the perfect finish for the day as well with a lovely meal that evening and lots of stories from the guests.  My favorite one was from my new friend Omid, from Cambridge, who had no plans whatsoever to participate in the event but wound up getting so excited and joining for the 200K with no training, no prep, etc.  A strong guy from rowing yeah, but no cyclist, yet he rocked up to the start gate and had a great ride and was all smiles in the evening when it was over.

If you want to do the Traka in 2026, better reach out to Artu or our crew at Moots as I can guarantee you won’t find a better way to experience Girona gravel in style.  Big thanks to the entire team at Artu for hosting such a wonderful experience!

 

Brent Whittington

entry.title: Lauren Hall: Legacy in Motion
entry.content:
There’s something about a Moots bike that stops people in their tracks. Maybe it’s the raw titanium finish, the clean lines, or -most often- the flawless welds that are truly in a class of their own. When I’m out riding, people recognize the brand immediately: “Moots! That’s Colorado, right?” Yes. And it’s more than a bike-it’s a legacy.

That word, legacy, had been on my mind a lot lately.

Last week, I had the privilege of returning to my hometown in Mississippi to attend my high school’s athletic banquet. I’ve known for some time that an award exists in my name – the Lauren Hall Award and Scholarship-honoring the most outstanding senior female athlete. But sitting in the audience and hearing the accomplishments of these athletes- how they’ve excelled in multiple sports, won state championships, and shown remarkable discipline and heart-was deeply meaningful.

This year’s recipient is Samantha Edwards, a standout student-athlete who will be attending Mississippi State University, my alma mater. I couldn’t be more proud to see her carry forward the values that matter most: hard work, determination, and the courage to lead by example.

We were-and still are-the St. Aloysius Flashes. That spirit of pushing boundaries and showing up with integrity lives on.

But none of this -my athletic career, the award, even the confidence to pursue cycling-would have been possible without my hero and mentor: my dad. He’s been the steady support and quiet inspiration behind it all. He showed up for every practice, every basketball, soccer, and softball game, every tennis match, every track meet. His presence taught me that consistency, encouragement, and heart matter most. He is a legacy I will always strive to emulate.

And it’s that same spirit I see in Moots.

Moots has built a legacy not just of beautiful, bikes, but of purpose-driven design and enduring quality. Just like those student-athletes, the Moots team shows up every day committed to their craft. Whether its’s refining a new geometry or hand-welding each frame in Steamboat Springs, they’re building more than just bikes- they’re building trust, community, and a standard for others to follow.

I’m honored to be part of that legacy, both on and off the bike. Here’s to Samantha and her bright future, to my dad and everything he’s poured into mine, to every rider who recognizes the excellence behind a Moots frame-and to all of us carrying forward something that lasts.

entry.title: Rider Spotlight: Mr. Keita Iwao
entry.content:
At Moots, we took the time to learn more about Mr. Keita Iwao—a passionate rider from Kagoshima, Japan whose connection to his Routt 45 runs deep. What started with a spark of inspiration online has become a lasting relationship built on craftsmanship, adventure, and personal meaning.

We hope you enjoy this glimpse into Keita’s story, his riding life in Japan, and the special bond he shares with his Moots.

WHERE ARE YOU FROM?

I’m from Kagoshima, Japan.

WHAT ORIGINALLY DREW YOU TO MOOTS?

My first encounter with MOOTS was around 2020. I saw an Instagram post from a bike shop and was instantly struck by how cool their bikes looked, thinking, "Can a bike really be this awesome?" From there, I delved into various content like blog articles and YouTube videos to learn more about MOOTS. As I discovered their honest approach to craftsmanship and the high level of customer satisfaction, I became more and more drawn to their appeal. I was thrilled when I found out that it was possible to purchase MOOTS even from Japan.

WHY DID YOU PICK THE ROUTT 45?

For me, my gravel bike usually serves two main purposes: either gravel rides with buddies and the occasional annual gravel event (race), or more leisurely-paced long rides. When I initially placed my order, the Routt 45 and Routt RSL were the only two frames that met my purpose. In my area, there's not much smooth gravel; most of the forest roads are littered with rocks and potholes. Because of this, I prioritized wider tire clearance over weight or nimble handling, leading me to choose the Routt 45. I was also strongly drawn to the bike's web catalog, which used the unique and playful expression "fast-paced lunch rides"—that sense of fun probably played a big role in my decision as well.

HOW DID YOU DECIDE ON THE FINISH? ARE THERE ANY DETAILS OF THE BIKE YOU ARE OBSESSED WITH?

I had always admired the STANLEY logo design ever since it first introduced me to the cool aesthetic of MOOTS bikes, so for me, there really wasn't any other choice.

What I particularly love are the pattern on the chainstay and the alligator graphic on the seat tube. There's a cuteness within their beauty, and all of these details together create a truly special feel.

DID YOU CUSTOMIZE YOUR BUILD? 

I purchased it as a frame, and since I wanted to try out Campagnolo Ekar, which was a hot topic at the time, I went with Campagnolo for everything, including the wheels.

CAN  YOU TELL US ABOUT A STANDOUT MOMENT THAT MADE YOU THINK 'THISI IS WHY I BOUGHT THIS BIKE'?

The Grinduro Japan in 2023 particularly stands out in my memory. The timed sections of that event had a lot of intense downhills, and many riders struggled. However, because I was using 45mm-wide gravel tires, combined with the excellent integrated feel of my bike frame, I was able to ride incredibly comfortably and fast. Many people complimented my bike, saying "That's a nice bike!" – so, the entire event was a great memory, largely thanks to my Moots.

WHAT DOES RIDING A MOOTS MEAN TO YOU? 

I believe it holds a special meaning, as if it colors my entire lifestyle, not just the time I spend riding.

WHAT TERRAIN OR TYPE OF RIDE DO YOU DO THE MOST ON YOUR MOOTS?

I primarily do hilly and rough gravel rides. 

TELL US ABOUT A MEMORABLE RIDE, OR TRIP THAT YOU TOOK YOUR ROUTT 45 ON. 

A memorable trip was definitely a bike camping adventure with friends, where I attached a bike trailer and loaded up my solo camping gear. One of my buddies also rides a MOOTS (a VAMOOTS RCS), and sitting around a campfire, praising each other's bikes, is a pretty rare and unforgettable experience.

WHERE DID YOU BUY YOUR BIKE? 

I bought my bike from a shop called KOGU Kagoshima.

 

IF YOUR BIKE HAD A NAME OR PERSONALITY, WHAT WOULD IT BE?

It's tough to give it a name, but I'm thinking of calling it Takamori, after Takamori Saigo, the great historical figure from Kagoshima. I believe his magnanimity and imposing, steadfast image perfectly align with the robust presence of this bike, a fitting tribute given Saigo's large stature and the MOOTS' sturdy, substantial look.

TELL US ABOUT YOUR BUILD! 

Drivetrain: Campagnolo EKAR

Wheels: Campagnolo Shamal Carbon

Tires: Panaracer Gravelking X1R 700x45mm

Handlebar: Thomson Alloy Gravel

Stem: Thomson ELITE X4

Seatpost: Thomson Masterpiece

Saddle: fizik Arione R1

Bottle Cages: SILCA SICURO Ti

Headset: Chris King

 

Inclosing, this bike will always remain special to me, not just because of its quality, but also because my son was born three months after it arrived. He's only two now, but when he grows up and shows interest in sports bikes, I want to proudly tell him, "This is the bike I bought when you were born." I plan to keep riding this bike until then, and I hope to share some of my biking adventures with him as well.

--

Thank you so much Mr. Keita Iwao for letting us get to know you and  your Routt 45 more. We look forward to hearing more about the adventures to come.

entry.title: The Moots Blackbird — A Modern American Classic
entry.content:
Each year, the ENVE Builder Round-Up challenges us to think differently—to build a bike that pushes boundaries while staying true to who we are. For 2025, we answered with a showstopper: The Moots Blackbird.


Introducing the Moots Blackbird: a bold, high-gloss showpiece built to turn heads and break the mold. Built exclusively for ENVE’s Grodeo event, the Blackbird fuses our high-performance heritage with striking visual design—and showcases just how far titanium can go when precision meets creativity.

At its core is the Routt CRD chassis, our flagship gravel platform known for clean lines, fully internal routing, and that signature Moots ride feel. We spec’d it with nothing but the best:

  • SRAM Red XPLR AXS drivetrain

  • ENVE Gravel IN-Route Fork

  • ENVE AR One-Piece Handlebar
